#9264. Young Climbers Bag Upcoming Routes, Including First Ascent, in Rolwaling

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (703 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Young Climbers Bag Upcoming Routes, Including First Ascent, in Rolwaling

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that an energetic foursome of young French climbers had a busy time recently in Nepal’s Rolwaling Valley, east of the Khumbu.
  • As soon as the climbers reached Rolwaling, they had to change their primary goal, which was in poor condition.
  • “Before long, the climbing turned vertical, and the ridge became razor-sharp and exposed,” Bazon wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that an energetic foursome of young French climbers had a busy time recently in Nepal’s Rolwaling Valley, east of the Khumbu. Eric Bazon, Pierre Girot, Sophie Jacob, and Kilian Moni did two latest routes, including a first ascent of a 5,205m rocky spire and one very difficult line. They then climbed another peak on a “rest” day.

As soon as the climbers reached Rolwaling, they had to change their primary goal, which was in poor condition. Their acclimatization was also progressing more slowly than expected. Instead, they focused their attention on a ridge they saw from their base camp every morning. On October 20, Bazon, Jacob, and Girot set off toward the summit, while Moni waited for them at the base.

“Before long, the climbing turned vertical, and the ridge became razor-sharp and exposed,” Bazon wrote. The climb took three days on the ridge, bivvies included, and led Bazon, Sophie Jacob, and Pierre Girot to the west summit of ChekiGo (6,128m). It took another full day and one more bivouac to reach base camp.

It has been revealed that cheki Go’s main summit was first climbed in 2005 by Bruce Normand of the UK and Oliver Von Rotz of Switzerland via the west face. A Spanish team led by Mikel Zabalza first reached the west summit via a direct route up the west face in 2017. The team had just returned from bagging the first ascent of Jugal II.

“It was quite an intense experience for a ‘secondary’ project: one that combined rock climbing on mediocre granite, improvised protection, and steep snow ridges, all while hauling our ropes on our backs,” mentioned Bazon.

According to recent reports, the ridge was technical enough to be a good start: 5c on rock and M4 on mixed terrain. In Alpine grades, the team assessed it as TD (very difficult).

The ridge on ChekiGo. Photo: Eric Bazon.

Since the weather forecast looked good for another four days, the team decided to continue climbing. They split into two teams: Bazon and Girot headed for a peak previously climbed by elite American alpinists Domen Kastelic and Sam Hennessey in 2014: Chukyima Go (6,259m). Like their predecessors, the French team approached the west face from the Naa Valley in Rolwaling.

“There was this direct, narrow, and obvious couloir that simply begged to be climbed,” Bazon reported.

The climbers at an open bivy. Photo: Eric Bazon.

The next morning, they found the west face in great condition, which allowed them to climb a direct route to the summit along rock cracks, steep ice, and varied mixed terrain.

It has been revealed that it took them two days (October 27-28), with one cold bivy on the face with their feet in their backpacks, to complete the route’s 23 pitches. Their West Face Direct route is 900m long, and the team assessed it as ED (extremely difficult), with M6 on mixed sections, and an Alpine ice grade of AI5.

The photo below demonstrates that the new French route, TchikitaMa Go, runs to the right of the previous line opened by the two Americans.

It has been revealed that left: the newly introduced route opened by the French team, compared, right, to the 2014 line by Domen Kastelic and Sam Hennessey. Photo: Eric Bazon/PlanetMountain.

Meanwhile, Sophie Jacob and Kilian Moni went for an unclimbed peak that also rose right in front of their base camp: 5,205m Janjmu. The pair completed the first ascent on an aesthetic 600m line up the north face. They called the route The Eternal Stars (“Les etoiles eternelles”) after some friends who had recently perished.

According to recent reports, “It felt just like being at home in the Alps, with the added challenge of high altitude,” the climbers reported. “We pushed ourselves to the limit, both physically and mentally, across demanding yet incredibly logical pitches.”.

It has been revealed that but this was still not enough for the pair. They squeezed in a final climb of Yalung Ri in what they called “a contemplative, active recovery” day. They then finished the trip by paragliding from the summit.

Industry observers note that kilian Moni flies from the top of Yalung Ri. Photo: Kilian Moni.

#9263. Duo Completes Baffin Island Circuit By Skiing, Hiking, and Packrafting

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (610 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Duo Completes Baffin Island Circuit By Skiing, Hiking, and Packrafting

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (610 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that caleb McDaniels, 25, and Henry Penfold, 22, have completed their impressive expedition around Baffin Island.
  • Sources indicate that the pair began and ended in Iqaluit, Nunavut’s capital.
  • The pair’s completed route around Baffin Island.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that caleb McDaniels, 25, and Henry Penfold, 22, have completed their impressive expedition around Baffin Island. The Americans combined skiing, hiking, and packrafting to almost circle the world’s fifth-largest island. McDaniels told ExplorersWeb they did about 20% skiing and the rest was evenly split between backpacking and packrafting.

Sources indicate that the pair began and ended in Iqaluit, Nunavut’s capital. The final section of their trip was also the longest, a 1,130km stretch with no villages after Igloolik to resupply. They made light work of it, knocking it out in 40 days and bringing their total distance to 3,262km over 145 days, from their late May start to their return to Iqaluit in mid-October. By then, the oncoming Arctic winter gave them few hours of light to work with.

The pair’s completed route around Baffin Island. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

It has been revealed that with no resupply points, the pair left Igloolik with 82kg of food. They hoped to do it in seven weeks but brought even more food, because they weren’t sure how long that giant giant section would actually take, explained Caleb McDaniels.

“With no way to carry that much weight in our packs, we loaded up our packrafts and paddled the first 400 miles [644km]. Then, for the final 300 miles [483km], we heaved on our packs to walk overland,” they explained.

According to recent reports, the paddling portion went swiftly, aided by some ingenuity. “Much of the time, we were able to sail using our trekking poles as masts and panels cut out of an old tent for sails. Speeding along at over five mph, we did some incredible downwinding, spray flying from our bows.”.

According to recent reports, using makeshift sails. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

According to recent reports, postholing through early winter snow back to Iqaluit. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

“It was more of a postholing session — we slowly picked our way across snow-covered boulder fields and partly frozen marshlands. Constantly breaking through thin ice over the tundra marshes, we walked in our drysuits to keep our legs and feet dry. Each morning required half an hour of chipping ice and melting out our shoes, which invariably froze solid,” they remarked.

McDaniels and Penfold had planned a roughly circular route around the island, but “we weren’t trying to circumnavigate Baffin,” McDaniels told ExplorersWeb. Two previous parties had circumnavigated the island by dogteam, but McDaniels and Penfold’s route was driven by aesthetic considerations rather than to satisfy a catchy trip definition.

Industry observers note that slogging overland. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

They chose their route after looking at satellite images and enjoyed both spectacular scenery and some special wildlife sightings, including at least one that was a little too close for comfort.

“One morning, as I went to fill our water bottles, I stumbled upon a sleeping polar bear hidden behind a low rise. Only a few yards away, it lifted its massive white head and glared at me for a moment before returning to its nap in the sun,” McDaniels wrote. “I carefully retreated behind the rise and yelled over to Henry to get the shotgun and flares out just in case. We quickly packed our boats and got on the water.”.

In Foxe Basin, they almost collided with a sleeping walrus, and on Nettilling Lake, they met one of the resident seals. “He was immensely curious and not at all afraid. He swam around our boats for half an hour, playing with our stern lines and swimming back and forth between us. At one point, I put my hand into the water, and he brushed it with his nose!”.

#9262. Latest Update: Americans Bag Major First Ascent in Pakistan

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (948 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Americans Bag Major First Ascent in Pakistan

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Americans Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler, awarded with a Piolet d’Or in 2025 after the first ascent of Yashkuk Sar, have done a similar monster 1,800m-long upcoming route on the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m).
  • According to recent reports, this first ascent of the peak’s north face included difficulties up to M7, WI5.
  • Meanwhile, the airline misplaced Winckler’s baggage — every adventurer’s nightmare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Americans Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler, awarded with a Piolet d’Or in 2025 after the first ascent of Yashkuk Sar, have done a similar monster 1,800m-long upcoming route on the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m). This time, Grant Stewart joined them for this off-season climb in the Karakoram.

According to recent reports, this first ascent of the peak’s north face included difficulties up to M7, WI5. The climbers had to overcome several obstacles before even setting foot on the face. Like many other alpine-style teams this season, they were originally planning to climb another peak. But instead of adapting because of washed-out trails, they had bureaucratic issues. Their permit, obtained 10 months earlier, was revoked some weeks before their departure. They had to swiftly find a different goal.

Meanwhile, the airline misplaced Winckler’s baggage — every adventurer’s nightmare. Somehow, the outfitter sent it to base camp some days later. Then, Steadman had to overcome serious Acute Mountain Sickness in base camp. Their acclimatization was hampered by freak spells of bad weather. Finally, the line on Sosbun Brakk they initially chose was too hard and risky because of a hanging serac they only spotted after they began.

The team’s lonely base camp. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“Back at BC, it was time to rest, regroup, and contemplate a totally different line that we’d seen from on the wall, which gave us new hope,” Steadman recalled.

Sources indicate that off to the north face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

On October 1, the three climbers set off on that potential upcoming line. “Instead of angling left up hard mixed ground above the cone as before, we made an arcing traverse right, across an ice apron, to gain runnels on the right side of the face,” Steadman explained.

The team gained 800m on that first day and set their first bivouac on a snowy arete, just in time to be slammed by a violent storm that kept them in their tent the whole next day.

According to recent reports, steep mixed terrain. Photo: Dane Steadman.

A tarp to protect the team’s bivouac from falling spindrift. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“In the morning, we made a gamble for the top by leaving the tent and starting up a massive gully system,” Steward wrote. “At its top, we reached another dead end in a huge serac barrier. To escape this, Dane committed to a visionary pitch, casting off up a blank slab to eventually reach an ice smear.”.

Chaotic, difficult rocky sections. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“A huge serac to our right and smooth slabs out left posed a serious question; eight meters of sideways teetering on tiny gneissic edges and a miraculous rock thread were the answer,” noted Steadman.

“We continued up the massive hanging glacier to reach the hallucinatory final headwall of steep ice/mixed climbing and mushroom-weaving lunacy,” Stewart continued. “One final traverse with 1,800m of exposure under our feet and a magically appearing, dead-vertical ice tongue led us to the summit ridge.”.

A totally vertical section. Photo: Grant Stewart.

Industry observers note that “The wild terrain on the upper mountain took longer than we wanted,” Steadman admitted. By the time they finally reached the summit, it was 4 pm, the storm was coming the following day, and they still had a long way (and many rappels) down.

Summit picture on Sosbun Brakk. Left to right, Dane Steadman, Grant Stewart, and Cody Wrincker. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“The sun would set around 6 pm, so we threaded the first of 35 rappels and started down. Long after dark, we finally arrived back at our bivy ledge at around 5,800m,” Steadman recalled.

The storm was not supposed to start until noon the following day, but it was already snowing at 8 am, with still 1,200 vertical meters of descent to go.

Rappelling down the route. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Recent findings suggest that “Before long, we were caught in a proper storm,” Stewart explained. “We committed to a faster and hopefully safer descent by rappelling down the west rib to the Sokha/Sosbun col. By the time we reached the col, we could barely communicate over the screaming southwest wind.”.

After some scary rappels in high winds down the serac band, the climbers finally reached a sheltered section of the face. They still had to deal with heavy spindrift coming from above until finally, at around 4 pm, they touched down on the glacier. And yet, the adventure was not over — especially for Grant Stewart:.

Following Dane, I took maybe 10 steps when I felt the ground under me crack. Instinctively, I jumped and landed on my stomach as a huge crevasse swallowed the ground behind me. Soaking wet, we began postholing into the wan light of a mesmerizing white out.

Industry observers note that [We stuck] to the center of the glacier as avalanches rumbled down all around in the whirling snow. After a strange eternity, the ragged colors of a tent appeared and we were greeted by ecstatic dancing, major hugs, and endless cups of chai from (our BC crew) Ibrahim and Idrees.

In a recent development, happy climbers and base camp crew after a safe return from the summit. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The team didn’t report their success and the details of the climb until they returned home. And then, the first words of appraisal were not for the route itself, but for the mountains and people of Gilgit-Baltistan.

Sources indicate that “It’s a unique place…where continents and cultures collide. Trips there, while often difficult, are rewarding in ways hard to describe simply,” Steadman said. This was his third trip to the Karakoram, a place he has fallen in love with.

#9261. Industry News: The Cheap FIRE Stereotype Deserves To Be Retired

📅 02 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2008 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Financialsamurai ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The Cheap FIRE Stereotype Deserves To Be Retired

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The popular image of a FIRE practitioner is someone eating rice and beans, clipping coupons, and driving a car older than their kids.
  • It has been revealed that there's some truth to it.
  • After 10+ years of aggressive frugality and a 50%+ saving rate, it's very hard to change your ways once you break free from the corporate grind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The popular image of a FIRE practitioner is someone eating rice and beans, clipping coupons, and driving a car older than their kids. All luxuries are shunned in order to grow their wealth as large as possible to break free sooner. FIRE folks are cheap and should enjoy life more critics say.

It has been revealed that there's some truth to it. To retire early, you usually need to save aggressively for 10 to 20 years. Along the way, you develop frugal habits that help you appreciate more of what you have. You may even start treating investing as an entertaining expense that motivates you to save even more.

After 10+ years of aggressive frugality and a 50%+ saving rate, it's very hard to change your ways once you break free from the corporate grind. I used to work late until 7pm all the time so I could eat free cafeteria food. Then I'd take some fruits and snacks out so I could save for breakfast the next day. So cheap.

Sources indicate that however, one day, you might discover your financial habits are much different from the narrative you've been telling yourself for years. Instead of thinking you're cheap after FIRE, you're actually spending aggressively.

I certainly did. And it made me realize the cheap FIRE stereotype is mostly wrong.

In a recent development, after I wrote about the hidden cost of buying a new car, a reader left a drive-by comment: “Just buy the car already. You've been talking about this too much.”.

According to recent reports, that's not happening. In the post, I shared that I scraped the front right side because I didn't see a bike rack sticking out three feet. My first reaction wasn't anger. It was relief. There's a wonderful feeling in not caring when an 11-year-old car gets another battle scar.

Still, his comment got me thinking. Am I being overly cheap, or even a little masochistic, by driving an old car with problems when I don't have to?

According to recent reports, my conclusion is no. The joy of not caring whether my car gets scratched or dinged outweighs the joy of driving something latest in a bustling city full of accidents. New expensive stuff just gives me more stress.

Then I looked at my spending on things that aren't necessary for survival. The total is far beyond what a stereotypical cheap FIRE practitioner would spend. And I have a feeling when you do a spending audit, you'll discover similar things.

Here is the key point applicable to ALL people who FIRE.

FIRE practitioners leave enormous sums of money on the table to do something else. From a financial point of view, they are paying a huge opportunity cost to sit on a park bench at 11 a.m. on a Wednesday and read.

So by default, FIRE practitioners are not cheap once they actually retire. And the more they made at their day jobs, the less cheap they are, because the opportunity cost is bigger.

Industry observers note that in 2012, I was paid a $250,000 base salary plus a discretionary bonus that ranged from $0 to $500,000. By walking away, I essentially spent all of it that year to be free from corporate politics, business travel, client pressure, and meetings.

Then I spent it again the next year. And the year after that. Over 14 years, that’s over $3.5 million in forgone base salary alone, before any raises. Add bonuses, and we’re talking about over $7 million in forgone compensation.

Most people are willing to sell their soul for money until age 61. Even if their tech giant is harming society, or could potentially kill all of humanity, it can be extremely difficult to walk away from a fat payday.

Sources indicate that and it’s not just the lost paycheck. When you leave, you also lose your employer’s subsidized health insurance.

It has been revealed that we pay about $3,000 a month for unsubsidized healthcare for our family of four. That’s $36,000 a year for coverage I used to get for a fraction of the price.

Choosing not to continue working is one of the most expensive purchases you can make.

So contrary to popular belief, anyone who actually takes the leap and FIREs is a big spender, not a cheap or frugal one.

Conversely, anyone who indicates they are FIRE and keeps working at a job they dislike for one more year is not. They are likely just fooling themselves. Because at the end of the day, your financial independence number is not real if you do nothing to change your life.

I hope this fundamental point is clear. Meanwhile, anything a FIRE practitioner spends beyond the basics necessary to survive should also be taken into consideration.

It has been revealed that let me share some examples, which are different for every FIRE person. However, here are likely the two biggest discretionary life expenses to consider.

If you rent or buy a house that's larger than a studio for yourself and a partner, or a two-bedroom if you have a couple of kids, you're spending beyond what's necessary.

Industry observers note that our biggest discretionary expense is the house we bought in 2023. It cost about 75% more than the house we bought in 2020 at the start of the pandemic.

We didn't need another bedroom or two more bathrooms. We also didn't need an enclosed front yard for our children to play outside safely. Nor did we need a larger lot with a view of the Golden Gate Bridge.

But I wanted it, and I convinced my wife it was a good idea. She was happy in our old house.

Sources indicate that we could easily save about $50,000 a year in property taxes, maintenance, and insurance if we had kept our old house. But the best time to own the nicest house you can afford is when you have the most heartbeats at home. Once the kids are gone, we can always downsize.

Anti-cheap FIRE spending: $50,000 a year more on housing.

In a recent development, some in the FIRE and personal finance community swear off kids because they are expensive and require a tremendous amount of time, money, and effort to. Kids can crimp the FIRE lifestyle. You can no longer travel as freely or do whatever you want every day.

Instead of going to food, things, and experiences for yourself, a lot of your passive investment income gets sopped up by little humans who often don't know how good they've got it. I get it.

According to recent reports, raising a child in an expensive coastal city can easily cost $1 million from birth through age 18. Add another $400,000 for college in today's dollars, and raising a kid can cost roughly $1.4 million through college graduation.

Industry observers note that of course, families can spend far less. Call it “only” $300,000 through age 18, or $500,000 through college. But that's still a lot of money going to someone other than you.

Industry observers note that nobody needs kids. But many of us want kids. Once we had one, we thought kids were so special that we had another. If I could rewind time to age 30, I would slap myself silly and shoot for one or two more. That said, being an older parent has its benefits, such as more maturity and financial means.

Anti-cheap FIRE spending on kids living expenses such as food, clothing, lessons, travel: $16,000 / year.

In a recent development, living in a nicer home and having kids aren’t outrageous excesses. Some would argue they’re foundational desires. We spend more time at home than anywhere else, and procreating is kind of necessary for the survival of our species.

But FIRE folks also spend plenty on things that are absolutely unnecessary. Like all things, there are levels to this.

Sources indicate that here are two more of mine, which may seem downright wasteful to some. But despite my temporary liquidity crunch, I’m not cutting back yet, especially after realizing how hard it is to spend money when you’re old.

According to recent reports, one of my biggest academic regrets is not taking Mandarin more seriously growing up. I lived in Taipei for four years while my parents were stationed at the American Institute in Taiwan, and I still blew it. Then I wasted seven years of Spanish from middle school through high school.

I’d pay a fortune to be fluent in a second language. So instead, I’m paying a fortune for my kids to have the chance I squandered.

We send both children to a language immersion school, which costs about $46,000 a year per child. It’s a lot of money. I’m a product of public high school, college, and business school, and I’m still a believer in public schools. I often wonder whether we’re making the right call.

A frugal FIRE parent would send their kids to public school and hand them a free language app. A really frugal one might even homeschool, which we did for 18 months during the pandemic. I can confirm it is not free. It just costs you your patience instead of your money.

Maybe this tuition is just expensive therapy for not studying harder as a kid.

Anti-cheap FIRE spending on education: ~$92,000 a year.

Living in San Francisco, we’re spoiled with great food. And since many of the delivery companies started here, getting it brought to your door is a breeze.

I love to eat. You should see my gut, which is why I joined a Dad Bod Challenge. I also love saving time and not slicing my fingers while cutting onions.

It has been revealed that so we’ve ordered delivery a couple of times a week for over 10 years. We could save money grocery shopping and cooking more. But we’d rather spend that time elsewhere. Clearly not at the gym.

Anti-cheap FIRE spending on extra food: ~$1,000 a month.

Here's roughly what our unnecessary spending looks like each year.

Add the $250,000+ in forgone base salary, and we’re spending over $420,000 a year on a lifestyle that strangers might call cheap. All because I drive an old car.

Industry observers note that here’s the kicker. Even with all this unnecessary spending, our excesses still cost less than the base salary I walked away from. And that assumes my base salary never went up after 2012, which is unlikely.

Oh, and I haven’t even included my wife’s forgone salary.

In a recent development, therefore, the mere act of retiring early and giving up a paycheck isn’t cheap. It’s prodigal.

Sure, I drive an old car and fly economy. But that’s because I feel stupid buying fresh or paying up for first class.

It has been revealed that the farthest I usually fly is five hours to Hawaii. Paying $1,000+ more for a premium seat feels ridiculous when I fit just fine in economy. That’s $200+ an hour for five more inches of legroom and a seat up to six inches wider. All so I can write a post, eat a meal, watch a movie, and take a nap. Things I can already do comfortably in coach.

It has been revealed that spending nothing on things you don’t care about isn’t cheap. It’s knowing what you value.

Sources indicate that so I’m declaring the cheap FIRE narrative dead. FIRE practitioners, especially the Fat FIRE crowd, are some of the biggest spenders in society. We could keep grinding to make more money. But we don’t, because we value our time more.

Giving up all that income every year to travel, create, or spend more time with our children is expensive. But we wouldn’t have it any other way.

Industry observers note that if your goal is to build enough wealth to buy your freedom, check out my USA Today bestseller Millionaire Milestones: Simple Steps To Seven Figures. It'll be the easiest and best personal finance book you'll ever read.

Weekend Warm-Up: Assynt

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Assynt, subtitled “Home is where the croft is,” is a short documentary that brings viewers to the Scottish Highland community of Assynt, where residents live on traditional crofts.
  • The croft is a uniquely Scottish term, describing the smaller, less fertile plots of land that poorer people were forced onto, following the infamous Highland Clearances of the 18th and 19th centuries.
  • But Lewis MacAskill, whom the viewer is soon introduced to, doesn’t see it that way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Assynt, subtitled “Home is where the croft is,” is a short documentary that brings viewers to the Scottish Highland community of Assynt, where residents live on traditional crofts.

The croft is a uniquely Scottish term, describing the smaller, less fertile plots of land that poorer people were forced onto, following the infamous Highland Clearances of the 18th and 19th centuries. Crofters lived on their crofts and farmed for subsistence, grazing sheep on shared land. Unable to support themselves on the croft alone, most also worked in fishing, kelp, or peat to support themselves.

It was a very hard life. But Lewis MacAskill, whom the viewer is soon introduced to, doesn’t see it that way. He is one of just over a thousand residents of Assynt, who chose to stay and continue the crofting tradition.

“I regard the croft as an extension of who I am as a person,” MacAskill explains.

Sources indicate that the small community of Assynt. Photo: Screenshot.

According to recent reports, macAskill introduces us to some of the other members of the community. Anna is a sheepdog owner and trainer, whom we see herding sheep using the same techniques people here have used for centuries. Stuart is a passionate fisherman, who shares his love of Assynt’s natural landscape with his young son.

Industry observers note that we also meet some of the creatives who have, MacAskill says, been drawn by the unique landscape and material culture. We see a potter using local materials, a fiddler, and a spinner on her spinning wheel.

Recent findings suggest that the spinning wheel came to Europe from the Middle East by the 13th century, and was widely adopted by the 18th century, replacing the older drop spindle and distaff. Photo: Screenshot.

In a recent development, macAskill moved to the croft a decade ago, and doesn’t regret it. Having grown up visiting every summer, he has always felt drawn to the land and knows others feel the same. But a small, isolated community like Assynt is constantly in danger of depopulation. MacAskill hopes that people keep choosing to move back and stay, heeding the same call he did.

The film ends on this note, with a montage of scenes from life in Assynt and the landscape it sits in, while an elderly crofter sings a traditional Scottish song of homecoming.

#9259. How To Keep Your Middle Class Membership Card

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2054 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Financialsamurai ↗ Open Full Page

How To Keep Your Middle Class Membership Card

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The middle class is the best class in the world.
  • According to recent reports, but once you get to the upper middle class, or the mass affluent class, those government benefits start going away.
  • If you need proof of the middle class’s power, look no further than this week’s midterms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The middle class is the best class in the world. It is the largest class, which means it’s the most crucial class. Politicians pander to us by saying nice things and giving us all sorts of random benefits, like the child tax credit or stimulus checks if you make a middle-class income.

According to recent reports, but once you get to the upper middle class, or the mass affluent class, those government benefits start going away. You make more than the middle class, but not enough more to avoid the sting of higher taxes and optional lifestyle choices, like paying for private school. And because you make more than the middle class, you are sometimes vilified.

If you need proof of the middle class’s power, look no further than this week’s midterms. Democrats just won both the House and the Senate.

In a recent development, the middle class is fed up with extremely wealthy politicians who provide tax breaks for their wealthy friends who don’t need them. Fed up with 28-year-old AI researchers buying $8 million homes in cash while their product threatens humanity’s existence. Fed up with high gas prices, high mortgage rates, a never-ending war, and a grocery bill that looks like a car payment.

It has been revealed that when the largest class in America gets angry, it doesn’t write a strongly worded email. It votes. And it flips Congress.

Industry observers note that the lesson is clear. If you want politicians to care about you, be middle class. If you want them to tax you, be rich. And if you want to be ignored and vilified at the same time, be upper middle class.

This is where we find ourselves with today’s post on how to be middle class and stay middle class, so you can feel safe, loved, and accepted.

Because based on the feedback from 3.5 million views and 1,400+ comments on X for my $408,000 budget post, I now clearly understand what is and isn’t allowed if you want to keep your middle class membership card.

Industry observers note that so you think earning $408,000 a year is a lot of money? After working 50+ hours a week, being stressed out of your mind, and barely seeing your kids, it might not be the dream income you imagined.Look how rapidly the money goes. $1/month left over.What would you cut? pic.twitter.com/AFGYHEdeQG.

According to recent reports, one of the biggest surprises from all the feedback on the $408,000 budget was that three weeks of vacation a year, two destination trips and one staycation, is considered an absurd luxury. The vast majority of commenters called it out of touch, ludicrous, or worse.

In a recent development, there was even a writer with 1.5 million Twitter followers who said he's never taken more than two weeks off in his life. He later explained it's because he doesn't make enough to take three weeks off. So if you needed more proof that writing doesn't pay, there it is.

Since 2009, I've considered three weeks of vacation a year the standard for anyone with a decade-plus of experience. This is a household making $408,000 with two kids. These aren't people fresh out of college. Taking 0-1 weeks in your first year or three, sure, that tracks. But after 10+ years in the workforce, three weeks off is not some wild ask.

Sources indicate that apparently it is. So the rule stands corrected: if you want to be middle class, cap your vacation at two weeks a year. Take a third week and you've officially graduated to out-of-touch elite. Congratulations, or condolences.

Not one of the 1,400 commenters gave this household credit for driving a paid-off Honda CR-V. A brand upcoming, nicely equipped CR-V runs about $38,000, compared to roughly $50,000 for the average new car in America today.

According to recent reports, so the verdict is in: the middle class are free, encouraged even, to spend more than they should on a car. This household is decidedly not following my 1/10th rule for car buying, the way personal finance nerds, the mass affluent, the rich, or the poor do.

In a recent development, ironically, the nicer the car someone drives, up to a point, the more middle class they appear. It's understood that the middle class take on debt, or at least stretch, for a car nicer than their income comfortably supports. That's the badge. Wear it proudly, on 72-month financing.

There was a genuine uproar about this household paying $5,000/month for their mortgage. If you live in an expensive coastal city, $5,000 is reasonable, maybe even cheap, for a single-family home. But the feedback was clear: $5,000 is too much, and so is 2,100 square feet.

In a recent development, three bedrooms and two bathrooms still reads as the quintessential middle class home to me, and I'll defend that. What's apparently not middle class is the 2,100 square feet of interior space. Plenty of commenters flagged that as immodest and far too significant.

So if you want to keep your middle class card, buy or rent something under 2,000 square feet. Ideally something starting with a 1: 1,600, 1,800, even 1,990 sqft works. Just don't let that second digit round up to a 2.

With a modest home and an expensive car, this household also isn't following my House-To-Car Ratio guide either. The typical American runs a ratio of about 9 to 15. I recommend readers aim for at least 50, ideally 100+, so you're minimizing a depreciating liability while maximizing an appreciating asset. The middle class, evidently, prefer it the other way around.

It has been revealed that since a huge amount of education is now available for free online, paying for grade school is an unnecessary luxury the middle class shouldn't indulge in. Same logic applies to paying full freight for private or public university.

A smart, motivated kid with engaged parents will likely do fine in almost any academic setting. So dropping serious money on private grade school tuition is, by this logic, mostly a waste. Save and then invest it so the tuition money grows to over $1 million by the time they graduate college.

Recent findings suggest that then again, having over $1 million to give your 23-year-old college graduate because you saved and invested the difference disqualifies you from being middle class. So instead of saving and investing the difference, feel free to spend it on whatever your heart desires. YOLO!

Of course this household earns their $408,000 the hardest way possible: two W2 salaries, taxed at near the top of the marginal bracket before a single dollar hits their checking account. Federal, state, FICA, all of it withheld before they ever see it.

Nobody in the comments seemed bothered by this part. And that's the tell. The middle class don't just tolerate a W2 job, they build an identity around it. Steady paycheck, steady withholding, steady sense that this is simply how adults earn money.

Recent findings suggest that ask them about starting something of their own, a side business, a rental, an app, anything with equity attached, and the answer is almost always the same: too risky. Better to let somebody else take the risk, and the upside, while you collect a salary and help build their dream instead of your own.

Entrepreneurship isn't guaranteed. But neither is a W2 job in a layoff cycle. The middle class would rather have the certainty of somebody else's risk than the upside of their own.

If you're a working middle class professional, the going rate is two kids, maybe. Every additional kid means more daycare, more food, more square footage you're apparently not supposed to have, and no extra help from the government to offset any of it.

It has been revealed that but stop working, or work little enough to qualify for subsidies, and suddenly more children becomes affordable again. Medicaid, subsidized childcare, food assistance, the EITC, all of it scales with need, not with effort.

The system isn't rewarding family size. It's rewarding low reported income, and if you're grinding away at a W2 job trying to move up, you're the one least likely to qualify for help raising the family you're working so hard to support.

So the rule holds. Two working parents, two kids, tops. Three kids or more puts you in the rich category. The middle class don’t have what some call trophy kids given it can take a fortune to raise them.

Recent findings suggest that curiously, there was a lot of pushback about the $408,000 household saving $16,000 a year for their two children's college tuition. Commenters asked why they'd bother saving for college when they're already paying $45,000 a year for private grade school per kid.

Sources indicate that my initial response was that college can be far more expensive than $45,000 a year. Some universities now cost $100,000 to $120,000 a year, all-in. So setting aside additional money for college isn't a bad idea. But critics noted the parents should just pay for college out of their day job income when the time comes.

Sources indicate that therefore, the middle class do not proactively save and invest for college in tax-advantaged 529 plans. And given many top private universities now charge $0 tuition for households earning under $200,000 a year, the belief that saving for college is unnecessary is, in fairness, somewhat logical.

What's illogical is assuming your kid has a real shot at one of these schools with a sub-7% acceptance rate. But the middle class are hopeful their children will defy the odds when such schools cater predominantly to the rich.

As an older parent, it never occurred to me not to save for college, because I don't strategy on working to pay for it when the time comes. When my youngest goes to college, I'll be 61. There's no way I want to be grinding from 61 to 64, paying tuition, as someone who left the workforce in 2012. So the only way for me to pay for college is to save and build passive income.

Therefore, it's clear the middle class don't focus on building passive income through a taxable brokerage account, a rental property portfolio, or other taxable investments. The middle class are solely focused on contributing to tax-advantaged retirement accounts like the 401(k), IRA, and Roth IRA, which is great, until you actually want to stop working before 59 and a half.

Industry observers note that having the grit to work forever, whether you want to or not, is truly a wonderful trait of the middle class. It makes employers proud.

Recent findings suggest that if any of this sounds absurd, that's the point. We judge other people's money and choices against our own experience, then call the mismatch a moral failing.

Personally, I love being part of the middle class, because nobody bothers you if you're like most people. But this exercise made me realize I've been too frugal in FIRE. I also need to build more grit by mentally preparing to work longer while spending more as a reward. So I'll do those things to retain my middle class membership card.

It has been revealed that the $408,000 family isn't doing anything wrong. They're just the latest Rorschach test for what the internet has decided “middle class” is allowed to look like. We shouldn’t ignore the opinions of the 3.5 million viewers and 1,400+ commenters.

And if working until 70 because you never built passive income is the price of admission, then welcome to the club. Just make sure to invest some money in our overlords to avoid being part of the permanent underclass. Now that would be unacceptable.

In a recent development, readers, do you agree with my conditions and descriptions of what makes someone middle class? What are some other conditions you might add?

Sources indicate that if you want an actual framework for these decisions, car versus house, rent versus buy, private school versus public, W2 versus building your own thing, instead of a crowdsourced vibe check, that's what I wrote Buy This Not That for. It walks through the exact tradeoffs above (the 1/10th car rule, the House-To-Car Ratio) without the 1,400 comments telling you you're doing it wrong either way.

Florida Man Finishes Four Corners Walk Across America

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After over three years of trekking 20,000km back and forth across the continental United States, endurance athlete Kyndal Ray Edwards has completed his ambitious Four Corners Walk.
  • Kyndal Ray Edwards, 33, is originally from Orange Park, Florida.
  • Sources indicate that over the next 15 months, Edwards walked to Long Beach, Washington, traveling 5,298km from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After over three years of trekking 20,000km back and forth across the continental United States, endurance athlete Kyndal Ray Edwards has completed his ambitious Four Corners Walk. His route took him from coast to coast, then corner to corner, starting in Florida and ending in Maine, where a crowd of supporters met him last week.

Kyndal Ray Edwards, 33, is originally from Orange Park, Florida. After struggling with drug addiction, mental illness, and the justice system during his early adulthood, he decided to become an endurance athlete and mental health advocate. On January 1, 2022, he began his walking project from the beach in Jacksonville.

Sources indicate that over the next 15 months, Edwards walked to Long Beach, Washington, traveling 5,298km from the Atlantic to the Pacific. His prepares expanded, and he undertook the challenge of walking to all four corners of the contiguous United States. From Long Beach, he headed to the northwesternmost point, Cape Flattery, also in Washington. After trekking south to San Diego, the next corner he headed for was all the way back in Florida, the southeast extremity.

Along the way, Edwards posted frequently on social media about his journey and his recovery from mental illness.

According to recent reports, on October 25, Edwards reached West Quoddy Head Lighthouse in Lubec, Maine. This is the northeast corner of the U.S., and the finish line for Edwards. He walked a total of 19,544 kilometers in 1,022 days, averaging nearly 20km per day.

Edwards and supporters at the finish line. Photo: Kyndal Ray Edwards.

A cross-country walking journey, Edwards claims, has been his dream since 2013. But with the end of his Walking Across America project, Edwards is already ruminating on future challenges. Online, he has proposed going on an adventure with a stranger in all 50 states, running more ultra marathons, and undertaking endurance challenges on every continent. However, he has yet to commit to one.

The end of Kyndal Ray Edwards’s journey came only days before Karl Bushby, another long-distance trekker, completed his 28-year Goliath Expedition. The pair also happen, Edwards pointed out, to share a birthday.

Appalachian Trail Gear Breakdown (Part 2)

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1888 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here is Part 2 of my Appalachian Trail Gear Breakdown.
  • The T-shirt I wore for the first 500 miles was from Patagonia’s Capilene Cool line, though I’m not sure what material blend it was made of.
  • Recent findings suggest that I was stoked about this purchase, but those who read my Day 44 post know mice chewed holes in it almost immediately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here is Part 2 of my Appalachian Trail Gear Breakdown. Did it take me a month to write and finally publish this post? Yes. Do I have an excuse? No.

The T-shirt I wore for the first 500 miles was from Patagonia’s Capilene Cool line, though I’m not sure what material blend it was made of. By the time I reached Damascus, it was already in tatters, so I switched to the SmartWool Merino Short Sleeve Tee.

Recent findings suggest that I was stoked about this purchase, but those who read my Day 44 post know mice chewed holes in it almost immediately. I still wore it for the remainder of the hike, and loved it. It was lightweight, breathable, and odor-resistant. It needed to be tossed by the time I finished the AT (partly from the mice, and partly from wear and tear), but I would repurchase one for a future thru-hike.

Industry observers note that my biker shorts and sports bra were cheap Walmart purchases, but both have held up incredibly well. The Avia sports bra was only $9 but is still in perfect condition after 2200 miles. It was a spandex-and-polyester blend and NEVER STUNK, though I know that’s incredibly hard to believe.

It has been revealed that I ran in my shorts for a few months before starting the trail, so by mile 600 they had holes along the seams. I bought the exact same pair from the Pearisburg Walmart to replace them, and they lasted the rest of the trail with no problems.

My fleece hoodie was from Squak, a small cottage brand based in Utah, and I found it to be warm, fairly lightweight, and very affordable. I never hiked in it, always keeping it 100% dry to wear as my baselayer at camp. My puffy jacket was the Patagonia Nano Puff, and I often wore this over my fleece on cold nights, or even while hiking on particularly chilly mornings.

In a recent development, the Nano Puff used synthetic insulation rather than down, making it slightly heavier but better at retaining heat when exposed to moisture from rain or heavy sweat. I found this beneficial for a trail as wet and humid as the AT. My only complaint is that the jacket did not have a hood, and I felt like I lost warmth without one.

In a recent development, I sent my fleece home in Daleville, VA (late May), and never felt like I needed it after that. My puffy jacket stayed with me the entire hike, and I think it’s important to keep one warm layer for the whole hike (even in the middle of summer). You just never know when you might need it.

Recent findings suggest that frogg Toggs were my rain gear of choice for my entire AT thru-hike, and I found them affordable and effective. The rain jacket was a great outer shell on cold days, though it traps a lot of moisture when you sweat. I wore the rain pants for the first time at Neel Gap (Day 5), but they ripped up the butt after about five minutes.

According to recent reports, other hikers remarked this is common, and I never replaced them. My advice would be to buy only the jacket and skip the rain pants altogether (but to each their own). I replaced the jacket once in Harpers Ferry, WV, and it was so cheap at Walmart that it was no sweat. You can also routinely patch small holes in the fabric with Leukotape.

I brought three pairs of socks for the trail, slept in one pair, and alternated the other two for hiking. Darn Toughs are the most popular option, and the lifetime warranty is definitely a perk. Numerous outfitters along the trail let you exchange worn-out pairs, no questions asked. Merino wool wicks away moisture and keeps your feet warm even when wet.

My trail runners were the Salomon XA Pro 3D V9 (say that five times fast). I first picked these up in Damascus, VA, and went through three pairs. For those interested in my journey to finding the perfect shoe, I wrote a full post about it (Day 99).

Industry observers note that my camp shoes were Xero sandals, and it was so nice to have something lightweight and breathable to wear each night. An added bonus of camp shoes is that they keep your trail runners dry through water crossings and give you something to wear when soaking sore feet in creeks and streams.

Last, but certainly not least, is my beloved AT buff. I got this for free at Outdoor 76 in Franklin, NC. This was the town where I stayed in my first hostel on the trail, and took my friend Cesare to the ER for his broken wrist. I started wearing it on Day 14 and didn’t take it off until after summiting Mount Katahdin (except for the occasional wash). It will likely come with me on any future hikes.

In a recent development, I collected water from natural sources in a 2L CNOC Vecto, then filtered it through a Sawyer Squeeze into two “clean” 1L Smartwater bottles. This method worked well and was what I noticed most other hikers doing. When I started the trail, I didn’t have the CNOC, so I collected water in one “dirty” Smartwater bottle and filtered it into one “clean” Smartwater bottle.

This was annoying because the bottles are made of hard plastic, and squeezing water through the filter makes them crinkle and collapse. The bottle’s suction also frequently pulled the O-ring out of my Sawyer Squeeze, which it needs to filter correctly. I didn’t have any of these problems when I switched to the CNOC Vecto.

Sources indicate that it’s a good idea to carry a few extra Aquatabs in your first aid kit just in case something happens to your water filter. It’ll taste like you’re drinking pool water, but at least you won’t risk getting sick. Aquatabs also kill norovirus, which the Sawyer Squeeze won’t remove. I used the tabs for a few days on the trail when everyone was getting sick, and I was worried that the water might be contaminated.

According to recent reports, my hygiene kit included a contact case, toothbrush, tweezers, nail clippers, one pair of glasses, and travel-sizes of toothpaste, Dr. Bronner’s unscented soap, hand sanitizer, and a hairbrush.

According to recent reports, this suited my needs, and I wouldn’t remove anything from my kit. The only item I would consider adding is a case for my glasses. They were scratched and basically destroyed by the end of the hike.

In my first aid kit, I kept a tick key, EpiPen, extra contacts (enough for the entire hike), my personal medications (all in labeled Ziploc bags), Tylenol, Aleve, triple antibiotic ointment, diclofenac gel, Band-Aids, Leukotape, and travel-sized bug spray. I did not use sunscreen on my thru-hike (bad, I know).

For pain relievers, I think it’s wise to keep both an NSAID (Aleve or Advil) and a non-NSAID (Tylenol) on hand so that you can diversify what you use. I probably prefer Aleve to Advil because it lasts 12 hours instead of 8. Diclofenac gel is also an NSAID, so it can act as a topical anti-inflammatory with less absorption into the bloodstream and less stomach irritation than oral pills (it worked great for my bursitis).

A small tube of triple antibiotic ointment helps prevent blisters and bug bites from getting infected. Band-Aids work for scratches, cuts, and blisters, and act as a good buffer between Leukotape and damaged skin. Leukotape holds bandages in place for long periods and can also repair gear and clothing.

Recent findings suggest that my advice would be to start with a three-month supply of your personal medications, because the pills weigh very little and getting off the trail to pick up prescriptions is a headache. This way, you will only need to resupply once during a thru-hike.

If you wear monthly or biweekly contact lenses (this won’t work for daily lenses), I recommend bringing a supply for roughly 6 months on the trail. Again, they weigh almost nothing and can fit in a small first aid kit. I was glad I didn’t have to worry about picking these up in a resupply box.

Sources indicate that within the first week on the trail, I ditched both my Kula Cloth and trowel. I never really reached for my Kula Cloth and found the whole concept a little gross (though I had friends who loved them). I much preferred packing out baby wipes I could use for numbers 1 & 2 and to wipe my legs at the end of the day. Instead of a trowel, I used my trekking pole, hands, or a stick to dig a cat hole.

For “personal protection,” I carried a pepper spray keychain on the front strap of my backpack. I never felt like I needed it, and considered throwing it away many times. But I think it gave me peace of mind on nights I camped alone.

It has been revealed that most hikers carry a Garmin inReach satellite communicator. You will likely have cell service at least once every day that you spend on the trail (with some rare exceptions). But I still had many nights camping without cell service. The Garmin was useful for sending my husband the occasional satellite text with my sleeping location and who I was with. It’s obviously also beneficial because you can hit the SOS button in an emergency, and rescue crews can locate you.

It has been revealed that per my Gear List, my base weight was 15.2 lb. Obviously, the gear you carry over a thru-hike varies by season, weather, etc. I sent home my mid-layer hoodie and wool leggings at the beginning of June, which lightened my load. But some weeks I also carried nail polish and temporary tattoos (lol), among other frivolous items.

I do think it’s important to carry as little weight as possible to prevent injury. You can really feel even just a few extra pounds when climbing mountains all day. But also, hikers can go overboard with the ultralight obsession. There is definitely a happy medium between weight, comfort, and having fun. Each individual has to figure out what that is for them.

If you have any questions or confusion about my gear and clothing choices, feel free to leave a comment, and I’ll try to answer them! Thanks for reading (:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as my public equity portfolio gets obliterated thanks to being overweight tech stocks, I started dusting off my resume to go back to flipping burgers at McDonald’s. Then halfway through the application, I wiped away my tears and took a deep breath.

As every long-time investor knows, the name of the game is survival. If you can make it through the downturn, good things usually await on the other side.

We're not in an official bear market, yet. But plenty of individual tech names have already fallen by over 20%, and when you're overweight those names, the index's official status doesn't matter much.

It has been revealed that so I thought it might be helpful for those who are retired, or who are close, to discuss the positives of going through a downturn. We'll also review how long downturns usually last so we can better prepare.

According to recent reports, as the midterm elections showed, a lot of people are not happy with the way our country has been led. But the discontent didn't appear overnight. The stock market was simply acting as a giant dose of Lidocaine.

Recent findings suggest that as long as stocks kept going up, we could more easily bear higher oil prices, higher food prices, higher housing costs, higher college tuition costs, and explosive medical costs. After all, our investment returns were growing faster than inflation. $6 for a gallon of gas stings a lot less when your brokerage account is up $50,000 for the year.

In a recent development, but that tolerance for rising costs disappears the moment our investments start losing money. Suddenly, $89 a pound for wagyu feels personal.

When the wealth effect vanishes, consumers cut back. Fewer dinners out. Fewer vacations. The newly introduced car gets pushed out another year. With declining corporate profitability, companies accelerate layoffs to protect margins. The newly unemployed tighten spending even further.

Rinse and repeat until economists officially declare a recession six months after everybody already felt it.

If you see the writing on the wall, you want want to get ahead of the layoffs by negotiating your own severance package. If you do, you will probably have an easier time getting a much better exit offer than being lumped with the masses.

Recent findings suggest that if you're newly retired, your biggest fear is sequence of returns risk. That's the risk of suffering big losses early in retirement while you're also withdrawing money to live on. Do that for too long and your portfolio may never recover.

Sources indicate that lose enough and you get forced back to work. Nobody who has tasted freedom wants to return to Monday morning status meetings and performance reviews from someone half their age.

According to recent reports, retirees who live off their investments should feel worse about a bear market more than the average worker. We don’t have a paycheck to cushion the blow. We may not have much spare cash flow to buy the dip either.

But here's the key point. If your investments can survive the correction or bear market, you should actually feel good during a downturn. Not ecstatic, but relatively good. Because the alternative is working hard for no financial reward.

How do you know if you can survive? Run through this quick checklist:.

In a recent development, so how long will the pain last? History offers some comfort, provided you have the patience of a parent waiting for a toddler to put on his shoes while already 15 minutes late.

According to Capital Group, the S&P 500 has dropped 10% or more about once every 18 months since 1954. A 20%+ bear market indicates up about once every six years.

It has been revealed that in other words, if you plan on a 40-year retirement, expect roughly 25 corrections and six or seven bear markets. Declines are the price of admission, not a sign the world is ending. Get used to them.

Source: Capital Group, S&P 500 data from 1954 through 2025.

It has been revealed that hartford Funds, using Ned Davis Research data going back to 1928, counts 27 bear markets. Stocks fell 35% on average and took 289 days, or about 9.6 months, to hit bottom.

It has been revealed that bear markets were far more common during the Depression era. Since 1945, there have been 15, or one about every 5.1 years.

Two caveats before you get too comfortable. First, these figures measure peak to trough. Getting back to your old high takes longer. Second, the 1973 and 1980 bear markets each dragged on for more than 600 days. Averages are nice until you're living through the outlier.

Recent findings suggest that but here's the part that should make everyone feel better. Every S&P 500 correction since 1929 has been followed by a recovery, and the average return in the first year after the bottom was 52%. And the recoveries are happening quicker now, if we include the 2025 Liberation Day and 2026 Iran War events.

Hartford also found that about 42% of the S&P 500's strongest days over the past 20 years occurred during bear markets. Sell in a panic and you'll likely miss the rebound.

My takeaway: In a realistic worst-case scenario, strategy on gutting out roughly 12 to 18 months of pain from peak to trough, with a longer tail to fully recover. That's why the one to two years of cash is fine, especially with interest rates still high.

The existential dilemma of a bear market is this:.

The correct answer is to work less hard and YOLO more. Let me explain using a concept I call Return On Effort (ROE).

During a bull market, working less hard actually increases your Return On Effort because your investments provide most of the returns. Unless you have a sales job or some other role tightly correlated to performance, an extra 15 hours a week rarely moves the needle. You're better off riding the organization's growth.

It has been revealed that during a bear market, working hard to run in place or lose money makes even less sense. There's nothing you can do to stem declining consumer confidence, latest socialist policies, higher taxes, and so forth. Your boss isn't handing out raises while revenue is falling. See Google's collapse after having such a huge lead in the AI race.

If anything, your extra effort earns you the privilege of doing the work of three colleagues who just got laid off. Congratulations on your 0% raise.

So you work less hard to protect your declining Return On Effort. Not because you're lazy. Because you're rational.

It has been revealed that with this logic in mind, who works the least? The unemployed, the traditional retiree, and the early retiree.

Sources indicate that therefore, so long as your investments can withstand the beating, you're going to be just fine. Psychologically, as a retiree, you must push yourself to do less and have more fun.

Happiness is relative. During a bull market, plenty of early retirees feel a twinge of FOMO watching former colleagues get promoted and cash fat RSU checks. During a bear market, that FOMO flips. Nobody envies the guy grinding through a reorg while his stock comp gets cut in half.

Whether you’re retired or still grinding away, a downturn offers some real perks.

Recent findings suggest that 1) Things get cheaper. When demand falls, so do prices for travel, hotels, and eventually real estate. Retirees with flexible schedules can travel off-peak and score deals that working parents can only dream about. Workers looking to buy their first home may finally face less competition.

Recent findings suggest that 2) You get to shop the sale. Retirees with passive income and a cash buffer get to buy when others are forced to sell. Workers get an even steadier advantage. Every paycheck and 401(k) contribution now picks up more shares at lower prices. Steady income plus a long time horizon makes you the natural buyer in a bear market.

According to recent reports, 3) Your kids get to buy the dip. I’ve written about how to use stock market downturns to make your kids millionaires. As a father, this is my favorite benefit of a bear market. Because the equity train finally stops long enough for kids to catch up and hop on board. A child has 50+ years of compounding ahead. A 30% drop today is a rounding error by the time they’re in their 50s.

According to recent reports, 4) Tax moves get better. Tax-loss harvesting offsets future gains. Roth conversions at depressed valuations mean you pay less tax on the same number of shares, and all the recovery happens tax-free.

Recent findings suggest that 5) The AI hedge is doing its job. Public AI stocks have gotten crunched. But there’s a flip side. If AI companies are struggling to justify their valuations, AI probably isn’t wiping out white-collar work as fast as everyone feared. That’s comforting for our kids, and for every worker wondering if their job will exist in 10 years.

Sources indicate that 6) You get humbled and build resilience. Being heavily overweight tech felt brilliant for years. Bear markets remind us we’re not as smart as we thought. My advice after every huge win is to go scrub all your toilets. Every downturn you survive makes you a calmer, better investor for the next one. If you’re still working, just make sure your emergency fund is solid, because layoffs tend to show up at the worst time.

You can’t control tech volatility, interest rates, or who wins elections. But you can control how you spend your time during a downturn.

Sources indicate that the market will eventually recover. It always has. When it does, the people who grinded through the downturn will be exhausted. Those of us who leaned into family, friends, and fitness will be well rested. Both groups will survive, which is what matters most.

According to recent reports, if you’ve been thinking about retiring, a bear market may be the best time to pull the trigger. It means that in spite of the carnage, your finances are strong enough for you to break free. Waiting for the next bull market can feel safer, but it’s backwards.

If your finances can support retirement while stocks are down 20% or more, your proposal has already passed the stress test. You’re not retiring on inflated numbers that could vanish in the next correction. And since bear markets don’t last forever, a recovery may carry your retirement forward with a tailwind instead of a headwind.

It has been revealed that compare that to the person who retires at the peak of a bull market, only to watch their portfolio drop 30% in the first two years. That’s sequence of returns risk at its worst.

Recent findings suggest that so go play in the park. Take your kids to the beach. A downturn is the best time to enjoy the freedom you worked so hard to build, and maybe the best time to claim it.

It has been revealed that are you finding it more comforting to be retired during a downturn, or more stressful? How much of your portfolio would need to fall before you'd seriously consider going back to work? Do you agree that working less hard in a bear market is the rational move, or is that just a cop-out for the lazy? And for those still working, has the market selloff made you rethink how hard you're grinding? Are you using the downturn to fund your kids' investment accounts?

If you want a roadmap for getting through downturns and coming out richer, pick up a copy of Millionaire Milestones: Simple Steps To Seven Figures, a USA Today bestseller. It covers how to keep investing when everybody else is scared, so you can reach financial independence sooner.

Recent findings suggest that the Electric Arms Race Has Gone Too Far: Tim Shuff questions the growing use of electric motors in outdoor adventure. While recognizing that electric assistance can make outdoor sports more accessible, he thinks that its wider use will change wilderness areas, reshape trails, and create pressure to build increasingly powerful equipment.

According to recent reports, jan Spicka descends from Huascarán Sur. Photo: Matej Zak.

A Czech Alpinist Describes How He Survived a Nightmare on Peru’s Highest Mountain: Climbing Peru’s Huascarán Sur turned into a tragedy for a group of five friends last July. Czech alpinist Jan Spicka describes how he and partner Matej Zak reached the 6,768m summit before he plunged into a hidden crevasse on the descent.

Matej’s quick reactions saved his life, but their three friends, Saul Mendoza, Chicho Ugarte, and Arti Salas, disappeared while attempting to descend by a different route. With no official mountain rescue in Peru, friends and volunteers pitched in. After 24 hours in the freezing conditions, they knew it was unlikely they would see their friends again. GPS tracks and later searches suggest they had fallen through a collapsing snow bridge.

It has been revealed that he Felt Stuck in New York. So He Started Walking to California: Feeling trapped by unemployment and a lack of opportunities in New York, 29-year-old Chantz Rivera began walking across America. He set off with a tent, sleeping bag, and some supplies in a shopping cart. Over 149 days, he walked to California, pushing his cart 32 to 40km a day along highways and through small towns, documenting his progress for his growing number of online followers.

In a recent development, this Mountain Race Makes Runners Carry 60kg of Beer and Supplies Uphill: Slovakia’s annual Sherpa Rallye is one of the world’s unique mountain races. Competitors have to haul heavy loads of supplies up a 5.7km rocky trail to a remote hut in the High Tatras, nearly 2,000m above sea level.

Industry observers note that men carry 60kg, including a 30-liter keg of beer, while women carry 20kg, with the loads secured to wooden frames. The race was started in 1985 by mountain porter Viktor Beranek. The event brings together the region’s nosiči (traditional mountain porters) and also helps stock the remote hut ahead of winter.

Gadd discusses the deaths of two close friends and challenges the underlying expectation that climbers should simply suck it up and carry on. After decades in the mountains, he has seen that the consequences of an accident extend far beyond the immediate incident, affecting survivors and their families and friends for years.

Recent findings suggest that two Hikers Dead in Bear Attack in British Columbia: Two hikers, identified as 48-year-old Jennifer Balcarras and her 20-year-old daughter Selah Reed, have died in a suspected grizzly attack near the Snooka West Trail in Bella Coola, British Columbia. Their bodies were found during a search after the pair were reported missing by their family.

In a recent development, this comes just a year after a separate grizzly attack in the same area severely injured four people, including three children. The trail remains closed as authorities continue their investigation.
