Latest Update: Day 35: Samaín: Halloween in Galicia

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Unable to sleep until my alarm, I was up and starting the long day ahead before 5:30.
  • With a lot of kilometers on the agenda, I took the planned route I discussed with my brothers and walked into the forest.
  • Most might’ve called it eerie, but because of the comfort I learned to find in the dark, I savored it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unable to sleep until my alarm, I was up and starting the long day ahead before 5:30. Triacastela had transformed overnight into a spooky Halloween town. Okay, not really, but the misty cloud that had sunk into the valley made me think so.

With a lot of kilometers on the agenda, I took the planned route I discussed with my brothers and walked into the forest.

There was a quiet stillness permeating throughout.

Most might’ve called it eerie, but because of the comfort I learned to find in the dark, I savored it.

Today was Halloween in the US, Día de Los Muertos in Mexico, and Samaín here in Galicia.

It has been revealed that in many traditions around the world, this time of year was believed to be when the veil between worlds was the thinnest. Today, I planned to lean into that energy and see what happened.

The sounds in the trees around me set the feeling of the day.

Birds I’d never heard before cawed and crowed.

Water droplets of cloud condensation pitter-pattered on the trees.

As the sun came up, I descended into another valley of clouds.

It was a town. As I moseyed along the streets through the dense fog, I came upon an old brick wall with rocks adorned with quotes. The phrases were wise and gave me something to contemplate. While reading them, I felt something brush my leg. I looked down and saw a puppy, ribs poking out a bit, and shaking. I bent down to pet it, and it jumped up, as if asking to be picked up. And so I did.

It has been revealed that after setting it down and walking a few steps further, I found the source of the quotes and the dog: Terra de Luz (Land of Light). It was an old blacksmith property now open for pilgrims to simply stop, rest, and reflect. They had a table of food, a permaculture garden, and signs offering yoga, meditation, and integration. It felt like a place I could spend my whole day, if I didn’t have the biggest day of walking ahead of me. For the five minutes I was there, though, I definitely felt a wave of peace.

Though the environment looked eerie, the energy I felt was light.

All different types of dogs approaching me for pets.

Giant slugs crawling their way along the trail.

Newly born calves staring at me with their tongues out.

A field full of giant pumpkins ready for harvest.

As I walked, I researched how the local traditions celebrated the holiday of Samaín.

According to recent reports, with roots in Celtic tradition, Samaín marked the end of the harvest. Roasted chestnuts (magostos) were eaten. Pumpkins and gourds were carved. And whispers of lore included witches (meigas) and mischievous spirits (trasnos).

Industry observers note that the theme of the holiday naturally continued as I caught up to my Italian brother. We picked apples from a tree along the trail and noticed the many flowers adorning the gravestones for the day of the saints.

When we got into the forest again, we came upon a magnificent tree that looked to be older than the country of Spain itself. Call me a tree hugger, but as I touched its branches and took in its magnitude, I could feel its wisdom.

Recent findings suggest that for the next portion of the walk, I chose to do it alone. I finished the last chapters of The Pilgrimage as I strolled under the many chestnut trees.

According to recent reports, when I finished this book the first time, I felt it had an anticlimactic ending. Now that I’ve walked the road he recounted, the ending of the book felt impactful, like I’d learned the same lessons that he concluded at the end of his journey.

My journey wasn’t over, and I knew I had more to glean, but I definitely knew I’d found what I had come looking for.

Sources indicate that and with those thoughts, I entered the most pilgrim-concentrated part of the Camino. Many people who didn’t have the freedom to do the whole route only had to walk the last 100 kilometers to receive a Compostela. This stretch would be busy, and I did my best to mentally prepare.

It has been revealed that well, that didn’t go super great. Many latest pilgrims I didn’t know, combined with not getting a lot of alone time, weighed on my mood.

I made it to the 100-kilometer mark from Santiago. It didn’t feel real. Didn’t I just start walking?

When I arrived in Portomarín, I was completely exhausted, both mentally and physically.

Then the brothers and I ended the night with a new tradition: Uno. We were all exhausted and delirious, though, so the fun didn’t last long.

Early to bed for another day closer to Santiago.

#9166. Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1699 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
  • Gribbin introduced his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
  • Sources indicate that the journey has not gone according to initiative.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

Gribbin introduced his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

Sources indicate that the journey has not gone according to initiative. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

It has been revealed that while he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

According to recent reports, given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid prepares. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

But this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

Roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

For most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

Northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

By the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and blueprint ahead.

The route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line demonstrates the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

Industry observers note that I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with new designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

Sources indicate that food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

In a recent development, safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

Industry observers note that the kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

Industry observers note that we have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

Recent findings suggest that successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

In a recent development, the huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

In a recent development, I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

You have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

In a recent development, we were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

There is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

How did you first get into the sport?

According to recent reports, I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

Back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

In a recent development, university changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

The decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

Recent findings suggest that the actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

Sources indicate that I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast.
  • In a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is rapidly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

It has been revealed that “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

In a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

It has been revealed that on the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

In a recent development, once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

Recent findings suggest that today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Wyoming man is serving 96 days in jail after he was convicted and sentenced on eight charges of wildlife violations this fall in Fremont County, according to a recent statement from the Wyoming Game and Fish Department.
  • In a recent development, dakota Jordan of Lander, who was found guilty of poaching deer, elk, and moose since at least 2021, now owes the state $18,000 in restitution.
  • Sources indicate that “I do think the penalties are appropriate for his complete disregard for wildlife,” Jon Desonier, WGFD game warden and access coordinator tells Outdoor Life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Wyoming man is serving 96 days in jail after he was convicted and sentenced on eight charges of wildlife violations this fall in Fremont County, according to a recent statement from the Wyoming Game and Fish Department.

In a recent development, dakota Jordan of Lander, who was found guilty of poaching deer, elk, and moose since at least 2021, now owes the state $18,000 in restitution. He has also forfeited the animal parts, firearms, and two vehicles used in his poaching sprees — a truck and a Jeep. Finally, Jordan lost his hunting and trapping privileges for life, a penalty that applies in all 50 states.

Sources indicate that “I do think the penalties are appropriate for his complete disregard for wildlife,” Jon Desonier, WGFD game warden and access coordinator tells Outdoor Life. “We take this stuff seriously. Guys aren’t just getting slapped on the wrist for serious wildlife crime.”.

Desonier, who was named wildlife officer of the year in 2025, started investigating Jordan after a man came to his office with information about an illegally killed elk cow and calf in November 2024. Word of a poached moose and deer were already on Desonier’s radar, but the dots weren’t connecting. That changed during an aerial deer survey. A crew counting wildlife from the air spotted the headless carcass of an elk.

According to recent reports, “We [had] spent a day walking around trying to find it and had no luck,” Desonier says. “We were not far, maybe 200 or 300 yards off, but they had a much better view from the air so it was easier to see.”.

It has been revealed that DNA from that kill site matched evidence found at Jordan’s property. Further DNA evidence proved damning: DNA from four other poached animals traced back to Jordan, thanks to a DNA database at the state-maintained forensics lab. Those hits included ivories from one elk, the leg bone of a second, meat from a third, and the European mount of a deer.

Sources indicate that “I’m so thankful for our forensics lab in Laramie,” Desonier states. “They held on to DNA evidence and analyzed a ton of evidence for us. If it wasn’t for them, we would not have success in this case.”.

Before the department could proceed with seizing the moose Jordan had poached, officials needed to determine if he’d killed it on state, federal, private, or reservation land. Using photos and GPS data from Jordan’s cellphone, investigators found the bones of a moose killed in 2022 and determined it had been poached on private land. The background of his photos included utility equipment, which was also key.

“We drove around looking for the transformer in the photo,” Desonier says. “A High Plains Power lineman saw the photo and sent us right to the kill site.”.

Investigators suspect Jordan poached more animals than those in his conviction, but they focused on the cases with the strongest evidence.

Recent findings suggest that “In my opinion, this guy shouldn’t be hunting,” Desonier claims. “He doesn’t have the mindset to respect wildlife. That’s how we got here.”.

Sources indicate that jordan’s father also lost his hunting privileges as a result of the poaching investigation. He is banned from hunting for five years and also owes Wyoming $5,370. At least two additional suspects are currently under investigation in a multi-state operation.

#9148. This Public-Land Virginia Hunter Chased the Same Massive Buck for 4 Years

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (896 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

This Public-Land Virginia Hunter Chased the Same Massive Buck for 4 Years

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (896 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that over many days of hunting a public mountain in Virginia this year Nick Dean had only seen three deer.
  • Sources indicate that “I had some trail camera photos of him, and on October 27 I had the buck at 40 yards, but it was too thick to shoot,” Dean tells Outdoor Life.
  • According to recent reports, dean was understandably frustrated that he’d missed his chance at the buck he’d been after for four years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that over many days of hunting a public mountain in Virginia this year Nick Dean had only seen three deer. But one of them was a giant whitetail buck he’d played cat-and-mouse with for multiple seasons.

Sources indicate that “I had some trail camera photos of him, and on October 27 I had the buck at 40 yards, but it was too thick to shoot,” Dean tells Outdoor Life. “He was following a doe, and I just couldn’t slip an arrow through the cover to take him with my crossbow – so I passed the shot.”.

According to recent reports, dean was understandably frustrated that he’d missed his chance at the buck he’d been after for four years. The public hunting area is steep, rocky, difficult to access, and there are not as many deer compared to other areas of Virginia.

“But in clubs I hunt I can only take one buck, and the challenge of taking a mountain buck is hard to resist,” states Dean, who works for an excavating firm. “I like hunting the mountains and I’ve been doing it there for 20 years. While there are not as many deer as some other places in the state, there are some substantial bucks.”.

Dean had another chance to take the giant buck a couple years ago during the muzzleloader season. But his black-powder rifle malfunctioned and misfired — again failing to capitalize on a close call with the buck.

Recent findings suggest that but on Oct. 28, the afternoon after he saw the buck this year, Dean climbed 2.5 miles up the mountain once again to try for the whitetail. He decided to climb a tree at a different location on the trail where he’d seen the buck the prior day.

“It was about mid-afternoon when I got where I wanted to hunt, because I had to work that morning,” he indicates. “I found a couple trails about 100 yards from where I’d seen the buck the previous day, and I climbed up about 15 feet in a super thick area.”.

According to recent reports, through his afternoon and evening hunt Dean heard squirrels chattering and scampering through leaves. He turned when he heard something behind him about 5:30 p.m. and when he looked he spotted the buck standing in a thick growth of mountain laurel.

“All I could see was his rack,” he indicates. “I pushed the safety off my Ravin crossbow, and when he heard that he looked right at me. He stared at me without moving for about a minute, but it seemed like hours.

In a recent development, “Then he put his head down, took a few steps into an opening. I raised my crossbow, put the scope crosshairs behind his shoulder, and pulled the trigger.”.

Recent findings suggest that the buck whirled and took off into a massive thicket of mountain laurel cover. Dean heard the deer plowing through the vegetation, then it became quiet.

Sources indicate that “I wasn’t very confident, and when I climbed down with my stand I went to where he stood,” Dean notes. “I found just a little blood, but no arrow. I called a few friends, and my dad, and a buddy who knew where I was hunting mentioned he would be there as quickly as possible.”.

His friend got there after dark, but with lights they found a slight blood trail leading into very thick cover.

“It was so thick we almost stepped on my deer,” Dean says. “The buck only went about 65 yards from where I’d shot it. But in the laurel cover you can’t see anything.”.

His 100-grain Beast expandable two-blade broadhead had been plenty lethal, piercing both lungs and the buck’s heart.

Recent findings suggest that “There was no dragging the deer anywhere in that laurel and steep rocky area,” Dean indicates. “We dressed and quartered the buck and packed him out like it was a Western hunt for elk.”.

It has been revealed that dean estimates his 17-point buck weighed about 180 pounds, live weight. He will have the deer aged by a state official. But he believes it’s perhaps 7.5 years old, and the same one he’d been after for years in that specific mountain area.

“There aren’t that many deer in that region, and even fewer major bucks,” he says. “In my mind, it had to be the same buck I’d chased for four years.”.

Industry observers note that read Next: A Veteran Bowhunter Finds Two Bucks Locked Together Deep Into Public Land. Should He Shoot Them?

According to recent reports, dean claims when his taxidermist was caping the buck for mounting, he found a wound on its neck. Dean believes that confirms his belief the buck is the same deer he’d chased for so many seasons.

It has been revealed that “Last year I was walking in to hunt and I jumped a doe, and behind it at 60 yards was the buck,” Dean indicates. “I shot at it as it faced me, and I was convinced I missed. But the slight flesh wound on the side of its neck found when it was caped, proves to me it was that same buck. My arrow must have grazed its neck.”.

No official measurements of the buck have been made, but eventually Dean will have it scored by Buckmasters.

#9145. Here’s Why You Shouldn’t Be Afraid to Harvest Does During the Rut

📅 07 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1183 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Here’s Why You Shouldn’t Be Afraid to Harvest Does During the Rut

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1183 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if there’s anything deer hunters can agree on, it’s that we love to argue.
  • Like many hunters this season, I’ve been patiently waiting for any mature deer to slip up during the craziness of the rut.
  • In a recent development, there are two lines of reasoning on why hunters should or should not shoot does during the rut.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if there’s anything deer hunters can agree on, it’s that we love to argue. There’s plenty to debate: scent control vs. hunting the wind, treestand vs. saddle hunting, compounds vs. crossbows — the list goes on. Unsurprisingly, the advisability of harvesting does during the rut is no different.

Like many hunters this season, I’ve been patiently waiting for any mature deer to slip up during the craziness of the rut. Because, alongside the lone Pennsylvania buck tag in my pocket, are plenty of doe tags. A couple days ago, after passing a few doe fawns and young bucks in hopes that a more mature doe or buck walked through, I began to wonder: How many hunters are purposefully passing does during the rut? And more importantly, is it a good idea to wait or shoot? That’s why I reached out to Lindsay Thomas Jr., chief communications officer of the National Deer Association, for advice.

In a recent development, there are two lines of reasoning on why hunters should or should not shoot does during the rut. The more does running around, one argument goes, the more bucks those does will attract. That camp passes does during the rut because a live doe might walk by and bring a massive buck in on her trail, or to the area you’re hunting when she goes into estrus in a few days.

I fall into the other camp. I agree that nothing beats a real doe’s scent — which is why I want to put a doe down nearby. Thomas agrees.

“My personal belief is there’s no better attractant for bucks during the rut than a doe on the ground in your hunting area,” says Thomas. “There is no better attractant. I don’t care what’s in a bottle. I don’t care what calls you’re using, nothing beats it.”.

Recent findings suggest that both Thomas and I have experienced just how successful dropping a doe near your stand during the rut can be. Last year I dropped a doe about 40 yards from my stand early into an afternoon rut hunt. About an hour later, two small bucks came in to check her out, both presenting broadside shots multiple times. I chose to pass those two, but had they been bigger, more mature bucks, one wouldn’t have been so lucky.

“Many other hunters I know have seen this strategy work,” says Thomas. “Dr. Grant Woods has got some great video that he captured showing a buck actually using its antlers trying to get the dead doe to stand back up. By understanding tending behavior, we know that when a buck separates an estrus doe from the other deer, she will typically bed down until she’s ready to breed. Oftentimes this involves the bedded doe laying for upwards of an hour or two just chewing her cud until she’s ready. So, a doe lying on the ground smelling like an estrus doe and looking like an estrus doe is not at all alarming to a buck this time of year. In fact, it’s totally natural.”.

If you’re interested in trying to fill an antlerless tag and shoot a buck during the same hunt, it’s notable to do your best to put that doe down close to your setup. It’s not unusual for deer to run up to 100 yards after the shot (particularly if you’re bowhunting). In my mind, if a doe piles up that far away, it lowers the likelihood that a buck comes into bow range if he cruises by to check her out.

True, it may not matter because a buck could follow her scent on the exact same trail she took and present the same great shot. It’s also just as likely that another buck cruising through the area catches a whiff of her where she fell and beelines straight to her. If she’s lying dead out of sight, you may never see him. Personally, I get down, tag her, and bring her closer to my setup as swiftly and quietly as possible. (Plus, in Pennsylvania, you have to tag the first deer you harvested before filling any other tags.).

Thomas is less inclined to climb out of his stand.

“I don’t think you want to get down and spend an hour blood trailing if it’s not going to be an easy blood trail,” says Thomas. “Walking all around that area is a ‘no’ for me, but if you saw her go down in some brush and know right where she is and you can make it quick, dragging her into the open where she’s visual from more areas might be a good thing for the remainder of your hunt.”.

It’s worth noting that it is a hunter’s duty to always ethically dispatch and recover the first animal you shot, so make sure to pick your shots wisely, make smart choices about the recovery, and, if you’re choosing to use the doe as an attractant, only do so on cold days where the meat won’t spoil while you sit for a few more hours.

Regardless of your opinions on rut tactics, the NDA has been a proponent of harvesting does as early in the season as possible to meet your properties management goals. Experts say shooting whitetail does during the rut can also support healthy deer herds. Since one adult doe eats 6 to 10 pounds of forage per day, managing the overall deer population becomes more crucial as winter approaches.

In a recent development, “There are three things that help produce good bucks: age, nutrition, and genetics. We can only control two of those, age and nutrition,” indicates Thomas. “And by taking a doe as early as possible, or even during the rut, you’re helping enhance nutrition. You’re bringing the overall deer density down [and] producing more forage for other deer to help get them through the winter.”.

Read Next: Quit Worrying About Genetics: How Successful Deer Hunters Think About Antler Growth, Cull Bucks, and Passing Good Deer.

It has been revealed that in short, shooting does early in the season leaves more forage for the rest of the herd, enhancing the health of your overall herd, and enhancing the nutritional output of the habitat for your bucks, resulting in larger, healthier bucks next season. It’s also more difficult to fill doe tags the later you wait into the season as does get spookier and harder to pattern during the late season due to hunting pressure and food availability.

Recent findings suggest that as we enter mid-November, many deer hunters across America are reaching the top of the bell curve of rut activity. In some areas, we may already be on the backside of peak rut. If you’re still holding your buck tag and a few doe tags, get out and hunt. If a massive doe piques your interest the next time you’re hunting, you can rest assured that putting your tag on her during the rut is only helping your odds that a big buck might just come into your area to check her out.

Industry News: This Is Why Your Trail Cameras Aren’t Working Properly

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (763 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Sources indicate that you’ve finally got your trail camera set up in the spot.
  • Sources indicate that it’s a new camera, the battery life seemed fine, cell reception was decent … What the hell?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Sources indicate that you’ve finally got your trail camera set up in the spot. Every day or two it sends you a photo of a giant old buck, and now all you’ve got to do is wait for the right wind to sneak in there and hunt him. And then, all of a sudden, the camera goes dead.

Sources indicate that it’s a new camera, the battery life seemed fine, cell reception was decent … What the hell? Welcome to the often frustrating world of modern trail camera use.

Industry observers note that I’ve been field testing and running trail cameras year-round for several years now and in my experience, there is no camera brand out there that’s immune to malfunctions and failures. But my experience pales in comparison to that of Rich Howell of Trail Cam Pro. Howell has been objectively testing and experimenting with trail cameras for more than 20 years.

It has been revealed that I recently interviewed Howell on the Outdoor Life podcast and he shared several reasons why hunters see so many camera failures in the field. Some of it has to do with how we’re using the cameras, and some of it has to do with how the cams are made (which is usually pretty cheaply). Plus, Howell hints at where he thinks the future of trail cameras is headed, and it’s all about making a system that is more affordable and useful to hunters. It’s a conversation worth listening to ahead of the heart of hunting season.

In the meantime, here’s why our cameras often go down in the field, and what we can do to fix them.

Industry observers note that standard alkaline batteries often don’t have the required power to keep a trail camera running reliably, Howell says. If you’re getting fine daytime pictures, but blank, black images at night, it’s a good sign you have a battery matter as there’s not enough power for the camera to fire the flash. This can happen even when the camera is displaying decent battery life.

More expensive lithium batteries can work well, but they too can have challenges. Howell noticed that about 1 in 20 lithium batteries would go bad very rapidly, (like within days of use) and sometimes this was enough to prevent the camera from working.

Howell now suggests that hunters use rechargeable lithium batteries, which have proven to be more reliable. Having a pool of these batteries on rotation will help solve many trail camera power troubles.

When hunters first jump into the cellular trail camera game, they often like to get their photos sent immediately. In the beginning it’s fun to get a notification and then have that instant gratification of seeing a deer photo.

But it’s usually more effective to have a cell camera batch send images every 12 hours or 24 hours. This is a key way to preserve battery life, and it’s also a more useful way to analyze trail camera data.

Personally, I like to have cameras send every 24 hours and then I review all the cameras everyday in the morning. Looking at all the cameras on the property at once helps me put together activity trends.

Howell indicates that solar panels definitely can help keep your camera powered, but they often have issues in the field. First, you want to make sure that they are facing south to capture as most sun as possible. This can be a challenge if you want your camera facing north. And second, squirrels have a tendency to chew through solar panel wires. If you’re setting up your camera and panel in the hardwoods, there’s a good chance a squirrel is going to get to it. In other words, solar panels can be a useful tool, but they’re not a silver bullet.

Read Next: Best Cellular Trail Cameras.

If you’re using the stock camera strap, you’re just asking for trouble. The tag ends of these straps always seem to come loose (triggering the camera) and you’re never able to position the camera perfectly on the tree with them. Plus, other hunters can easily spot the strap, which is an important consideration if you’re hunting public land. Howell suggests using an adjustable tree mount to make sure you can position the camera exactly where it needs to go. You can find a wealth of  trail camera information on the Trail Cam Pro website and by subscribing to their newsletter.

📅 07 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2604 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Hunting the ‘Old Ripper’ Was Almost More Adventure Than I Bargained For

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2604 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I had just come back from the service in 1954.
  • In a recent development, old Ripper was a large black wild hog that lived in the nearby Fowltown Swamp.
  • Sources indicate that old Ripper got his name because there seemed to be absolutely nothing he couldn’t rip up or utterly destroy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I had just come back from the service in 1954. My wife was expecting our first baby, and I was running a general store on Highway 97 just outside of Bainbridge, Georgia. Hardly a day went by that someone didn’t come in and tell tales of Old Ripper.

In a recent development, old Ripper was a large black wild hog that lived in the nearby Fowltown Swamp. That hog tore up more fences, broke more gates, broke the backs of more female hogs and was chased by more hunters than any critter there has ever been in this country. Ripper had been shot by several people. My Daddy fired at him seven times with an M-1 carbine and believed he hit him, but the hog never fell. He had been hunted with dogs and he had killed plenty of dogs. There never was a hog hound that could hold him. The last time the boar was run with hounds, he killed two of the best hounds in the county with his slashing tusks, so no one else ever put their dogs on Old Ripper.

Sources indicate that old Ripper got his name because there seemed to be absolutely nothing he couldn’t rip up or utterly destroy. Farmers around Bainbridge went to the hardware stores and bought brand-newly introduced aluminum gates to put in the gaps he made in their fences. Within a week, the gates were often all bent and torn up where that crazy boar had stuck his nose under and bent them to get into a pasture or field. There was no hog wire or barbed wire fence that could keep Old Ripper out.

That boar was walking destruction. The farmers hated him not only for tearing up fences and gates, but even more because of what he did to their sows. Ripper would break into a pig parlor, tear up the pens and release all the sows. Then he would take them off for a stroll in the woods. Old Ripper weighed 438 pounds. So when he mounted some of the young sows, he broke their backs. Then the sows would have to be destroyed. The sows he did breed threw shoats that were as wild and crazy as he was. The piglets wouldn’t fatten and brought almost nothing at the market.

Recent findings suggest that everybody was out to get Old Ripper. My dad was accustomed to catching wild hogs. We used to catch them in the Fowltown Swamp, fatten them and sell them at the market. My daddy knew about trapping hogs. He built traps to catch Old Ripper. On two separate occasions Old Ripper did go into one of daddy’s traps, but he tore up the wooden stockades and broke out both times. My daddy wouldn’t stand for that, so daddy got a steel bear trap and set it for Ripper. When daddy went back the next day he found the giant tracks of Old Ripper and followed them to the trap. But instead of catching a renegade hog, he found the bear trap had been sprung by the big boar.

One reason Old Ripper became a legend was his ability to outthink the farmers and the hunters in our area. He had been around humans so much that in many cases he just outthought folks instead of using brute force. The people around our place began to think Old Ripper might be a supernatural creature. He was a boar, but he was a smart boar. No dogs could hold him, no stockades could enclose him, no fence could stop him and no man had been able to kill him for seven years.

According to recent reports, other episodes added to the legend of Old Ripper. One of the meanest things Old Ripper ever did involved Mrs. Ella T. Hand’s daughter-in-law, who was five months pregnant. She was in her kitchen and heard a disturbance out among her sows. She went out to the pig parlor and saw Old Ripper trying to tear the planks off the posts where she had her sows penned up. She picked up a rock and threw it at the old boar to try and run him off. When he saw her, he turned, looked straight at her and charged. Only a few steps away was a giant red oak stump that stood about three feet off the ground. The lady climbed up on the stump and began to scream for her husband. All the while, Old Ripper was going around the stump, snorting and blowing. He attempted to rear up on that stump and get to her but she stayed just out of reach of his razor-sharp tusks. For an hour the hog circled the stump as the lady screamed for help. Finally her husband came home. When he saw what was happening, he grabbed his shotgun from over the fireplace and ran toward the hog. At less than 10 yards, he shot Old Ripper in the side of the head with birdshot. The hog merely shook his head, looked at the man and trotted off.

To say Old Ripper was hated by everybody in the community would be a vast understatement. Every man and boy dreamed of killing that old boar, and plenty of work was forgotten by the men who hunted him. All it took to organize a community hog hunt was for someone to report that they’d seen Old Ripper. Every man and boy within earshot would grab a gun and head for the swamp.

According to recent reports, I would have liked to have hunted Old Ripper, but I had mouths to feed. I didn’t have time to waste on that renegade boar. I had just bought a brand-upcoming lever-action Marlin .30/30. I was proud of that gun and took it out behind the store to test it out. On that particular day, Mrs. Ella T. Hand happened to be sitting out in front of the store. Mrs. Hand was close to 80 years old. She always wore a sunbonnet, a long dress and about 90 percent of the time, she had a dip of snuff in her mouth. Mrs. Hand saw me kill a crow sitting in the field about 150 yards away with that rifle. I knew I’d made a lucky shot, but she didn’t. She told everyone for a month about how good I could shoot with that new .30/30.

“If that old wild hog comes back around my sows, I’m going to come and get you, Jack, and let you kill him with that new rifle,” she told me.

Well, about a month later, here comes Mrs. Ella T. in her 1949 pickup truck.

According to recent reports, “Jack, that old boar is up in my field with some sows he run off,” she told me. “Now I don’t expect you’ll have any better luck than anybody else who has tried to kill him, but I sure wish you’d bring that latest rifle up to the field and give it a try.”.

In a recent development, I closed up my little country store and got into the front seat of that pickup truck with Mrs. Ella T. to try my hand at Old Ripper. I had five cartridges with copper-jacketed lead-headed bullets in my gun—the kind that open up but still go on through. There wasn’t any doubt in my mind that if I could hit that boar, the bullets would do the damage needed to put him down.

We drove to Mrs. Hand’s 40-acre peanut field, which backed up to the edge of Fowltown Swamp. I saw Old Ripper out in the middle of the field with four sows he had just broken out from their pen. The five pigs were all rooting in the peanuts. There was a hog wire fence around the field, with barbed wire on the top. The field, which was about 250 yards wide and about twice as long, was on a hillside. Old Ripper and the sows were up close to the top of the hill and I was down near the bottom. There was a dried-up creekbed that ran under the fence. From the tracks in the wash, I figured this was where Old Ripper and the sows had gotten into the field. The creekbed was only about two or three feet deep, but it was big enough for me to crawl under the fence and still stay out of sight. I could lay down in the bottom of the wash, crawl along on my stomach and Old Ripper wouldn’t be able to see me.

Recent findings suggest that until that day, I had never seen Old Ripper. I had looked at fences he had torn up and I had seen mud on the sides of the trees where he had rubbed. I knew he was a big boar, but I never realized just how big. When I saw Old Ripper standing there in the sun, his black bristles gathered in the rays of light and made him look a deep royal blue. He was a magnificent animal standing about four feet high, and he completely dwarfed the sows following him.

Recent findings suggest that I said to myself, “Doggone your hide, Old Ripper! I’m going to try and get a little closer to you.”.

The wash meandered from the bottom of the slope where I was uphill to where Old Ripper was rooting in the peanut patch. Lying flat on my belly, I would crawl for 10 yards and then peep over the edge to see where Old Ripper was. Each time I looked, the old boar was about 10 yards farther from the place than he had been before. It was just like he had a sixth sense that warned him of danger. He kept the same distance away, about 230 yards from me, from the time I first saw him until I decided to shoot. After I had crawled 30 yards, Old Ripper and his band of runaway sows were within 10 yards of a thick broom sedge field. I knew that if he got into that field, I wouldn’t be able to see to shoot him.

It has been revealed that the wash was shallower and just barely kept me out of the boar’s view. The shot had to be over 200 yards. So I laid the rifle down on the lip of the wash, looked through the open sights and aimed at the top of Old Ripper’s shoulder. When I squeezed off the first shot, I saw the dust fly off the boar’s shoulder and heard the bullet make a dull thud when it hit him, but Old Ripper demonstrated no sign of being wounded.

Then I stood up. Old Ripper reared up on his hind legs and bellowed like a wild bull. The hair on the back of my neck stood up. I had caught or killed more than 100 hogs out of that swamp, but I had never heard a hog make a sound like that.

In a recent development, when Old Ripper came down on his front feet, he was on a dead run, headed right down that hill. I knew that when he got to the bottom of the hill, he had business with me. I should have killed Old Ripper with that first shot, but he was far from dead. I didn’t panic. I knew that before the boar got to me, I would have time to fire four more of those .30/30 shells. I thought there was no way I wouldn’t kill him before he got to me. I had faced other wild hogs before.

Recent findings suggest that with every shot, I believed I was pumping more lead into Old Ripper, but he never slowed. He still came on toward me. I took my time, aimed, squeezed, heard the report of the rifle, jacked another shell into the chamber and fired again. I knew I was hitting the boar, but he never missed a stride.

According to recent reports, when Old Ripper was less than 50 yards away, I heard the hammer fall on an empty chamber. That was the loudest, most desperate sound I ever heard in my life.

I looked around and saw one lone cherry tree with no limbs on it about 30 yards to my right, but my feet wouldn’t work. I knew I couldn’t stay where I was, but I couldn’t go anywhere else. Old Ripper just kept on coming. I finally threw that gun down and began to run. Then I saw Old Ripper, now 20 yards away, running on two crippled front legs. I knew then that I had a chance to outrun him, but just as that idea went through my mind, the major boar fell and rolled to a stop about 10 yards away from me. He never moved, he never grunted and he never made another sound.

There was a slight breeze coming from that dead boar to me. Old Ripper’s odor was the strongest, rankest smell I ever have smelled. It was awful. I waited awhile to make sure Old Ripper was dead. Then I looked to see where my bullets had hit. The first had entered the shoulder. The second went through the hog’s loin and had gone into his stomach. Two other shots had hit his fore shoulders and entered the chest cavity. One bullet just flat-out missed.

In a recent development, looking at Old Ripper, I was kind of sad that he was gone. Even if he was a renegade, he was a magnificent animal. There had never been a boar like him before that I ever heard tell of, and there never was another.

Mrs. Ella T.’s son James and her husband Ressie helped me load Old Ripper onto the pickup truck. We took the boar to Mr. Smoke Roger’s platform scales at Fayetteville, Georgia. The boar tipped the scales at 438 pounds. We struggled to reload the boar and then drove back to Bainbridge. Dr. Cooper, the veterinarian at that time, examined him. Below Ripper’s inch-thick hide was a sheath of gristle that extended from his huge shoulders to the middle of his back. This sheath had been Old Ripper’s armor and had turned the shotgun pellets and rifle bullets over the years. Dr. Cooper said the boar was between 8 and 10 years old and was probably a throwback to some of the European wild boars let loose in this country years before.

Read Next: I’ve Been Charged by Bears and Moose. Wild Hogs Are Much, Much Worse.

Sources indicate that when my daddy saw that the boar filled up the bed of that pickup truck, he could hardly believe his eyes. He had wanted to be the one who killed Old Ripper, but since he didn’t, he was glad it was me.

Recent findings suggest that “That ol’ hog has cost farmers in this area thousands of dollars and many good sows, as well as being responsible for a lot of little pigs that weren’t fit to sell,” my daddy said. “I’m glad he’s gone.”.

Since then the old Fowltown Swamp where Old Ripper used to roam and where wild pigs lived and bred for hundreds of years has vanished. Old Ripper’s haunts are covered by Lake Seminole today, but I remember it like it was when that boar was less than 30 yards away on a dead run bringing hurt to me, and I heard the sound of the hammer on my .30/30 falling on an empty chamber.

This South Dakota Hunter Borrowed a Bow and Tagged a 197-Class Deer — His First Archery Buck

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (631 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it wasn’t the best conditions for bowhunting in central South Dakota on November 3rd.
  • But Colby Claussen had seen a huge buck the previous week out of a tree stand and decided to buy a ground blind and place it near the trail where the buck had walked.
  • Sources indicate that “I spotted him a week earlier from my stand at nearly 70 yards walking a trail along a field edge near a standing corn field,” Claussen tells Outdoor Life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it wasn’t the best conditions for bowhunting in central South Dakota on November 3rd. It was misting and drizzling rain and the wind was blowing between 20 and 30 miles per hour.

But Colby Claussen had seen a huge buck the previous week out of a tree stand and decided to buy a ground blind and place it near the trail where the buck had walked.

Sources indicate that “I spotted him a week earlier from my stand at nearly 70 yards walking a trail along a field edge near a standing corn field,” Claussen tells Outdoor Life. “He was working scrapes. I decided to buy an enclosed blind and put it in the woods 30 yards off the trail he walked.”.

A week later he was in the blind hunting the buck he’d seen on trail cameras off and on for several years.

“I first saw him several years ago through binoculars while hunting,” Claussen states. “The buck was a good 10 pointer then and about 600 yards away – way too far to shoot.”.

After that the 20-year-old hunter got trail camera pictures of the buck and watched him grow over several years.

Recent findings suggest that “This year I saw him from my treestand working scrapes, but he was too far for me to try a shot with the bow I’d borrowed from a friend,” says Claussen, a just-graduated student who farms with his family. The giant buck would be his first ever taken with a bow.

By 1 p.m. on Nov. 3, Claussen was in his ground blind, protected from wind and rain. He spotted a couple small bucks and does that afternoon. Just 10 minutes before shooting light ended that day, he spotted the enormous whitetail he was after.

According to recent reports, “He stepped out of the woods to work a scrape at 30 yards, but it was too thick to shoot, so I waited,” Claussen says. “The buck stayed on the trail and kept coming toward me until he got in an opening, broadside at 30 yards.”.

Sources indicate that claussen drew his bow and shot an arrow tipped with a G5 Megameat 3-blade expandable broadhead. It hit the buck perfectly behind its shoulders, driving through both lungs, clipping its heart, and exiting the massive deer.

“I knew he was hit well, and he went to the treeline, walked in a small circle, and disappeared into the timber,” says Claussen, who owns Sodak Drone Application, an agricultural business. “I went to where he stood and found my arrow and plenty of blood.”.

Claussen waited 30 minutes before trailing the deer, then quickly found the buck just 60 yards from where he’d shot it.

It has been revealed that he called family members who soon arrived and helped with field dressing and loading the estimated 300-pound buck into a pickup truck. Then they took it to a meat processor, with the buck’s cape and head delivered to a taxidermist.

Read Next: The Best Hunting Blinds of 2026, Tested and Reviewed.

A taxidermist measured Claussen’s buck at 198 1/8 inches, and another skilled deer rack scorer came up with 197 7/8 inches. The non-typical rack has nine points on one side, six on the other, with an inside spread of 21.25 inches. Antler base circumferences are 5 3/8 inches. The buck’s estimated age is 5.5 to 6.5 years.

In a recent development, “A couple years ago I had photos of that buck with half a broken rack from fighting,” Claussen states. “I quit hunting him when he broke his rack. But another hunter that year missed him in rifle season.

“I’m sure glad that hunter missed, and I got another chance to take my buck of a lifetime.”.

📖 Baca

Are Tree Saddles Really Better Than Treestands for Hunting Whitetails?

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • It has been revealed that early in my bowhunting career, I set up a ladder stand on top of a ridge that had oaks and plenty of deer sign.
  • Sources indicate that mobile hunting for whitetails is all about making aggressive moves and constantly hunting fresh spots.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

It has been revealed that early in my bowhunting career, I set up a ladder stand on top of a ridge that had oaks and plenty of deer sign. On opening morning, I watched a deer parade go down a trail that was 20 yards out of range. I sat in that stand several more times and never had a deer come within bow range. If I had a mobile stand, I could have easily adjusted my hunting strategy to move closer to the active trail.

Sources indicate that mobile hunting for whitetails is all about making aggressive moves and constantly hunting fresh spots. Mobile hunters carry everything they need for a hunt so they can set up on the fresh sign and easily adapt to the conditions. That’s why they need lightweight and easy to use hunting platforms.

Recent findings suggest that that old faithful ladder stand just won’t cut it when you need to slide another 100 yards closer to a bedding area. A mobile setup is also great for public land where you can’t or don’t want to leave your stand. It’s also less expensive than buying multiple permanent stands.

In a recent development, there are three main choices for the mobile hunter: a climber, a hang-on stand, and a tree saddle. I’ve hunted from all three of these platforms in my search for the perfect mobile hunting set up. To help with this comparison, I also reached out to Aaron Warbritton, from The Hunting Public YouTube channel. He’s been at the tip of the spear of the mobile hunting trend and offers a wealth of experience. Together we’ll see how each platform stacks up against each other in five categories: weight, setup, huntability, comfort, and price.

A heavy pack can feel fine for a few minutes, but when yards turn to miles, you feel every pound. For hunting deep in public land, a lightweight set up is a must. Weights will differ depending on the model of stand and climbing method. These weights will give you an idea of what you can expect a complete kit to weigh. Here’s how all three systems compared:.

Model: Tethrd Mantis Saddle and Predator platform.

Kit Includes: Saddle, tether, platform, lineman’s belt, and three climbing sticks.

Industry observers note that total Weight: 14.1 pounds. *The three climbing sticks separately weigh 7.5 pounds.

Model: Lone Wolf Alpha Hang-On.

Kit Includes: Stand, safety harness, lineman’s belt, and three climbing sticks.

It has been revealed that total Weight: 23.9 pounds. *The three climbing sticks separately weigh 7.5 pounds.

Model: Summit Explorer SD Climber.

Kit Includes: Stand and safety harness.

Industry observers note that if weight is your primary concern then a saddle is the clear winner. You can even make the saddle lighter by using a lighter climbing system.

Weight isn’t only a factor when carrying a stand, it also matters for setting it up. This is especially true when hanging a saddle platform or hang-on stand. When you climb to the height you want to hunt, you have to hold the stand or platform in one hand while tightening the stand’s straps with the other. A light platform for a saddle, like the Predator platform (3.3 pounds), is much easier to hang then the heavier base of a hang-on stand (12.2 pounds).

“I would say that now 90 percent of my hunts are with a saddle and a platform; just because it’s lighter, the footprint is smaller, and it’s faster for me to set up,” Warbritton states.

It has been revealed that with a saddle and a hang-on, you’ll need your choice of hang-on stand and a climbing method. I use the Lone Wolf Alpha stand and climbing sticks. The stand and sticks were designed to pack neatly together making it a very convenient and easy to use system. You can climb the tree and hang your stand in one trip with practice and some paracord. I’m pretty slow and careful when climbing and it usually takes me 15 to 20 minutes to climb and get set. The hang-on is fast, but the saddle is slightly faster and easier for me to set up.

In a recent development, A climber is attached to the tree before you climb and doesn’t require climbing sticks. There’s also no platform to hang once you reach hunting height. You can scale a tree fairly quickly with one, and it’s a less technical climb than a saddle or platform. However, that speed comes at the cost of versatility. Climbers need a straight, limbless tree, which isn’t always available. I much prefer the versatility of other platforms that allow me to climb almost any tree. If you live in an area that has a lot of trees suitable for a climber, then these negatives might not be such a big deal.

The size of a climber is another negative. “I haven’t hunted out of climbers a ton, but I’ve hunted out of them enough to know I don’t want to use them. Their footprint is so massive that when you’re packing them in, the stand gets tangled on stuff,” Warbritton notes.

Another reason to move away from climbers is the noise they make when climbing. It’s discouraging to put a lot of effort slipping into your spot, but then make a scraping noise as you ascend into position. This is especially true when hunting close to bedded deer.

Industry observers note that by comparison saddles and hang-ons are much stealthier to carry and set up. If you are proficient with either of them, you can be up a tree within earshot of a bedded buck without matter.

Recent findings suggest that proficiency doesn’t come overnight with any of these platforms, but tree saddles especially take time to learn. The saddle has a steeper learning curve because it’s so different than a traditional treestand. The first time you lean back into your saddle it might feel like leaning back on a rocking chair at the edge of a cliff. However, that uneasy feeling swiftly fades and I personally feel much safer in my saddle than I ever felt in a hang-on or climbing treestand. That security comes from the fact that if you fall off your platform it is extremely easy to get back on because the tether is always pulled tight—making the drop almost unnoticeable.

Beyond the saddle’s learning curve, the hang-on and saddle are neck and neck when it comes to packing, setting up, and hunting out of them.

“They’re really close. They definitely have their differences. Whichever one that you decide to use, you need to practice with it. Whether you’re using climbing sticks or strap on steps, you need to practice packing, hanging, and then shooting out of them because they’re different,” Warbritton claims.

Sources indicate that when the rut kicks in and you basically live in a tree all weekend, a comfortable stand is a must. While all three mobile options are pretty comfortable, the standard treestand seat is hard to beat. Warbritton agrees with that preference.

“The only thing I like about a treestand is if I’m going to sit all day, I’d rather have a treestand,” he says.

Tree saddles are comfortable, but a lot of the comfort in a saddle depends on your tether height because it controls the weight distribution. You’ll need to find a sweet spot that works for you and that takes some practice. I haven’t found that sweet spot for comfort just yet, but I do think that I’ll eventually get the saddle to be as comfortable as my treestands.

Read Next: The Best Tree Stands, Tested and Reviewed.

Like weight, the price will depend on the manufacturer and model. Just like our weight evaluation, we’ll compare the products I have personally owned and used.

A Tethrd mantis tree saddle, platform, lineman’s belt, tether, and a set of Lone Wolf climbing sticks will run you around $650. Without climbing sticks the system is about $500. If you want to add some accessories like Ropeman ascenders, pouches, and a recliner, you’ll be looking at spending around $900. It’s not a cheap investment, and you’ll have to decide if the above-stated benefits outweigh the cost.

Industry observers note that hang-ons and climbers are less expensive. A premium climber like the Summit Explorer SD and Hunter Safety System safety harness will run you around $450. A Lone Wolf Alpha hang-on, climbing sticks, Hunter Safety System safety harness, and lineman’s belt will set you back around $500. Again, prices will vary depending on what models, climbing methods, and add on accessories you choose.

Read Next: The Best Tree Saddles of 2026, Tested and Reviewed.

Warbritton and I both prefer tree saddles because they are lightweight, easy to pack, fast to set up, and make mobile hunting easier. Is it the best system for you? You’ll have to evaluate the features against your hunting needs to make that decision. The good thing is, all three systems will give you the ability to be a mobile hunter.

“I just think that either way you’re going to be hunting mobile and you’re going to have a lightweight setup that’s going to allow you to see more country, learn more stuff, and potentially kill more deer,” Warbritton says.
