Hunters Can’t Really Improve Wild Whitetail Genetics. Here’s Why

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2515 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that it was the year we’d been waiting for at the family deer camp.
  • Sources indicate that still, there was probably a faster way to get here.
  • Recent findings suggest that typically, a cull buck is one that deer managers have identified as genetically inferior and should be removed from the wild herd.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it was the year we’d been waiting for at the family deer camp. All summer and fall we pulled trail camera photos of more—and bigger—bucks than had ever been seen on the property. It was a far cry from the early 90s, when the bucks my dad and uncles did spot tended to have a signature narrow spread with tall, skinny tines. Now, nearly 30 years later, we’re finally seeing a caliber of deer we weren’t even sure the property was capable of supporting. It’s taken a lot of intensive habitat improvement and discipline, but it’s working.

Sources indicate that still, there was probably a faster way to get here. It should have taken years, not decades, to improve our whitetail habitat. And there are still things we’re trying to figure out—like how to kill those bucks now that we’ve got them. So, I decided to find out what a lot of whitetail hunters get wrong by talking to some hunters who have been succeeding at the management game for a long time.

Recent findings suggest that typically, a cull buck is one that deer managers have identified as genetically inferior and should be removed from the wild herd. This might be a deer whose antlers are too small or too funky to keep in the gene pool. Studies show that killing these deer solely on the basis of selective harvest (rather than for the traditional reasons of fun, meat, etc.) is ultimately a waste of a good buck tag.

Industry observers note that “Many hunters simply believe that you can influence antler quality through genetics in the wild,” says Kip Adams, chief conservation officer of the National Deer Association (formerly QDMA). “We know very clearly that yes, behind a fence—when you can pick which buck is doing the breeding and which doe is doing the breeding—[you] absolutely can influence the genetics. In the wild, it’s very clear we cannot do that.”.

Recent findings suggest that this is for a few reasons. For one, does are contributing half the antler DNA to buck fawns. (If you can identify which does have favorable antler genes from your treestand, please share with the rest of the class.) Also, the rut doesn’t lead to quite as many fawns as you might think.

“It’s not like the biggest buck out there dominates all the does and sires the most fawns,” Adams claims, noting that the average U.S. fawn recruitment right now is .59, or less than one fawn per doe. “Research shows that most bucks sire very few fawns during the course of their life. We can’t dominate the gene pool that way.”.

“We can’t predict what a buck’s son will have—from an antler standpoint—by looking at a buck’s antlers,” states Adams.

It has been revealed that let’s say that again for the hunters in the back: Just because a buck has significant antlers doesn’t mean his offspring will. And just because a buck has small antlers doesn’t mean his offspring will have small antlers. (Part of that goes back to the fact that you can’t tell what kind of antler genes a doe is carrying around.).

It has been revealed that that all boils down to Adams’ original point: A hunter cannot influence the genetics of a wild deer herd. Selective buck culling to optimize antler size doesn’t work. So, what can hunters do, if they want to shoot bigger bucks? It’s a simple two-part proposal rooted in the classic QDM refrain. First, let deer get older.

“We tend to see and hear about more bigger bucks than ever before because older deer are encompassing a higher percentage of the total buck harvest today than ever before,” Adams says. “Hunters today are letting deer get older at unprecedented levels, and that’s the reason that, across the whitetails’ range, we see, hear of, photograph, and shoot bigger deer than ever before.”.

The 2021 Deer Report reveals that during the 2019-20 deer season, 39 percent of all antlered bucks harvested were at least 3.5 years old. That’s the highest national average ever recorded.

The second thing you can do if you want to increase antler size? Increase the available nutrition for deer. This means increasing habitat quality, decreasing the number of deer using the habitat (that is, shooting more does), or both.

According to recent reports, it’s all good and well to recommend passing bucks to let them mature, but what does that look like on the ground? Some of the most successful significant deer hunters follow this advice, and with good results.

Brothers Brent and Justin Cearlock, two of the Illinois hunters behind the world-record whitetail, enjoy considerable success year after year. Part of this is because of where they live, in the prime significant-buck county of eastern Illinois. But it’s also because they pass more bucks than they shoot, even with two buck tags apiece per season.

Read Next: Two Years After the World-Record Buck, the Cearlock Brothers Are Still on a Roll.

“I have no intention of shooting a deer younger than five, unless it has just a substantially huge rack,” says Justin, who mostly relies on trail camera history to help him establish age estimates. “I don’t care if I think the deer is four. I’m just going to let him get to five, just to see what happens.”.

In a recent development, this past season, Brent made the call on a stud buck that didn’t meet this age threshold. Instead of picking up his bow that morning, he grabbed his phone and shot some video.

It has been revealed that “I passed a phenomenal deer—the biggest buck I’ve ever let walk in my life,” Brent indicates. “He was already in the mid-160s, flirting with the 170-inch mark as a 4-year-old deer. I called him Will, because I didn’t know if I would have the willpower to pass him.”.

In a recent development, the guys could only imagine what Will might look like in fall 2021. Brent ended up killing a lower-scoring buck that same day: a deer that was at least seven years old, and that he had history with.

“We’re very fortunate to have access to the properties we do. If you don’t have good properties, you’re not going to shoot substantial deer,” Brent claims. “But we do put a lot of effort into it and we pass deer that most people probably wouldn’t pass. There are a lot of guys that say they’ll pass a deer like that. But when they’re standing there and it’s getting dark, they’re like, I’m shooting that deer.”.

Brent didn’t regret his decision—the older buck meant a lot to him—but he couldn’t help feeling torn when he learned a neighbor shot Will a few weeks later.

“Passing a big one comes with risk, and I am genuinely happy for the other hunter to get a great buck like that,” Brent says. “But I’d be lying if I said part of me isn’t sincerely disappointed that we just lost what we thought might be our No. 1 target buck next year.”.

Often the decision to pass a deer is fraught because of the property itself. Other hunters with permission and neighboring hunters are just two of the many factors that reduce a deer’s odds of surviving into the next season. And the Cearlocks don’t begrudge anyone who wants to shoot younger bucks: They’ve been those guys themselves, earlier in their hunting careers. But the knowledge that a neighbor might shoot a buck isn’t enough to make them abandon their management strategy in the heat of the moment.

“There’s a lot of things that can happen,” Brent acknowledges. “But if you shoot them, they’re definitely not going to make it to five.”.

Recent findings suggest that this past deer season, Rick Dahl secured access to a latest whitetail property in central Missouri. Dahl believes the new farm, which is in the same county as the parcels he currently hunts, actually holds better potential for bigger bucks. The new property is promising for a few reasons, including its superior soil quality, fewer neighbors to compete with, and the anecdotal evidence that massive bucks are being harvested nearby. The fact that the new property doesn’t have any shooter bucks on it yet doesn’t seem to faze him.

“The food supply is very limited on the latest farm,” Dahl indicates, who is a lifelong Missouri deer hunter and chairman of the NDA board. “[But] it’s in the right area and, if we give the deer there what they need to eat, time will tell whether we’ll be able to produce a bigger-antlered deer there.”.

It has been revealed that although the property has fertile soil, Dahl claims the food supply is limited because it hasn’t been managed for deer yet. A mature forest canopy has prevented understory growth, and many of the tillable fields were used as cattle pasture. Dahl’s no biologist, but he still knows good soil is crucial for growing big deer.

Dahl conducted a trail camera survey late last year, which revealed a relatively even age-class distribution of deer—and some clues to support his hunch that nutrition is currently a limiting factor for antler growth. The photos of yearling bucks seem to be mostly spikes, instead of fork-horns. And, with the exception of one deer with an extra point, not a single buck on the property seemed to have more than eight points.

According to recent reports, “That was really interesting to me,” Dahl states, who noticed four bucks in the 4- and 5-year-old age class that probably scored 140 inches. “It takes a significant 8-pointer to score like that. So, there’s clearly an 8-point genetic thing going on there. I will be really interested to see what transpires over the next three to five years as we begin to introduce more food.”.

Read Next: 9 Ways to Score Permission on Private Property.

What confused me about this particular endeavor—investing time and money in a whole new property that’s going to need careful timber, habitat, and food plot management—is that Dahl at the moment has a 4.5-year-old minimum age limit agreement with his hunting buddies on the excellent properties they’ve already got. Why not just raise the age limit for shooter bucks to five, like the Cearlock brothers?

Industry observers note that “I’m at the point where I think five and a half is the right age [for me],” Dahl notes. “But I also realize that everybody’s at a different stage in the maturation process that we all go through as hunters. My hunting partner is a perfect example. He hasn’t shot a lot of bucks. And if we say we’re not going to shoot anything less than five years old, well, what are we doing? We just went from five deer out there we can hunt to two. At some point you’ve restricted yourself. And for me, if there’s only one deer on the farm that I’m willing to shoot, then the question becomes, ‘Is it really fun anymore?’ And maybe that deer jumps the fence and gets shot by the neighbor on October 30. What do you do? Are you just done?”.

Happily for Dahl, he doesn’t have to pick. He can tinker with the newly introduced farm, and see if those nutritional improvements eventually support the 4.5-year-old bucks he’s interested in.

The Northeast isn’t exactly known for dedicated deer management. This is a combination of multiple factors, including high hunter numbers in states like Pennsylvania and poorer soil quality. But Neil Dougherty, the president of NorthCountry Whitetails consulting services, finds the challenges of creating QDM programs for clients that much more rewarding.

Sources indicate that “Iowa is like Disneyland—it’s fake,” Dougherty laughs. “It’s such a wonderful place in those areas where deer have the ability to explode like that, but it’s not the everyman’s hunt. It’s such a foreign thing to most people who are trying to play this deer game.”.

Industry observers note that when Dougherty examines a deer property, he takes into account 17 different factors—from native habitat to huntability—to determine the property’s potential. He can almost always improve a property to help “unlock the genetic potential” of the deer that are there. But he’s not a magician, either.

Recent findings suggest that “There’s a magic intersection with the amount of food that’s produced on a property, and the amount of deer that are there to consume that food,” Dougherty notes, “The problem is, in some major woods country, that could be eight deer per square mile. That kind of hunting sucks.”.

While almost all the properties Dougherty works on need some serious rehabilitation of the natural habitat, the biggest problem with a fresh property usually lies not with the land, but the client.

Recent findings suggest that “When I show up, there’s almost always a hunting strategy that’s flawed,” Dougherty claims. “Just about every property has a hunting strategy that does not lend itself to the intersection of the hunter coming in contact with 5-year-old deer. [Those hunters] just haven’t been exposed to 5-year-old deer. They don’t understand what it takes to speak the same language.”.

If you broke down those flaws, Dougherty estimates poor understanding of the wind is to blame about 40 percent of the time. That’s a major improvement compared to even 10 years ago. Today’s hunters are generally much more sophisticated at hunting downwind, he says, and being aware of steady or swirling wind patterns.

Recent findings suggest that “Access is the biggest problem I’m finding. It’s super hard to get out of these spots—getting in isn’t that hard to do, but getting out in the dark and not blowing up the area? That requires a lot of discipline. And sometimes we’re limited by the physical characteristics of a property.”.

Sources indicate that while Dougherty is a habitat expert, his consulting work involves much more than recommending where to put food plots and what to plant in them. At the end of the day, he’s teaching clients how to hunt.

It has been revealed that “I would encourage people to not get caught up in this whole genetic thing,” Dougherty advises. “Learn what your [deer] potential is on the property you hunt, know what you’re doing when it comes to habitat, and just be happy with what you’re doing.”.

So, even if the stars align and you end up with major deer consistently using your property, the question remains: Can you kill one of them?

It has been revealed that as it turns out, I couldn’t last fall. When I did finally get the biggest buck on the place in front of me, I choked. Painful lesson though it was, it was a reminder that managing for mature deer isn’t like shooting fish in a barrel. Sure, it can be a lot easier when you’ve got 5,000 acres and no neighbors or public land for miles around. But that’s unrealistic for most hunters. Even some basic habitat work and personal discipline can improve the number and quality of deer where you hunt.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The backpacking equivalent of “happy wife, happy life” is “happy feet, happy hike.” So today, I’m going to help guide your decision-making when selecting footwear for your next backpacking trip.

In a recent development, hi, I’m Andrew Skurka. I’m a former thru-hiker. I was the first person to do the Great Western Loop, the Alaska-Yukon Expedition, and the Sea-to-Sea Route.

If you’re watching this before Saturday, December 5th, 2026, and if you live in the Denver metro area, we’re going to have a great time, and you can get tickets here.

Finally, before we get started, we’re opening applications for our 2027 guided backpacking trips on Monday, December 7th. You can find more information here.

In a recent development, footwear plays an outsized role in your backpacking trip. It’s one of the most crucial decisions that you’ll make as a backpacker when selecting your equipment, and just honestly, it’s really difficult to enjoy yourself on a backpacking trip if every step hurts or feels uncomfortable.

In a recent development, and it doesn’t help that the industry also uses a lot of technical jargon to describe their shoes. It can be pretty overwhelming if you’re not familiar with how shoes are constructed and the different features of them.

Before we talk about backpacking footwear, I think it would be worth looking at some of the other outdoor sports that we might be familiar with. So, for example, biking or skiing or running.

And if you know a serious skier or a serious biker or a serious runner, you know that they don’t have just one pair of shoes. They have multiple pairs of shoes. And when we talk about not just shoes, but multiple skis, multiple bikes, and when we talk about their collection or their quiver, they’ll say their quiver of skis. Each of those sets of skis, each of those bikes, has a specific application or purpose.

So, as an example, let me just kind of walk you through my little collection of running shoes.

Recent findings suggest that let me start with my trail running shoe. You’ll notice that the shoe has a narrower foot shape to give me good control laterally when I’m on uneven terrain. It also has an aggressive outsole for good traction on dirt and rocks.

This is what I would consider to be like my bike trail or gravel path trail shoe. The outsole is much less aggressive, and it’s a more comfortable upper. It’s a little bit wider, so I can run in the shoe for more time without feeling like my foot’s being constricted.

This is my road shoe. This outsole is almost nonexistent, has very little traction, and the major highlight feature about the shoe is all this thick foam so I can run on pavement without breaking my bones.

In a recent development, and then the last shoe I have with me, this is my racing shoe. This has some fancy, super high-tech foam that has a lot of energy rebound and makes me faster. And then the upper is also very minimalist, very minimally designed, very lightweight, so that it doesn’t slow me down over the course of those 26 miles.

So that’s just one example. These are my running shoes.

It has been revealed that if you meet a biker or a skier, they’re gonna have the same thing. A skier’s gonna have their cross-country skis and their skate skis and their alpine skis and alpine touring skis, and then their, you know, you name it.

There’s, I think, what’s the saying? “n+1” is where you should stop buying skis.

In a recent development, and then bikers are gonna be the same way. They have their road bikes, their mountain bikes, their gravel bikes, their townies. Okay, same thing.

Now, interestingly, when we talk about backpacking shoes, there is really no consideration in the industry of what the optimal application is of a backpacking shoe.

According to recent reports, if you look at backpackers who are on the cutting edge of backpacking, what you’ll see is that they don’t wear boots. The footwear that they choose isn’t actually designed for backpacking. The footwear that backpackers who are on the cutting edge of backpacking wear, they’re trail runners. They’re not even designed for backpacking. And it just happens to be probably the closest thing that is suitable for our particular activity.

What I want to emphasize to you when you’re looking at shoes, first, is that you want to be looking at what the optimal application of a particular shoe is.

So I’ll walk you through the features of a shoe and talk to you about the different conditions in which those sorts of features excel.

And then the other consideration when you’re buying a shoe is that you need to make sure that it fits you.

So at the end, we’ll talk about fit and how to make sure that it’s not just like the best backpacking shoe of 2026, but it’s the best backpacking shoe for the trip that you’re going on and that fits your foot.

Before we talk about how to pick a shoe for the right conditions, let’s actually talk about the parts of the shoe.

Let’s start with the outsole. This is going to be on the bottom of the shoe. It’s where literally the rubber meets the road.

Recent findings suggest that it is going to be typically made out of some kind of rubber compound. There is a trade-off between sticky rubber and durable rubber. So just be aware of that trade-off when you are looking at shoes.

The other thing to be looking at with your footwear is going to be the lugs, including the lug pattern, the lug depth, and also the lug volume.

Generally speaking, for softer surfaces like mud or sand or snow, you want lugs that are taller and that have shorter edges to them.

In a recent development, and then the opposite is true, too. If you’re going to be walking on flat benched trails, your lug pattern doesn’t need to be as aggressive.

Industry observers note that the next part of the shoe I want to talk about is the midsole. This is going to be made out of foam.

Recent findings suggest that and when you’re thinking about the midsole, you want to be paying attention to the height of the midsole. And you sometimes might find the specs called stack height. So you might see like 30 millimeters on the heel and, say, 22 millimeters at the front.

The taller the shoe, the more wobbly it wants to be. However, the taller the shoe, the more cushioning you’re going to have. So that itself is a little bit of a trade-off.

Another thing you want to be thinking about with the midsole is just the firmness of this midsole.

Recent findings suggest that this midsole here, this is a HOKA shoe. This is very plush, forgiving, soft, versus the midsole foam that’s used in this La Sportiva.

Industry observers note that this is pretty firm. And that results in this shoe being more comfortable to wear and absorbing more of the ground, for example, like when you step on a rock.

Sources indicate that however, this shoe gives you better ground feel. Your feet definitely feel more connected to the ground, more sensitive when you’re wearing this.

The third part of the shoe to be looking at is going to be the upper.

The upper, more than probably any other part of the shoe, is responsible for how this shoe fits you, so particularly its shape and its patterning.

It’s going to be made out of fabric and perhaps some faux leather.

The things to be looking at with the upper of a shoe are whether it’s breathable or whether it’s described as waterproof.

For some environments, you also want to be considering whether it’s sand-resistant.

And then the last thing is you want to be thinking about what the expected durability is of the upper.

Recent findings suggest that in my experience, the upper of a shoe is typically the thing that blows out first. It develops holes. Sometimes if you snag it bad enough, a whole section of it can rip. Sometimes fabrics just kind of slowly fray apart.

So this is the first part of the shoe that blows out. You really want to give some consideration to this part of the shoe if you need to be using it for a very long distance.

So now that we’ve talked about the parts of the shoe, let’s actually talk about how different design decisions with each of these shoes make them optimized for particular environments.

The shoe that you choose for, say, the Appalachian Trail may not be the best shoe for, say, hiking in southern Utah. And the shoe for hiking in Utah might not be the best shoe for, say, hiking in the High Sierra or for Alaska.

So let’s talk about specific conditions that affect footwear choice.

Industry observers note that are you going to be hiking on compacted dirt or, like, coarsely ground mineral sand? Are you going to be hiking on slippery roots, rocks, and mud? Are you going to be walking on sharp talus and scree? Are you going to be walking through loose blow sand?

If you were planning a trail hike that was mostly on compacted dirt or ground-up mineral sand, such as what you might find on the East Coast or in the northern woodlands or, say, in the High Sierra, a shoe like this without a particularly aggressive outsole would be just fine.

However, if you are planning a trip where there’s going to be slippery rocks, roots, mud, slippery tundra, having an outsole with a more aggressive lug pattern would be better, something like this.

Or if you’re going to be, say, hiking on a bunch of slickrock or doing scrambling, you might want to be using some kind of shoe with an outsole like this where there’s flatter sections of rubber that give you more of an approach-style shoe with a lot of surface area that’s going to give you extra traction on those surfaces.

The next condition that you should be thinking about is going to be the typical surface angle of whatever you’re walking on.

So if you are walking on, say, a really high-quality benched trail, I’m thinking of something like the John Muir Trail, which is, even though it’s going up a lot, up and down a lot, it’s often switchbacking, and they have benched the trail into the mountains, so the trail itself is actually pretty flat.

In that case, a shoe, something like this, that kind of has a wide last on it, is going to be great because this is going to translate to more comfort.

It’s going to be a looser-fitting shoe. It’s going to give your foot places to move around, and you’re not going to be as prone to getting pinched or any constrictions in your shoe.

So this would be a good trail shoe.

Of course, the classic example, and I don’t have a pair with me because I don’t wear them, would be the Altra Lone Peaks.

And for me, personally, it feels like I’m wearing clown shoes, but I totally get why they’re so popular among long-distance hikers who are on those really high-quality trails.

If you go to the other side of the spectrum, imagine you’re hiking off-trail in steep mountain country. It behooves you to have a shoe with a much narrower last.

This is the La Sportiva Bushido. There are a lot of people out there who cannot wear these because their feet just aren’t narrow enough, or they’re not willing to deal with the discomfort of having their foot kind of wedged into a shoe.

This is a much more appropriate shoe for a high route or for early-season conditions when you want that lateral stability of your shoe.

To take it to an even more extreme example, this is the La Sportiva TX Guide, and this is even a narrower last than the Bushido, which limits its application for, or suitability for, longer days on the trail, or just longer days in general, which makes it really excel in terrain that tends to be highly technical.

So we’ve talked about the walking surface. We’ve talked about the surface angle.

The last consideration that affects the suitability of footwear would just be a number of different environmental factors.

So let me give you some examples.

Industry observers note that if you’re going to be in an area with a lot of spring runoff, so I’m thinking of, say, anywhere, like any mountain environment in the springtime, there tends to be high runoff of creeks. In that case, you’re going to be looking for a breathable shoe, not a waterproof shoe. (We’ll talk about waterproof shoes a little bit later and why my preference is for breathable shoes even in wet environments.).

Another environmental factor would be spring snow.

So if you’re going to be up in the mountains, say, in the West, if you’re going to be there in May or early June, you’re going to want a shoe with an aggressive outsole that’ll give you good bite and traction on that snow.

Another environmental consideration would be loose sand.

So I’m specifically thinking right now about the Four Corners of the United States or the western U.S. and places like southern Utah, which have that really fine, powdery blow sand.

There are shoes that, for example, like this one, are effectively sandproof even though they are still breathable.

And then there are other shoes, like this one, that are basically, they just, you wouldn’t believe the amount of sand that passes through the upper of a shoe like this.

So if you’re hiking in an area like that, you want to be aware of that consideration.

And then the last environmental factor that I would throw out there would be scratchy brush or vegetation.

This is gonna be more of an glitch if you’re hiking off-trail, but anytime you’re walking through brush, so that might be willow or manzanita or chaparral, that is really hard on the uppers of the shoes.

So that’s a real argument then for going with a shoe that has a really durable, robust upper, not something that you would necessarily see on a road running shoe that has been given a few extra features to make it suitable for trail running.

So let’s rabbit hole for a few minutes about this discussion of waterproof or breathable shoes.

So-called waterproof shoes, they’re, it’s generous.

Let’s just assume that the shoe itself is waterproof. The problem is that there’s this big hole in the top of the shoe.

Industry observers note that I would also argue that waterproof shoes don’t end up being waterproof long-term. Just the torsion that you put on a shoe from normal wear and tear breaks down that waterproof-breathable fabric.

The other thing that happens with waterproof shoes is that your feet get wet from the inside because of your perspiration.

So my recommendation to everyone has been my recommendation for, boy, going on like 20 years now.

Instead of trying to keep your feet dry in the backcountry, just embrace the fact that they’re going to get wet and learn how to manage wet feet.

Let me give you four ways that you can manage wet feet in the backcountry.

First, you can wear a breathable shoe. A breathable shoe will expel water faster, and it will also dry out faster because more air will be passing through the shoe, not just through the top, but also moving through the fabric in the upper.

Second, when you are taking a break during the day, so at rest stops, remove your shoes and socks. Just five minutes, 10 minutes, 15 minutes of fresh air to your feet can be really nurturing for your feet that otherwise are just squeezed into a wet shoe all day long.

Third, at night you want to have a dedicated pair of sleeping socks, and you want to make sure that your feet get warm and dry at night and that they stay that way.

Fourth, you can bring out a balm. So this is GurneyGoo. This is just one example of many.

According to recent reports, and use this balm to recondition your feet at night. The way that you do it is you get to camp, you do all your dinner stuff, you go into your tent, you take off shoes and socks, you let your feet dry out for a while and get them nice and dry, and at that point you put the balm on.

And that’ll basically recondition your skin, and then in the morning the bottoms of your feet will feel a lot more restored than if you had just let them air out and get really dry and crispy over the course of the night.

Quick plug that we have done a couple of videos in the past about managing wet feet in the backcountry.

At the top, I made the argument that your footwear needs to do two things for you.

In a recent development, the first is that it needs to be appropriate for the conditions and optimized for your application. And then the second thing that it needs to do for you is that it needs to fit.

It has been revealed that footwear fit is highly personalized. It’s really unlike any other type of backpacking clothing or anything else that you wear.

So as an example, if I took this shirt, which isn’t a backpacking shirt, but it’s going to convey the idea.

If I took the shirt and I gave it to another male who’s about six feet tall and 160 pounds, it probably would fit them just fine and they could wear the shirt.

However, if I were to give them this shoe, this size 11-and-a-half shoe, they might put it on and it might fit them horribly.

And that’s because fit is very personalized.

And there are a couple of things going on here.

Part of it is the shape of your particular foot, like whether you have, say, a narrow heel and a big toe splay, or maybe something that’s a little bit more ruler-shaped.

Also, what is the volume of your foot? Are your arches high? Are they low?

In addition to the shape of your foot, your gait plays into this as well.

What exactly is that process of lifting your foot in the air and putting it back on the ground? Are you pronating? Are you landing flat? There’s just lots of options in this.

Another consideration with fit is going to be your Achilles, the flexibility and strength of your Achilles tendon.

And that’s going to affect how much tolerance you have for this angle, whether you can do a right angle, or whether, like with a zero drop, you’re actually a little bit more than a right angle, or whether you need something with a little bit of a lift so that it’s a greater-than-90-degree angle.

That just is impacted by, again, the flexibility and strength of your Achilles.

And then finally, the last thing with fit is just personal preference.

Like my tolerance for squeezing my foot into something like that La Sportiva TX Guide might be higher than the next person who just isn’t willing to deal with that constant squeezing tightness for the performance gains that those shoes offer in particular environments.

So how should footwear fit you? What are you looking for?

It has been revealed that the first is that when you put it on, out of the box, it should immediately be comfortable. It should feel like someone had a mold of your foot, and they created a shoe just for you. It shouldn’t pinch. It shouldn’t be applying pressure in places where you don’t want it. And you should be able to be very comfortable in the shoe, again, out of the box without aftermarket insoles.

I know a lot of people like their aftermarket insoles. I’ve just always felt that the designers design the shoe for a foot, and the aftermarket insole changes the intended user, and you probably shouldn’t do that. You should probably just go find another shoe.

And then the other criteria for determining whether a shoe fits you really well is you take a walk around the shoe store or around your house and try, if available, to go up and down some things. That way, you can replicate more of a true hiking environment.

And you want to feel like you can walk naturally in that shoe, that your heel-to-toe transition feels really natural, that it’s locking your heel down the way you want it to. It should feel like you’re walking in a slipper in an optimal situation.

It has been revealed that now, the one little caveat that I would add to fit is not every shoe is going to feel super comfortable right out of the box. And that’s just going to be a trade-off of the shoe.

So, for example, when I put on these La Sportiva shoes, this feels comfortable right out of the box. It feels like a slipper. It feels like it’s made for me.

I put on these TX Guides, I’m like, okay, they’re a little tight. I wouldn’t mind a little bit more room. But I just know that in certain environments these shoes are phenomenal.

And I’m willing to deal with maybe some slight discomfort, nothing that’s going to be trip-ending, just something where it’s more like at the end of the day, I’m looking forward to taking them off.

The other thing about fit and comfort: if you’re trying on two different sizes, and one size almost fits you perfectly, you just feel like it’s a little bit tight, and then you go up to the next half size, and that definitely feels too big, I would actually lean more towards the smaller shoe.

What you’ll find is that most shoes have enough foam in them, and maybe even some, not just foam in the midsole, but also some open-cell foam in the heel cup.

And those materials pack out a little bit with use, and that will give you that extra breathing room that you’re looking for.

Typically for backpacking, your backpacking shoes are going to be about a half size bigger than casual shoes.

Industry observers note that so, for example, I’m size 11 in these shoes. I’m size 11-and-a-half in these shoes. That’s pretty typical.

You need a little bit more room in your backpacking shoes to account for foot swelling.

The other thing is you don’t want your feet jamming into the front of your shoe, assuming that you like to keep your toenails.

Sources indicate that when you’re sizing your shoe, one way that I typically will do it, I’m going to demonstrate here, is I’ll put on a shoe, and I’ll jam my feet into the toe box. And if I can get my index finger down the back of the shoe, that typically is about right.

It shouldn’t be a really easy depression into the back there, but you want some friction on it.

But you shouldn’t be able to wiggle around and not be in contact on both sides of your index finger.

If you find that the shoe mostly fits, but you need just a little bit of extra heel lock, you can mess around with your lacing systems.

So, for example, let me bring this close.

This is a heel lock that I added to the very back of that shoe.

Another thing that I sometimes do, if you’ve been watching these videos, sometimes what I’ll do is I’ll basically just remove the lacing from this part of the shoe, and that relieves the pressure over that bunion.

So you can mess around with your lacing system if you need to kind of optimize the fit of your particular shoes.

Like you found the shoe, it’s almost perfect. You’re just trying to really get that last five or 10% of fit in.

We’ve talked about fit. We’ve talked about sizing. Let’s next talk about the toe box.

This topic gets a ton of attention in the backpacking community. And understandably, because backpackers, they’re spending like 10, 12 hours a day in these shoes, putting lots of miles on them, and some discomfort caused by the toe box can have big repercussions.

So just realize right now that there is a trade-off.

If you go with a very wide toe box or something like an Altra, which is going to, you know, come out to here, yes, that gives you a lot of room in that toe box.

It allows your toes to splay, and how wonderful that feels.

But it also leads to a really sloppy fit. You are going to be moving around in that shoe if you’re putting that shoe on level walking surfaces.

So the Altra Lone Peak, classic thru-hiking shoe, and also highly appropriate to trails like, say, the Pacific Crest Trail.

Probably less appropriate for something like the Appalachian Trail.

And when we see our clients, some of our clients come out with the Lone Peaks and try to take them off-trail in places like Alaska or southern Utah and walk on steep slickrock or steep alpine tundra or off-trail in the Sierra on high routes, they just don’t work that well.

In a recent development, some clients can do them, can wear them. They’re capable in them. But for a lot of clients, it just leads to unsteadiness that isn’t helpful. So in that case, you want to be looking at a shoe with a narrower toe box.

And again, you’re dealing with that trade-off of a narrower toe box.

It’s going to be a little bit less comfortable, but you need to be considering, or your thinking needs to be, am I willing to endure the tightness and constriction of that narrow toe box for increased performance?

Or do I not need that performance, in which case I can go with that really wide toe box?

So the last topic when it comes to fit is going to be the heel-to-toe drop.

According to recent reports, if you have a zero-drop shoe, so this shoe, this is just an Adidas street shoe. This is, I believe, a zero-drop shoe.

Which means that the stack height of the midsole and the outsole in the heel is the same as it is in the forefoot.

That’s a very natural style of footwear. Like if you were barefoot, that’s what it would be. You’d have zero drop.

To the contrary, this shoe here, this is a road marathon shoe. And I believe this has a heel drop of 12 millimeters. I think it’s 28 or 30 in the back and maybe 20 in the front.

And as a backpacker, here’s the way to think about this.

If you have a zero-drop shoe, your lower leg is at a right angle, or at least it wants to be.

But when you put a backpack on, you actually need to be leaning forward to counteract or counterbalance the weight of that backpack.

So if you are wearing zero-drop shoes when backpacking, just realize you’re going to probably forward lean and your Achilles is going to be at something less than a 90-degree angle. That could put a lot of stress and strain on your Achilles, especially if you’re not used to it. That would be the major thing.

You can build up to it, but if you’re accustomed to shoes like this, or running shoes or trail shoes or any kind of shoes that have significant heel-to-toe drops, and then you try to get in a zero-drop shoe, there is a buildup period.

It is going to hurt if you just suddenly start trying to put on lots of miles.

Industry observers note that I think for backpacking, probably the most natural heel-to-toe drop is going to be something in a moderate range. So maybe six millimeters, maybe eight millimeters, because that kind of naturally lifts the shoe a little bit. So, for example, the shoe would be lifted because the heel would have some more rubber under it.

In a recent development, and at that point, you’re able to be at still a little bit of a forward lean, but that forward lean creates only a 90-degree angle, or maybe even a little bit less than a 90-degree angle. So it’s gonna put less strain on your Achilles.

Sources indicate that so that’s a personal preference thing. But I do think probably naturally some mild drop is probably best for most people.

When you’re buying shoes, the heel-to-toe drop would not be on my top three list of considerations.

I think that you’re mostly looking for just that out-of-the-box comfort, how well the sizing works for you, and the shape of that toe box.

That heel drop is probably pretty far down the list.

That was a lot of shoes and a lot of foot talk.

But hopefully at this point, you have a better sense of what you’re looking for when you’re selecting backpacking shoes for your next trip.

‘Not Your Daddy’s 22.’ This Is The Best 22 Creedmoor Ammo for Deer Hunting

  • Sources indicate that people get a lot of big feelings when you broach the subject of shooting big-game animals with .22-caliber rifles, so it’s vital to talk about what we mean, and what we don’t.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

In a recent development, latest cartridges like the 22 Creedmoor and 22 ARC have been developed alongside the modern practice of leveraging heavy-for-caliber bullets into better downrange performance and, as it turns out, the 22 Creedmoor is a stone-cold deer killer. There are still relatively limited factory ammo options compared to legacy cartridges, and if you’re looking for the best 22 Creedmoor ammo for deer specifically, there are a couple of key considerations. Here’s a look at five of the solid options we have tested for accuracy and velocity, using the bullets that have killed deer and other big game with. Being that Hornady brought the cartridge to SAAMI for standardization, they have the widest variety of factory ammo, but there are other good options too.

Sources indicate that people get a lot of big feelings when you broach the subject of shooting big-game animals with .22-caliber rifles, so it’s vital to talk about what we mean, and what we don’t. There have undoubtedly been thousands of deer killed with various varmint bullets and .22 rimfire cartridges with a wide variety of results.

That’s not what we’re talking about here.

As numerous insightful old timers discovered by loading cartridges like the .220 Swift, .22/250 Remington, and .223 Remington with more purposeful bullets — sometimes requiring tighter twist barrels — .22-caliber centerfires kill deer very effectively.

The 22 Creedmoor, with the same bullets and barrel length, will leave even the great Swift in the dust, and it’s specifically designed to work best with modern, long, high-BC bullets that maintain their speed and terminal effectiveness hundreds of yards beyond what traditional 40- to 60-grain .224 bullets could. These bullets are perfectly capable of delivering decisive penetration and trauma on any reasonable shot at a deer.

Sources indicate that there are a couple important things to consider when picking the best 22 Creedmoor ammo for deer. First is bullet weight and construction. There isn’t currently a plethora of 22 Creed factory ammo on the market, but it’s wise to avoid the varmint-specific loads. Many varmint bullets are designed specifically to be fragile. At some of the velocities you’ll see from these 22 Creed varmint loads, the volatile bullets can sometimes not penetrate well.

An example of this is Hornady’s 62-grain ELD-VT, launched with the 22 ARC in mind. According to Hornady their shooters, after killing hundreds of coyotes, noticed that they saw a higher percentage of them running after being hit when the 62-grain ELD-VT was used in the 22 CM than when it was launched slightly slower out of the ARC. The problem was remedied with a slightly heavier 69-grain slug. Deer aren’t exceptionally significant or dense animals, and there are other ammo options that will work well.

According to recent reports, the other consideration isn’t as straightforward, and is one significant drawback of the 22 Creedmoor. Its standardized twist rate of 1:8 accommodates those more fragile bullets at high velocities while generally stabilizing the heavy-for-caliber 80-plus-grain bullets — but not always. At low elevations and in cold weather, your bullets can lose stability, and your accuracy can go to hell completely.

According to recent reports, I first noticed this while shooting at about 28 degrees Fahrenheit and 1,000 feet of elevation. This barrel consistently printed 20-shot samples under an inch with the 80-grain ELD-X, but, beyond 600 yards, my bullets were dropping way more than they had been doing a few days prior when it was warmer. Later, at 0 degrees Fahrenheit, groups at 100 yards opened up to nearly 6 inches with the same bullets. I’ve documented this instability, which varies from barrel to barrel, in several guns now.

The takeaway is that if you are going to be hunting late season at low elevation in cold temperatures, either choose a bullet that will work reliably in a 1:8-twist barrel, or at least test your rifle and ammo in those conditions before hunting.

In a recent development, the 80-grain ELD-X is one of the best all-around .22-cal performers for larger game. This bullet follows the same general design as other ELD-X bullets, featuring a lead core and mechanical internal locking ring to control expansion. It has Hornady’s heat shield tip with DRVT for more consistent drag. This is one of the most efficient hunting-specific .22-cal bullets there is, with a BC that allows it to stay above 2,000 fps for over 600 yards in the 22 Creedmoor. The most unique characteristic to this bullet — compared to the ELD-X in other calibers — is that it has a proportionally thicker jacket. This was to ensure controlled expansion even at velocities over 3,000 fps.

This bullet has proven to penetrate well and do a lot of damage. I shot a whitetail buck with the 80-grain ELD-X loaded in a .223, which would have been the equivalent of about a 450-yard shot from the 22 Creed. It hit the buck, which was quartering to, through the front shoulder and exited halfway back the ribs on the opposite side. I’ve also executed a similar shot on a huge black bear from about 15 yards with a 22 ARC — leaving the bullet under the offside hide after about 18 inches of penetration.

This is an all-around performer in the 22 Creedmoor, but is more optimal in a 1:7-twist barrel. If you’re planning on using it in cold weather, you should test it beforehand.

According to recent reports, many hunters will intentionally steer clear of match ammunition and Hornady does not recommend this ammo for deer hunting. Sometimes folks try stuff without asking permission, however, and it ends up working pretty damned well. Now, seeing how well the 80-grain ELD-X works, I’m not compelled to choose the nearly identical ELD-M bullet over it. They have the same BC and often have nearly the same point of impact and velocity. But this load has crushed a lot of bucks and is a favorite of Derrick Ratliff of Horizon Firearms and one of the big players in bringing the 22 Creed to the commercial market.

In a recent development, the ELD-M bullet will generally be more fragile than the ELD-X, and it creates even more violent wound cavities. This doesn’t mean it explodes on shoulders and won’t penetrate — that’s not the case. But when seeing the holes it puts through deer, you may want to tone it down. There’s no harm if you choose a more rigidly constructed bullet, and you should always be thoughtful about the shots you do take by keeping your bullet construction in mind. Still, this ammo is out there killing bucks with authority.

If you need or want a monolithic copper bullet, this will likely be the only factory option you can find. It uses a 65-grain CX bullet, which is a comfortable 1:8-twist bullet. In testing, Hornady found the 70-grain CX — made for the 1:7-twist 22 ARC — doesn’t stabilize well. I was able to shoot a pronghorn with this bullet, handloaded for an 18-inch 22 Creedmoor, before factory ammo was available. The bullet passed through both shoulders and the buck was dead before he hit the ground.

If you’re a fan of shoulder-shooting deer, this is a bullet you will be very happy with. The CX is designed for high weight retention and won’t produce a wound as violent as the ELD-X or ELD-M, but it is a penetrating son-of-a-gun. The 65-grain CX has a lower BC than the 80-grain lead-core bullets, but has enough velocity to help it maintain a similar effective range. For most deer hunters choosing a 22 Creed, you’ll be hunting at distances where that lower BC won’t come into play.

We’ve been substantial fans of the Federal Fusion line for deer ammo because it’s affordable, shoots well, and delivers great terminal performance. Federal just announced this 22 Creedmoor deer ammo, but I saw the press release a few days after buying some in a local store, so it should be available for rifle seasons. This is probably the most affordable 22 Creed ammo that’s deer-appropriate, and it features the same plated jacket as other Fusion bullets.

I’ve gone through a couple boxes of this and the ammo shot pretty well. It averaged 3,100 fps from a 22-inch barrel, which would put it around 125 fps slower than box velocity of 3,300 fps in a 24-inch barrel. Velocities can vary depending on several factors, but it does track with a lot of factory 22 CM ammo in the 70-80-grain range which ranges from 3,050 to 3,200 fps from 20-inch barrels — the most common contemporary barrel length.

If maximizing efficiency is crucial to you, there are better bullets, but this should work comfortably at any temperature in a standard 1:8 twist barrel, and will deliver great performance for the needs of most deer hunters.

Industry observers note that another excellent option for deer would be Nosler’s 70-grain AccuBond offering. This is more of a legacy bullet — made for 1:9- or 1:8-twist barrels — that’s also loaded in .223, rather than one of the more optimized 22 Creedmoor options. I would love to see Nosler come out with a heavier, more efficient option that leverages the Creed’s case and chamber design and load this to a bit more competitive speeds. Still, this is a deadly and effective bullet at normal deer-hunting distances, and would be a good choice.

Industry observers note that modern bullets are what really make the 22 Creedmoor shine as a deer cartridge. We have options that are more efficient with more predictable performance than ever. If you want to hunt deer with a 22 Creedmoor, pick ammo that will fit how and where you hunt.

Read Next: Best Ammo for Deer Hunting, Tested for Accuracy.

Most people won’t have to worry about bullet stability with factory ammo, but it’s something you need to pay attention to at low elevation in temperatures below freezing. As with any hunting rifle and ammo, the most key factor is you. Pick a rifle and ammo you like and get out there and practice.

#9126. ‘It’s a Different Race of Deer Up There.’ A High-Country Mule Deer Hunt for the Ages

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3399 w)

‘It’s a Different Race of Deer Up There.’ A High-Country Mule Deer Hunt for the Ages

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3399 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “IT’S A DIFFERENT race of deer up there,” Tim Trefren mentioned as we pulled dusty saddles and sweaty blankets off our horses.
  • It has been revealed that the ridge is called the Greyback.
  • According to recent reports, whatever its derivation, the Greyback presides over gamey country in the Wyoming Range of western Wyoming.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“IT’S A DIFFERENT race of deer up there,” Tim Trefren mentioned as we pulled dusty saddles and sweaty blankets off our horses. Tim’s mount was a classy roan named Red. They called mine Propane Tank, both for his rotundity and for his habit of releasing an audible quantity of gas with nearly every step. “Up there” was a high ridge above the wall tents and lodgepole corral of Tim’s remote Wyoming hunting camp. We had just ridden down that steep ridge in the dark, our horses’ hooves throwing sparks every time their shoes nicked a rock in the trail. To me, in the dark atop a farting horse, the sparks looked like terrestrial versions of the shooting stars we had seen early that morning as we ascended the ridge, the Milky Way smeared across the sky.

It has been revealed that the ridge is called the Greyback. Geologists would tell you it’s the upthrust portion of a subduction zone, vertical evidence of one of the continent’s growth plates. I’d guess it got its name because the miles-long hogback is punctuated by rocky heights that make it look like a giant’s backbone. And because it separates the Greys River watershed from that of the Hoback River to the east.

According to recent reports, whatever its derivation, the Greyback presides over gamey country in the Wyoming Range of western Wyoming. Tim, owner of Trefren Outfitters, and I had hunted elk since daybreak in the timberline basins that slide off the eastern side of the ridge. We had been in elk all day, and had seen moose, black bears, and even bighorn sheep on the distant red-rock slopes of Hoback Peak. Looking north from the highest points of the ridge, we could see the jagged crest of Grand Teton hovering above the town of Jackson like a snowy fang. We hadn’t gotten a shot at a bull, but soon after we mounted our horses for the long switchback ride down the ridge, we spotted a heavy-antlered animal crossing the trail in front of us. In the weak light of evening, it looked like a bull elk.

Sources indicate that “That’s a helluva buck,” Tim whispered from the saddle, watching the mule deer disappear into the dark. “A helluva buck.”.

Now, at the corrals, brushing down the horses and hanging saddles in the tack tent, Tim talked about the deer.

“We used to see bucks like that pretty regularly, back in the ’50s and ’60s,” Tim remarked. “Some hunters called them mossbacks, but most around here called them greybacks. They were just bigger—maybe 50 percent larger in body size than your typical mule deer. And their antlers… Well, there were some mighty fine racks that came out of that country back there.” Tim waved his curry brush back up toward the ridge.

I knew some of that history. The one-time world-record mule deer hailed from the Hoback. Back in the 1920s, a hunter killed the wide-racked buck for meat and left the skull behind. The antlers were picked up and found their way to a succession of bars, ending up at the Jackson Hole Museum, where you can still admire their dimensions: 217 inches of bone, enough to remain in the record book as the third-largest typical mule deer buck of all time.

In a recent development, “This was all horse country back then,” Tim continued. “If you wanted to hunt the Hoback, you had to initiative to spend a week on your horse. Then the Jeeps started stabbing in, and the trails turned into roads. A guy in a chained-up Willy could hunt the Hoback in a couple days. Those massive deer started getting harder and harder to find, to the point I’d almost say they’re extinct.”.

Tim bucked his saddle on to its rack in the tack tent and spilled oats out of a Folgers can for the horses.

“Be something to turn up one of them greybacks.”.

In a recent development, that was six years ago, but I never forgot about that buck. I didn’t shoot a Hoback bull with Tim, but later that season I killed a cow in the tech giant of Tim’s son, also named Tim and called Junior around camp. In that season and over the next couple, I got to know the Trefrens and their main guide, Greg Kriese, like extended family. Tim Jr. kept inviting me to hunt with him, and I kept going—sometimes by myself, sometimes with friends—with a nonresident deer tag when I could draw one, with an elk tag when I couldn’t. Usually they gave me Propane Tank to ride.

In a recent development, my friendship with the clan grew so strong that I felt the blow when Tim Jr. called with the news. “Dad died last night. Funeral is in Thayne on Saturday. It would mean a lot to all of us if you could make it.”.

I can’t recall the obligation that kept me away from Thayne that day, but I still feel guilty that I wasn’t there to send off Tim Sr., his empty saddle cinched on Red, his body in a horse-drawn hearse driven down Main Street by his son.

Industry observers note that I also can’t recall what kept me from hunting with Tim Jr. and Greg that year, but I was determined to return to the Wyoming Range last fall. I had a preference point for a deer tag and had set aside a week in September for the Region H buck season. Then my friend Mike Stock called with a proposition. Mike is the centerfire ammunition product manager for Winchester, which has a longtime partnership with Browning. He had advised Browning on the development of a newly introduced line of ammunition. The iconic Buckmark would be imprinted on the cartridges’ headstamps. Mike is also one of my favorite hunting partners, and we try to get out in the field together at least once every season.

Let’s go deer hunting, Mike mentioned, and be the first hunters to use Browning’s newly introduced Buckmark ammo in the field. Where should we go?

The answer leapt from my lips: The Wyoming Range.

Industry observers note that that’s the abbreviated story of how Mike and I found ourselves pulling into the Trefrens’ wall-tent camp in late September, Browning rifles and ammo ready to go to work atop the Greyback. As I drove into camp, sun sifting through the lodgepole pine needles and little grey squirrels sprinting across the road, I felt a little like I was coming home. I wondered which horse I’d get dealt this year.

Sources indicate that mike hadn’t been a hard sell on Wyoming. There are other great places to hunt big mule deer—southern Utah, Colorado’s Western Slope, Arizona’s Kaibab Plateau, Oregon’s Blue Mountains, southeastern Idaho—but few with the history of the Wyoming Range.

I told Mike about my own background with the place—not only the monster buck I had spied with Tim Sr., but even before that, the pictures of heavy-racked, non-typical Greys River deer I had drooled over as a young Western hunter obsessed with massive mule deer.

The Wyoming Range is legendary among trophy mule deer hunters. Maybe it’s the reputation of the Hoback Buck, but for years the range was known for its high-­country muleys—tall, heavy, non-typical bucks that summered in the subalpine basins of wildflowers and jack pine and wintered in the sagebrush desert that stretches east toward the Wind River Range.

Sources indicate that then word started trading among deer hunters that the Wyoming Range’s reputation was slipping. The state is issuing too many hunting tags, remarked some. It’s the drought, said others. But there was one undeniable consistency: Too many deer were dying out on the winter range.

Over the past couple of decades, much of that high-basin sagebrush has been impaired by gas wells, service roads, and power lines. When habitat becomes fractured, long, hard winters can be catastrophic for mule deer, especially when they follow droughty summers that leave the animals in poor physical condition. Trophy mule deer need five or six years to reach maturity, and tough winters come around about once a decade. The math suggests that weather and winter-range energy production may have as much impact on the Wyoming Range’s mossbacks as Jeeps had.

After I explained this dynamic to Mike, I could tell he was deflated. We were here to hunt substantial mule deer, but I made it sound like he should shoot the first forkhorn he saw.

“Relax,” I stated as we settled into our canvas wall tent. “If any folks know significant deer, it’s Junior and Greg.” But silently, I was worried. I had hunted here for years and had never had a deer in my sights that I wanted to shoot.

Industry observers note that the camp’s daily ritual isn’t for night owls. Up at 4 a.m., breakfast in the cook tent, then in saddles by 5 and on the Greyback trail a couple of hours before light. The idea is to be in the high basins by sunup, glassing with binoculars for deer moving to their day beds. My horse this year: Hoback. Mike’s: Dickhead. Matt Nager, our photographer, rode Ugly Betty. Junior had to attend to work in town, so Greg, astride Red Ryder, guided us.

On our first morning on the ridge, Greg spotted a heavy-racked 4-point moving across a bowl, and it seemed a cinch to circle around the back side of the basin and shoot him when he walked into view on a game trail just below us. Only, after we waited a couple of hours, the buck never showed.

In a recent development, it’s like that in these high parks. What appears from a distance to be a featureless meadow is cut with gullies and fissures deep enough to funnel a deer out of danger.

So we hiked back to our horses and rode south in the midday heat, planning to eat lunch at the head of a series of basins that Greg stated might be productive. Lunch is a highlight of any hunt with the Trefrens. Two sandwiches with condiments, a couple bags of chips, candy bars and granola bars, little pudding cups. Fruit Jell-O. An assortment of hard candies. It’s any fourth-grader’s fantasy grab bag. And it was all mine, in the most handsome lunchroom a significant-game hunter could imagine.

In a recent development, as I settled against a fir trunk with my lunch bag, Greg pointed toward a strip of stunted pine that ran 1,000 yards away, from the middle of the steep basin toward the rim. “Keep an eye on that cover,” he said. “I guarantee there’s game in there.”.

The sun was hot and the sandwiches tranquilizing, and every 30 minutes or so, I roused myself out of a haze to glass the jack pines. In midafternoon, I heard Greg whisper from behind his spotting scope.

“I got something here.” An urgency in his voice made me sit up straight. He fiddled and focused the scope and let out a deep breath. “Holy hell. That’s a giant.” Just like that, my lunch lethargy was gone as Mike, Matt, and I fought for position behind the scope. I scrunched my eyes in the optic. The heat was throwing up a shimmer, so the animal bedded in the shade of the pines looked like a deer in a fever dream, swimming in and out of focus. But I could make out its blocky body, double throat patch, and tall antlers blonde as straw.

In a recent development, if you’ve ever seen a trophy animal at an impossible distance, then you know that two things happen. First, you can’t stop looking at him, sizing up his headgear and wondering just how you might actually kill him. Second, you get a little paralyzed. To sit there and stare is easy and without consequence. To actually make a move ruins the perfection of possibility. What if he sees us and bolts? Or what if we blow our stalk and run him out of the basin. Or what if he simply walks into the scrubby pines and out of our sight? For nearly an hour we admired him, shooting video on our cell phones through the spotter and debating his dimensions.

I knew we’d have to move to kill him. We were 925 yards away, with no way to get closer on a straight line. We’d have to drop off our little ridge, hike to the top of the basin, and either take a long shot from above or work down into the basin without busting him.

Sources indicate that I led the way, moving with purpose, with the others behind me. Here was possibly the largest mule deer I had ever seen in the flesh, and he was alarmingly aware. As we had watched him for that hour, he had gotten up from his bed three times. Every time he bedded back down, he situated himself so that he could scan the rim of the basin. Watching him, I realized here was a deer who knew the source of danger—the horse trail at the top of the ridge—and he knew how to avoid it, by staying in cover all day. The only place to spot him was from our lunch perch.

To kill him, we’d have to do everything right, so I made sure my profile was hidden by the ridge, that I didn’t knock an errant rock down the slope, and that I had a blueprint.

That initiative was to gain the rim of the bowl and then to range the buck. I reckoned we’d be about 600 yards out, a long shot with my .30/06 and 185-grain Browning bullets even if I wasn’t shooting at an extreme downhill angle. But maybe, just maybe, a solution would reveal itself from the rim.

Sources indicate that by the time we climbed to the top and assessed the situation from the rim of the basin, the sun was sinking low in the west. Worse, the buck was obscured by a little finger of rocks we hadn’t factored in from below. If I was going to kill this deer, I was going to have to enter his world: the steep, stony heart of the bowl.

Industry observers note that I’d have to go alone, leaving my crew behind at the top to watch the action. But I’d also need an assurance the deer was still in the pines. So Greg sent Mike back to the spot from where we had originally seen the buck. If he was still in sight, Mike would raise his arms like a football referee signaling a touchdown. If he wasn’t there, Mike would sweep his hands horizontally, as though signaling an incomplete pass.

According to recent reports, I dropped my pack and binocular, stuffed extra shells in my pockets, and pulled leather gloves on my hands. I felt like an Olympic mogul skier, about to drop into the run, so steep and gnarly was the terrain in front of me.

Industry observers note that I took a couple of steps downhill and immediately knocked loose a fist-sized rock. It tumbled, caught air, and then clattered down the bowl, sounding like a lawn chair thrown down a stairway. No deer would stand for a racket like that.

I took a couple more mincing steps on the slope, trying to keep my balance and retain my stealth. Another rock rolled. How would I ever get to that rise of rocks undetected? I steeled myself. I’d simply have to sprint and hope to intercept the deer. I started to stride, only it was a cartoon sprint, on a 60-degree slope, the ankle-turning cobble trying to spill me on my butt, and rocks careening into thin air. My beautiful high-country buck surely must be in Idaho by now.

Then something surreal and impossible happened. Mid-stride, hyper-aware of the cacophony I was causing, I heard a noise quite unlike clattering rock. It was sudden, shrieking, and sky-fillingly loud, and I immediately realized it would cover my noise. I pitched down the bowl, windmilling my arms, using my rifle as a counterweight to keep my feet, dead-set on making the outcrop.

I reached the rock just as the source of the noise—two fighter jets—screamed over the Greyback, low enough for me to see rivets in their wings. I have no idea whether their low-altitude run is a regular occurrence, only that their timing this evening was a godsend. Just as swiftly as they’d arrived, they were gone, and the high-mountain silence returned. I peered over the rock, and there was the line of pines 200 yards below me. But there was no buck in sight. I glassed through my riflescope, hoping to see an antler or an ear. Nothing. I was losing light fast, and felt a little surge of panic. Was the buck gone?

According to recent reports, I turned and looked back up at the rim at Greg. Four hundred yards above me, silhouetted by the glowing sky, I could see Greg’s sign, his hands high in the air. The buck was still there. I was stuck on my rock, unable to move without dislodging more scree. My only choice was to wait and hope the buck might rise from his bed while I still had enough light to shoot.

Read Next: Mule Deer Hunting Tips.

It has been revealed that I laid my leather gloves on the rough granite, and then the forend of my .30/06 X-Bolt on the gloves. I could only wait, and fret about the failing light.

It has been revealed that when I saw the deer, he was feeding uphill, most of his body obscured by pine branches, but I knew it was him by his blocky body and tallow-ivory antlers. With no clear shot, I had to wait excruciatingly long minutes, glassing through my riflescope, until he was clear of bullet-deflecting obstructions. He was quartering away at a distance I estimated at 260 yards, but my rest was literally rock-solid. In the echoey bowl, my rifle shot sounded louder than the jets.

In a recent development, I waited for Mike to reach my perch, and the two of us walked to the buck while Greg and Matt came with the packs. The deer had cartwheeled down the scree after the hit, and it was nearly dark when we reached him. Normally, I would have held his antlers first, but what took my breath away was his body size. He was as large as a spike bull, with immense hindquarters and a barrel chest. I was marveling at his physical dimensions when Mike started laughing. “He looks just like the Buckmark,” he mentioned, and I noticed that he did: The deep forks and long tines of the antlers might pass, in this flimsy light at least, for the iconic logo of the bullet I had just used to kill him.

When Greg and Matt arrived, we took photos and then started taking apart the deer. Our backpacks weren’t stout enough to haul all the meat, and it would take too long to hike out of the basin for the horses. So we quartered the buck and draped meat across the boughs of subalpine fir trees. I tied an orange vest to a tree and then urinated all around the little grove. This is lion and bear country, and I hoped the scent might deter scavengers until we could return in the morning with a pack horse.

Sources indicate that in the dark of a moonless night, the hike out of the basin was long and strenuous. We reached the horses at midnight. I can’t recall a more enjoyable ride than that one, my hands caked with deer blood, the only sounds the tick of horses’ hooves on rocks and the creak of tired leather. I’m pretty sure my smile could have been seen from the satellites that streaked overhead, little pinpoints of light arcing against the deep stars.

Sources indicate that I had killed my biggest mule deer, in one of my favorite hunting grounds, with a group of close friends. I could almost hear Tim Sr. ahead of me on Red. “Be something to turn up one of them greybacks…”.

This story was originally published in the September 2016 issue of Outdoor Life.

Tech Report: This Traditional Archer Tagged a Major 8-Pointer With a Longbow and Stone Point Arrowhead He Made Himself

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was the evening of October 25 when Joe McConnell, a traditional bowhunter from central Ohio, climbed into a ladder stand with a backdrop of heavy cover.
  • McConnell was hunting with a longbow in a narrow strip of woods that he owns.
  • “I was really after a nice 10-point buck I had on trail cameras,” McConnell tells Outdoor Life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was the evening of October 25 when Joe McConnell, a traditional bowhunter from central Ohio, climbed into a ladder stand with a backdrop of heavy cover.

McConnell was hunting with a longbow in a narrow strip of woods that he owns. The spot was overlooking a travel lane deer were using to enter a large field of standing corn.

“I was really after a nice 10-point buck I had on trail cameras,” McConnell tells Outdoor Life. “The wind was perfect that evening, blowing right in my face. I was looking forward to filling my first landowner tag with a deer on my own property.”.

It has been revealed that “I’d made a mock scrape in front of my stand, with a licking branch above it about 12 yards from my ladder,” says the 38-year-old archer. “I heard him in the corn about six rows in, and he came to check the scrape.

“I saw his rack above the standing corn field coming to me, and when he stopped broadside quartering away at 12 yards, I took my shot.”.

It has been revealed that the buck was not the 10-point he was after. Instead, it was a dandy 8-pointer that McConnell couldn’t pass up.

According to recent reports, mcConnell drew his 64-inch, 55-pound longbow he’d made from an Osage orange tree limb. Then, shooting instinctively, he released a 26-inch arrow he’d made of cane and fletched with white turkey feathers.

His arrow hit the buck perfectly behind the shoulder, the super-sharp stone broadhead he handmade drove deep into the deer’s chest.

Sources indicate that “I saw him race and tear through the corn field,” notes McConnell, who owns a hardwood flooring and restoration business. “I heard him crashing away through corn stalks, and then nothing.”.

The bowman found a good blood trail where the buck stood, and the trail was easy to follow through the corn.

Sources indicate that “He only went about 75 yards before falling dead,” he indicates. “My stone broadhead did an incredible job, driving through its liver, a lung, and smashing into a rib on the opposite side of the buck. The arrow point hit bone and stopped or it would have completely gone through the buck’s hide on the opposite side.

“Everything really came together for me with that deer. I’ve taken lots of animals with the bows and arrows I’ve made. But it’s the first deer I’ve taken with a stone broadhead that I knapped myself – and it was devastating.”.

Recent findings suggest that mcConnell has taken plenty of deer and wild hogs with traditional archery gear he’s made. He also shot a buffalo with his traditional equipment, and a stone point head he’d made specifically for the hunt.

It has been revealed that he called some friends who helped get his big 8-point buck out of the field. The field-dressed buck weighed 180 pounds at the processor. It had an estimated live weight of well over 200 pounds.

He will eventually have the deer scored via Buckmasters, and his taxidermist estimated the rack to be about 140 inches.

Read Next: Killing a Grizzly the Old-Fashioned Way: With a Longbow and a Stone-Point Arrowhead.

Sources indicate that mcConnell models his canted bow shooting style after legendary archer Howard Hill. He leans forward when drawing his bow, anchors his arrow at the corner of his mouth, and uses his bare hand holding his bow as an arrow rest.

Sources indicate that “I got started in archery when I was only 14,” McConnell states. “It’s been a lot of fun learning about making bows, arrows, and now stone broadheads. Traditional equipment is remarkably efficient bowhunting gear.”.
