Traveling 290 Miles on Foot in 4 Days? John Kelly Sets Upcoming Benton Mackaye Trail FKT

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (642 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ultrarunner John Kelly, 42, set an unsupported and overall Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the Benton Mackaye Trail last month, completing the 288-mile route through the southern Appalachians in 4 days, 5 hours, and 48 minutes.
  • When he completed the trek on October 22nd, Kelly became the fastest person ever to complete the Benton Mackaye Trail (BMT), even besting the supported speed record of 4 days, 21 hours, and 25 minutes set by Tara Dower in 2022.
  • He also beat the previous unsupported speed record set by Bob Stewart in May of this year (5 days, 5 hours, and 21 minutes) by more than 24 hours.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ultrarunner John Kelly, 42, set an unsupported and overall Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the Benton Mackaye Trail last month, completing the 288-mile route through the southern Appalachians in 4 days, 5 hours, and 48 minutes. “Unsupported” means Kelly carried all his own food and gear for the entire journey and received no outside help. His pack weighed 27 pounds on day one, with roughly 50% of the weight coming from food.

When he completed the trek on October 22nd, Kelly became the fastest person ever to complete the Benton Mackaye Trail (BMT), even besting the supported speed record of 4 days, 21 hours, and 25 minutes set by Tara Dower in 2022. Supported records are normally faster than unsupported ones because athletes can carry less weight and benefit from support crews.

He also beat the previous unsupported speed record set by Bob Stewart in May of this year (5 days, 5 hours, and 21 minutes) by more than 24 hours.

Recent findings suggest that the BMT starts at Springer Mountain, Georgia and ends at Significant Creek in Great Smoky Mountains National Park. According to Kelly’s own tracking data, he climbed nearly 63,000 feet, burned 38,000 calories, and slept for just 6 and a half hours total in his four-plus days on trail.

Kelly’s trip report indicated that he only committed to the BMT attempt one month ahead of time and told no one except his wife, his coach, and Bob Stewart, who held the unsupported FKT at that time. (“He was so genuinely kind, helpful, and thrilled to see someone getting out on this trail,” Kelly wrote of Stewart’s reaction when Kelly told him he was coming for his record.).

It has been revealed that he started the trek on October 18 and finished on October 22 but didn’t publicize his tracking data and trip report until eight days later. “I considered keeping this quiet. You know, just go for a hike like most people do. But I knew this would also be one of the best ways I could continue my AT fundraiser for Western Youth Network, supporting kids in western North Carolina,” he wrote. He has raised $15,000 for the nonprofit and is matching donations 100%.

Kelly has previously set FKTs on trails including the UK’s Pennine Way and Vermont’s Long Trail. He is also one of only a few dozen athletes ever to complete the infamous Barkley Marathons and one of only three to complete the course more than once (he finished in 2017, 2023, and 2024).

In his BMT trip report, Kelly described experiencing auditory hallucinations on the way down from the final summit, running out of food with 5 hours to go in the trek, visualizing a large meal at Cookout to keep himself going, and regretting not packing more Nerds gummy clusters.

Recent findings suggest that kelly credited his wife, the crews who maintain the trail, and fellow athletes like Bob Stewart with making his record possible. “Even unsupported,” he wrote, “it’s not really solo.”.

#9120. Tips for Hunting Mature Bucks Over Bait (Plus the Ethics of If You Should)

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1314 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Tips for Hunting Mature Bucks Over Bait (Plus the Ethics of If You Should)

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1314 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that during the 2023 deer season, I shot my biggest buck ever: a Kentucky main-frame 12-pointer with a couple extra points that scored 168 6/8 inches.
  • Industry observers note that and as I write this, I can hear blood boiling and I can see the angry comments coming.
  • In a recent development, the National Deer Association published an article explaining how baiting deer can spread disease: “By design, baiting and supplemental feeding concentrate deer and other wildlife species for the purposes of hunting, trapping, viewing, or simply increasing nutrition available to the animals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that during the 2023 deer season, I shot my biggest buck ever: a Kentucky main-frame 12-pointer with a couple extra points that scored 168 6/8 inches. And I shot that substantial sum-buck over a yellow pile of ear and persimmon-flavored shelled corn. I even dropped a protein block in the middle and seasoned it with scent for good measure.

Industry observers note that and as I write this, I can hear blood boiling and I can see the angry comments coming. Hunting whitetails over bait is still a controversial topic across much of deer country. It is, of course, illegal in many states in the Midwest, Northeast, and West. And even in places where baiting is legal, some argue that hunters should avoid using it.

In a recent development, the National Deer Association published an article explaining how baiting deer can spread disease: “By design, baiting and supplemental feeding concentrate deer and other wildlife species for the purposes of hunting, trapping, viewing, or simply increasing nutrition available to the animals. Some argue baiting and feeding have positive attributes, but no one can disagree they have numerous negative implications to a deer herd, including altering animal behavior, degrading the habitat near bait and feed sites, increasing the susceptibility to predation, and greatly enhancing the opportunity for disease transmission.”.

According to recent reports, the NDA’s formal position on baiting deer is this: “The NDA opposes the expansion of baiting where not at the moment legal. The NDA will not work to repeal baiting where currently legal, except where CWD (or other known diseases) is present. The NDA supports the use of baiting by wildlife professionals conducting scientific research. The NDA supports continued research on the effects on baiting in deer management programs.”.

Recent findings suggest that baiting is legal and very popular in many Southern states. All hell broke loose when Kansas regulators began discussing the potential of banning deer baiting. Hunting deer in Texas is synonymous with hunting over a feeder. But still, many folks don’t understand how big bucks relate to bait piles.

Two comments I always hear when the bait debate pops up go something like: “Oh, you bait, bro? Must be easy killing those major bucks.” Or, “Bait won’t kill big, mature bucks, Jack.”.

I scoff at both of those statements. Neither are true, and it’s far easier to screw up on a mature buck with a poor baiting strategy than it is to fill a tag with one. Like other tactics, baiting is just another tool in the arsenal. It isn’t a cheat code.

Sources indicate that I know because I’ve been baiting Kentucky whitetails most of my hunting career, and it took a long time before I started experiencing success on mature deer. Here is how to bait deer and, more specifically, how to bait a monster buck—plus some considerations if you’re on the fence about legal baiting.

The early season is my favorite time to bait a monster buck. Hunting pressure is low. There’s plenty of cover for concealment. Deer are on predictable bed-to-feed lines of movement. There’s no better time to catch a buck off-guard over a bait pile.

Target warm-season bedding areas, such as north-facing slopes or low-lying areas near water that offer a high stem count. Then, determine what destination food source deer are targeting, such as green soybeans, fresh-cut corn, or dropping white oak acorns. Place the bait between the bedroom and dinner table.

Industry observers note that don’t overlook the pre-rut. This is a great time to bait a monster buck. Bucks are moving more but aren’t running wild just yet. So, capitalize on that buck’s rising testosterone levels. Often that leads to increased daylight travel.

In a recent development, as with the early season, it’s still all about bed-to-feed patterns. But now, deer are likely settling into their fall bedding areas and food sources. So, find these locations (which vary greatly by region and habitat type) and plant bait stations along lines of travel.

Once the rut hits, you might get a buck to hit a bait pile. But most of the time, a rutting buck is more interested in scent-checking does that have been through the buffet line. Because of this, bait stations are still effective during the rut, but you must hunt them differently.

Recent findings suggest that usually, I prefer to place bait piles on the downwind sides of doe bedding areas. Or locate the bait between two doe bedding areas. Bucks like to travel these locations anyway, so it’s a no-brainer game plan.

Once the rut is over, and the late season arrives, it’s all about the food again. But still, focus on late-season bedding areas. Think solar bedding (south-facing slopes) and thermal cover (dense stands of coniferous trees). Also, consider what deer are eating now, including remaining waste grain, green plots, remaining acorns, but most importantly, woody browse.

Recent findings suggest that once again, the best bet is placing bait piles between bedding areas and destination food sources. Use these as staging areas to intercept bucks during daylight. At this point, they aren’t likely to reach destination food sources before dark. But if your bait site is located close enough to bedding, they might hit that corn pile during legal shooting hours.

Read Next: 35 Deer Hunting Tips to Read Before This Season.

Recent findings suggest that no matter the time of year, there are certain tactics that apply to virtually every baiting scenario. Of course, you have to locate a big buck before bait will help you. No volume of bait will bring in a monster buck if he doesn’t already live there. But once you’ve got a big buck located, follow these tips.

Sources indicate that some people say deer hunting over bait isn’t ethical. But here’s the thing: Some hunting ethics are situational. I’m not talking about taking poor shots or breaking hunting laws. Those ethics are clearly black and white.

In a recent development, for me, baiting deer is more of a gray area. First off, if it’s legal, it’s legal. When analyzing the differences of state-to-state guidelines on baiting, you’ll see regional discrepancies just like you will with crossbow regulations, the use of deer urine lures, and season structures. So if your area allows baiting, then it’s likely that agency wildlife managers for that area have decided baiting is not detrimental to the deer and deer hunting.

Second, it’s key to realize that it’s not like you can just throw out bait at any random spot in the woods and start shooting trophy bucks. It’s far from a canned hunt. If you live in an area that permits baiting, understand that bait has several different applications. Where legal, it can be used to help you attract deer, hold deer, feed supplemental nutrition, take inventory of deer, and more.

In a recent development, as for effectiveness, people commonly say bait stations are either fool-proof or that they turn bucks nocturnal. In my experience, neither are true.

Whitetails are smart, especially around bait piles. They learn to approach bait piles downwind and they pick up on hunters’ scent in the area. Yes, they will often hit bait at night. But no buck is 100 percent nocturnal—that’s a myth.

It has been revealed that if you suddenly start seeing a target buck avoiding bait during daylight, it’s likely because you screwed up and disrupted that deer. Or, he started bedding elsewhere. Or, he started targeting a different destination food source. Or, maybe he’s just being a wild, unpredictable deer.

The point is, hunting over bait is still deer hunting. Anything can happen, and most of the time the significant buck wins. But if you understand how to bait deer and you execute a well-crafted game plan, then baiting just might lead to the biggest whitetail of your life.

#9116. These Popular Bass Fishing Myths Were Debunked Decades Ago

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3184 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

These Popular Bass Fishing Myths Were Debunked Decades Ago

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3184 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Missed him,” I said and groaned as I reeled in a slack line.
  • Sources indicate that “Rerig and toss it back in there,” Ralph Manns directed me.
  • Recent findings suggest that manns was right.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Missed him,” I said and groaned as I reeled in a slack line. Setting the hook after I had felt a gentle tap had produced nothing but a mangled plastic worm.

Sources indicate that “Rerig and toss it back in there,” Ralph Manns directed me. “Another one might hit it.”.

Recent findings suggest that manns was right. The next time I set the hook I was rewarded with a pleasantly bowed rod. After a short fight, a five-pound largemouth bass thrashed in the landing net.

“Now, you get one,” I said and grinned as my bass splashed in the live well.

Sources indicate that manns complied with a cast that dropped his worm beside the same rotted stump. The line twitched, the rod arched and he promptly landed a twin to the first bass. Not a bad start for our first look at Texas’ Lake Livingston—especially after my traumatic and almost sleepless night.

Industry observers note that it had begun innocently enough with my arrival at Livingston’s Penwaugh Marina the previous evening for a meeting of the Texas Outdoor Writers Association. Luck of the draw had placed me in the same room with fisheries biologist Ralph Manns, a pleasant mild-mannered gentleman I was meeting for the first time. I had no idea that our meeting would alter the course of my fishing life.

It has been revealed that an insatiable appetite for more facts about bass behavior had prompted Manns to become a full-time student at Southwest Texas State University after retiring from active duty in the Air Force where he had spent 20 years as an intelligence officer and a political scientist. At the time of his retirement he was a lieutenant colonel.

En route to a masters of science degree in aquatic biology, which he earned in 1981, Manns conducted a study of black bass in Lake Travis in 1977 and 1978. The study team used electronic transmitter tags and receivers to track 14 bass while divers recorded the behavior of another 935 bass. Manns’ team also used angling techniques to obtain detailed reports on an additional 289 bass. Data on more than 20 different types of behavior and the environmental conditions that might influence the fish were fed into a computer to compile and analyze the results.

Industry observers note that manns’ exhaustive studies of scientific literature on bass and his extensive two-year study have led to rather innovative and sometimes controversial conclusions. During my first few hours with him, he crumbled the foundation of my bass fishing knowledge with solid scientific evidence that contradicted many generally accepted fishing theories.

Sources indicate that those first two bass we caught from Lake Livingston, for example, were taken from classic bass structure—a stump on the upper edge of a submerged creek bed. The bass probably had not migrated from the depths, however, to feed in the shallower water as a popular myth would have us believe.

The hypothesis that bass live in deep water, migrate to shallow water on a daily basis to feed and then return to deep water along established migration routes is generally credited to Buck Perry, the gentleman rightfully recognized as the father of structure fishing. His methods of catching bass have been so successful that other anglers and writers have perpetuated his migration theories.

It has been revealed that ralph Manns agreed that such structures are good places in which to fish but the analytically minded biologist could find no scientific literature to substantiate a deep-water migration theory. Manns wanted a better explanation for the appearance of bass at certain underwater structure.

“Sure enough,” Manns related, “our tracking studies verified data available in at least 15 other studies that revealed the predominant movements of black bass are parallel to the shorelines and contour lines and not perpendicular to them. The movement, moreover, usually is at a nearly constant depth.”.

A national magazine recently published a story entitled “When the Sun is High, the Bass Go Deep”. The author surmised that because more bass are caught in deep water during midday hours, bass obviously migrate from shallow to deep water as the sun brightens. And that’s how myths get started.

Manns’ study of Lake Travis bass showed no such tendency.

“Our research showed some bass at shallow depths, some at medium depths and some in deep water at all times,” he revealed. “And they tended to remain at that particular depth whether active or inactive. Bass do move vertically but not routinely. A deep fish might pop to the surface to run through a school of shad, but it will grab two or three and almost immediately dive to its original depth because that’s where it has established its equilibrium and can suspend without effort.”.

A bass can hover effortlessly at a particular depth because its air bladder is balanced at that depth and it gets out of balance if it varies much from that point. According to Manns, it takes hours for the air bladder to adjust to a major depth change. The more out of balance a bass gets, the harder it has to swim to maintain its stability.

It has been revealed that manns noted that black bass usually move along contour lines for only short distances and tend to stop at any bisecting lines of structure that obstruct their movement, such as a fence, stump or rock. By casting to a fence, an angler increases his odds simply because moving bass are likely to pause there.

According to recent reports, most anglers will catch more bass, Manns maintained, if they fish on the better bisecting structures for several minutes during activity periods. Additional schools often stop at the same structure long enough for the anglers to catch more fish.

Industry observers note that some fishermen consider schools of black bass a rarity. Limit catches might be rare but, according to Manns’ underwater observations, most bass are in either a school or an aggregation.

“There are almost no loner bass,” Manns says. “The few single fish we observed underwater were either very sick, very large or totally inactive. The sick ones obviously couldn’t keep up and the larger bass were probably unable to find compatible partners in their size range.

“Rule one,” he continued, “if you catch a bass, assume it is not alone. As a minimum, it is in a group of two to five fish. Actively striking bass are usually feeding and moving bass. They tighten up their aggregations and move in small schools.”.

During activity periods, of course, almost anyone can catch bass by tossing an edible-looking lure in the path of a feeding school. It’s the inactive periods that separate expert from novice bass fishermen.

According to recent reports, “Fishermen should remember that bass are inactive most of the time, even if their stomachs are empty,” Manns claimed. “Unlike humans who have a predictable three square meals a day, a bass may be forced to exist for days without eating. That little bit of minnow it ate three days ago must last the bass a long time and it does not waste it!”.

Sources indicate that the fact that a fish is inactive doesn’t mean that it won’t eat, Manns admitted. If something passes closely and in front of a bass’ mouth, it will usually eat because bass are opportunists. But an inactive bass probably won’t move more than a few inches to hit a lure. An angler who is fishing a spot that holds inactive bass may have to cast 15 or more times before the lure passes through that tiny strike zone in front of an inactive bass.

In a recent development, A fast-moving crankbait offers good odds of getting a lure to an active bass. Because active fish may chase lures for 10 feet or more, each cast effectively covers a wide path on each side of the bait’s track. The same lure retrieved past inactive bass, however, may pass by many fish without eliciting a strike.

Recent findings suggest that the success of an angler’s technique, then, depends on how active the bass are. Anglers who cast and crank at wide intervals over inactive bass will usually get few strikes. Fishermen who flip worms or jigs to the base of cover objects where inactive bass may hold, however, get close enough to take a few fish. If the same anglers continue to flip slow lures while bass are in an active state, though, they cannot hope to hook as many as those with fast lures. Thus, an angler must match his lure and his technique to the activity level of the bass.

Sources indicate that one widely accepted myth claims that bass avoid sunlight because they have no eyelids. Manns’ underwater observations indicate otherwise.

In a recent development, “It was clear to us that bass have no requirement to live in shade,” Manns declared. “Moving bass were as likely to stop at a sunny spot as a shaded one. Although bass have no eyelids, their eyes have pigment mechanisms that compensate for excessive light. Water is an excellent light filter, too. Unless a bass is in very shallow, calm and clear water, the water serves it well as a pair of sunglasses.”.

It has been revealed that bass that anglers catch from beneath piers, boat houses and docks are probably there for cover or food rather than for shade. In fact, even slightly colored water refracts sunlight sufficiently to destroy any distinct shade line within a few feet. Even in moderately clear lakes, bass down more than 10 feet experience little or no shading from objects at the surface.

This means that bass a fisherman finds beneath floating structures will probably hold tightly to the bottom of the structure—unless, of course, there are other attractive structural elements on the bottom. Lures retrieved just beneath floating structures, then, will probably be more effective than lures retrieved along the bottom.

Sources indicate that although bass do not need to avoid sunlight, Manns’ records indicate that more bass are caught from shaded areas than from sunny ones. He stressed that this statistic is not contradictory because inactive bass may suspend in either shade or in sunny open water. But for an angler to cast his lure near enough to inactive bass to make them strike, he usually must find bass that are suspended close to an identifiable target. While the target creates shade, the shade itself is incidental and not the reason the bass are there.

Another concern of bass anglers is that bass will move when they hear noise coming from above them. Manns’ study, however, clearly demonstrated that bass learn to ignore any sounds that don’t represent a threat. Bass frequently swam beneath docks where workers were pounding with hammers or sailors were stomping in boats. Bass also ignored outboard motor noises in Lake Travis, which is heavily used by recreational boaters. Surprisingly, however, some of the lake’s bass had learned to move away from boats with electric fishing motors and it was difficult to approach such bass unless they were pushed against cover objects.

Industry observers note that manns suggests that a great myth of angling literature is that bass seek out preferred temperatures, water clarity, structure and so on. He stressed that the part of a bass’ brain that processes every piece of visual or physical information is about the size of a thumbnail. A bass simply does not have the ability to be intuitive.

According to recent reports, “A bass will not run across a lake to an area that has a better temperature level,” Manns claimed, “because it doesn’t know it’s there. Now if a bass is wandering around and finds a more comfortable area, it might think, ‘Wow! Isn’t this temperature nice?’ And if it can stay there without getting hungry, it may hang around long enough for the angler with a temperature meter to catch it.”.

In Manns’ study, bass did not move to deeper water to avoid surface temperatures in the 84° to 88° range. In fact, when all other factors were equal, black bass (including smallmouths) preferred the water temperature to be between 78° and 86°, not the 72° that is popularized in most fishing literature. Manns’ findings are corroborated by at least 20 other scientific studies published during a 40-year period. Bass found in cooler water are there because of a better food supply or because they are unable to compete with larger predators present in warmer water.

In a recent development, manns admits that there are optimum chemical environments for bass but in most lakes the fish must be satisfied with less. They merely move into someplace tolerable, adapt to it and once they’ve adapted to that condition, any change is a negative change to those fish.

In a recent development, “Most people don’t realize that a bass is constantly adapting to its environment,” Manns declared. “The chemistry of its body adapts to temperature and water conditions and, if any factors change, the fish is temporarily out of balance. When cold fronts go through, for example, sudden drops in temperature disturb the fish’s equilibrium and it becomes slightly sick until it adapts to the new condition. That helps explain why bass normally don’t bite as well after a cold front.”.

A common dream of anglers is catching bass on almost every cast from a “hotspot” where hungry largemouths eagerly await the next cast. The nearest thing I ever found to that fabled “hotspot” was on Lake Sam Rayburn back in 1968. My partner and I found a timbered flat near a river channel where every cast with our crankbaits hooked a chunky bass. We tied the boat line to a limb and promptly caught 60 largemouth bass from an area no larger than the average living room. In that era of 15-bass limits it was the first chance I had to cull bass to improve a stringer.

Sources indicate that our hopes for a repeat performance the next day were short lived. Our first few casts hooked bass, but the action ceased and we never relocated the bass. Nor did any of our friends ever find fish there on many subsequent trips. Manns offered an explanation for the phenomenon.

“They were probably transient bass, which is a major cause of confusion to anglers. Bass are generally thought of as having one type of behavior pattern. Actually, though, there are two types of black bass: transient bass and home-range bass. The concept is an old one that indicates up in scientific literature as far back as 30 years ago.”.

In a recent development, manns theorized that the fish’s health or its ability to catch prey determines whether it is a home-range or transient bass. Healthy fish establish territories and hold them, moving as little as possible. They conserve energy by feeding quickly and remain in the same general location unless there is a major change in water conditions or the food supply.

Large bass populations or shortages of prey create competition for food, however. Those bass that feed less efficiently must feed longer and move often to find forage. A transient is one because it is a loser.

There are many transient bass in our better bass lakes and they almost always school. An angler who finds such a concentration can catch great numbers of them at one time but he should not necessarily label the area as a great fishing hole. Such catches can be the result of chance meetings with transients.

Manns says that an angler should not spend much time returning to the site of a major catch unless he has reason to believe, such as repeated success, that the place is a home-range area. An angler can more consistently catch bass by returning to locations where he has taken one or two fish over and over again. Those are probably spots that have enough food to hold home-range fish day after day.

Manns stressed that bass reactions vary according to how hungry they are. A very hungry fish will probably strike at any lure it can get in its mouth. A bass that has been feeding on shad for 20 minutes, however, will probably only take something that is similar to the shad.

Although bass can see colors, anglers should remember that bass do not perceive them as a human would. Manns recalled a day when he and his partner followed a large school of bass feeding heavily on shad. The two cast all of the traditional shad-color lures without a strike. As soon as Manns put on a gold lure, though, he caught fish on almost every cast.

Industry observers note that the bass obviously responded to some flash of gold from the shad caused, perhaps, by the angle of sunlight. The bass had enough color discrimination that they triggered to the tiny variation. Manns, therefore, suggests that anglers who are unsuccessful in catching obviously active bass should change lure colors, sizes and actions until they find one that triggers the fish. Bass are not ambush predators as are halibut, angler fish and sculpin; nor are they chase predators such as tuna or striped bass. A black bass is a compromise fish designed to do a lot of things—none of them perfectly but all of them well. The bass is a seeker with a short sprint. It enters cover for protection and to rest, not to ambush prey. Cover actually limits and hinders a bass’ ability to strike and that is why prey fish hide in such areas.

Recent findings suggest that the standard hunting pattern of a bass is to move around structure objects to see if anything strays far enough from cover to become vulnerable. It assesses its ability to catch individuals of prey and strikes only at those it thinks can be caught. The bass ignores prey that are likely to dodge and thus escape. A bass will ignore a lure that looks like a healthy bluegill just as it would ignore a real bluegill under the same circumstances.

Industry observers note that “Bass fishing is very mathematical, very predictable,” Manns claimed. “It is a problem to be solved. Most of the false concepts arise because writers intellectualize about bass. The reaction mechanism of bass is actually very very basic: a reaction to a stimulus and a response, nothing more.

Read Next: Old-School Tips for Catching Substantial Bass Right Now.

“A bass can’t outsmart you. All you have to do is find something that will stimulate it, put it where it will stimulate it and you will catch a bass. There’s really nothing more to fishing than that.”.

Manns makes it sound simple and it looks simple enough when you watch him in action. He merely works the odds, covering as much favorable water as possible with a wide variety of lures. But he seems to catch many more bass than the average fisherman. The years he spent in their living quarters are paying off.

This story was originally published in the November 1983 glitch of Outdoor Life.

#9114. ‘8 Different Hunters Had Been After It.’ Giant Nontypical Buck Taken in Indiana

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (854 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

‘8 Different Hunters Had Been After It.’ Giant Nontypical Buck Taken in Indiana

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (854 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Joe Merritt, age 41, of Middletown, Indiana had some target bucks he was after the first week of November during the state archery deer season.
  • “On Tuesday, November 3 I got a trail camera photo of a huge buck sent to my cell phone from a very small woodlot that was my least favorite place I had to hunt,” Merritt tells Outdoor Life (he did the interview after just spending a morning hunting rabbits with his beagles).
  • The next day the same cell phone camera got photos of the buck again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Joe Merritt, age 41, of Middletown, Indiana had some target bucks he was after the first week of November during the state archery deer season. This is the first year he had cell cameras out to monitor multiple areas, and they proved to be a critical tool for taking the buck of a lifetime.

“On Tuesday, November 3 I got a trail camera photo of a huge buck sent to my cell phone from a very small woodlot that was my least favorite place I had to hunt,” Merritt tells Outdoor Life (he did the interview after just spending a morning hunting rabbits with his beagles). “The photos were of a huge buck that I’d never seen anywhere before.”.

The next day the same cell phone camera got photos of the buck again. And the next morning, Nov. 5 at 3:55 a.m. he got photos of the huge buck again from the same camera in the same small wooded area.

It has been revealed that “I knew I had to go after that buck right then,” notes Merritt, who owns a coffee distribution company. “I left immediately and was in my saddle hanging from a  thin tree well before dawn.”.

Merritt listened to deer in the woods around him long before daybreak. He wanted to be in his stand early to not disturb deer. He believes the spot was a bedding area near a sanctuary of private property where no hunting is allowed.

As an overcast dawn broke, he had a small 8-point buck come by his stand. Almost an hour later a doe revealed.

Sources indicate that “She kept looking behind her as she moved my way,” says Merritt. “She kept coming to me and flopped down and bedded just 35 yards away. The whole time she was looking back, and I was a little puzzled until the giant buck I had on camera highlighted up.”.

But the giant buck moved toward the doe and bedded down near her, just 37 yards away.

“That’s when the chess game began,” states Merritt, who is also a dedicated houndsman who’s pursued raccoons and bears with dogs. “I was hanging from a very small diameter tree, and both deer were bedded close, and there was no chance for a bow shot while they were lying down.”.

Merritt sat in his stand, quiet and still, for four hours before the doe finally got restless, stood, and walked toward Merritt. She was feeding on browse as she moved his way.

Recent findings suggest that “That’s when the buck stood up, and started following her,” Merritt notes. “The doe was right underneath me watching back at the buck when he turned and gave me a full broadside shot at 22 yards.”.

Merritt made a perfect shot on the biggest deer of his life.

“I saw him running and blood was blowing out everywhere,” noted the bowhunter. “I didn’t see or hear him fall. But I knew the shot was perfect and the buck would be easy to find.”.

The doe was still feeding under his stand after Merritt shot and the buck ran.

Sources indicate that “I just broke down in the stand, shaking and talking to myself about what just happened,” he notes. “It took about 10 minutes for me to de-escalate and comprehend what had just happened.”.

Then he climbed down to the ground and walked to where he’d last seen the buck. He walked right to the downed animal that was only 60 yards from where his arrow had struck it.

It has been revealed that “I walked up to him and placed my hands on his rack and thanked the Lord for what had just happened,” states Merritt. “Then I phoned my wife and friends.”.

Shortly, his close pal Jared Leppink joined Merritt in the woods and the two of them loaded the buck into an UTV. Then they shot photos of it, dressed the deer, and caped it.

While the buck has a massive rack, Merritt mentioned the deer only weighed about 200 pounds – not a significant animal for east-central Indiana, which regularly gives up 250 to 300-pound whitetails.

According to recent reports, “I don’t think the buck was that old,” Merritt notes. “The teeth were not very worn. I think he was between 3.5 to 5.5 years old.”.

When pictures of his buck hit social media it created a wave of folks contacting him.

Sources indicate that read Next: Indiana Is Now the Top Trophy Whitetail State. Here’s Why.

In a recent development, “I had to turn off my phone for 24 hours,” he says. “About eight different hunters had been after that buck and showed me photos of it. Some had shed horns from the buck from prior years. We figured I shot my buck 12 miles away from one hunter who thanked me for shooting the deer.

It has been revealed that “I asked him why he was thanking me. He remarked, ‘Well now I know you got him, and I don’t have to keep passing other good bucks waiting for the 23-pointer to show up.’”.

#9111. The Gun Industry Is Divided Over Federal’s Upcoming High-Pressure 6.5 Creedmoor Ammo. Here’s Why

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3301 w)

The Gun Industry Is Divided Over Federal’s Upcoming High-Pressure 6.5 Creedmoor Ammo. Here’s Why

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3301 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Late last month Bergara became the first gun manufacturer to explicitly state Federal’s 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak ammo is not approved for use in its bolt-action rifles.
  • The 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak, introduced this summer, has the same dimensions as a traditional brass 6.5 Creedmoor cartridge and was specifically designed by Federal Ammunition for use in existing 6.5 Creed rifles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Late last month Bergara became the first gun manufacturer to explicitly state Federal’s 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak ammo is not approved for use in its bolt-action rifles. This reverses earlier guidance that the new high-pressure cartridge technology was compatible with Bergara’s existing 6.5 Creedmoor rifles.

The 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak, introduced this summer, has the same dimensions as a traditional brass 6.5 Creedmoor cartridge and was specifically designed by Federal Ammunition for use in existing 6.5 Creed rifles. It is not a fresh cartridge, but an improvement to an existing cartridge. This unusual dynamic is part of the regulatory and potential liability concerns right now vexing the gun industry.

Federal’s proprietary steel-alloy case technology contains higher pressures that drive bullets at faster speeds for better performance. Plus Peak operates at 80,000 psi, compared to about 62,000 to 65,000 psi for brass 6.5 Creed cartridges. This is possible because the Peak Alloy case material that Federal has developed is much stronger than brass. It acts as a containment vessel insulating the action and barrel from the extra pressure without inflicting extra stress on the rifle.

Related: They Built a Rifle Cartridge That Could Change Hunting and Shooting Forever.

In a recent development, the ammunition has undergone substantial testing by Federal, a dozen gunmakers and component companies, the U.S. military (which has ordered 40 million cases), and other industry professionals.

According to recent reports, and indeed, Bergara rifles were originally deemed “compatible” with this 6.5 Creed Plus Peak ammo, according to previous guidance from Federal and media coverage of the ammo’s launch in June. But on Oct. 29 Bergara announced that the upcoming ammunition “is NOT approved for use in any Bergara rifle chambered in 6.5 Creedmoor.”.

The reason Bergara cites is spec-based:.

“These cartridge pressures haven’t been evaluated under SAAMI’s standard development process,” reads the statement, referring to the Sporting Arms and Ammunition Manufacturing Institute. “Ammunition operating outside SAAMI pressure standards for its caliber should not be used in any rifle unless Bergara formally confirms compatibility for that model.”.

Industry observers note that SAAMI sets the gun industry’s self-imposed guardrails with voluntary performance standards for firearms, ammunition, and suppressors. Bergara did not cite any incidents of catastrophic failures or injury related to shooting the newly introduced case technology through its rifles. (No one we spoke to for this story reported being aware of a catastrophic failure while testing the Plus Peak in existing 6.5 Creed rifles.).

Recent findings suggest that bergara confirmed in 2025 it would launch rifles in 7mm Backcountry, which debuted the same high-pressure cartridge technology as the Plus Peak. Various online distributors and retailers indicate Bergara’s HMR Pro and MG Lite models would be available in the 7BC, but the organization doesn’t currently offer any rifles chambered in 7BC on its website. It’s unclear if any preproduction or production models were ever manufactured. Bergara declined to comment for this story.

In a June statement, SAAMI acknowledged the development of the 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak and the creation of a working group — at Federal’s request — to evaluate the new case technology on “performance, pressure, testing, and interchangeability standards.”.

SAAMI and its member companies are also discussing “the technical challenges and opportunities presented by advanced cartridge case technologies and their interaction with existing firearms and suppressors.”.

The organization stopped short of taking a position on the ammunition and instead urged hunters and shooters to contact their rifle’s manufacturer before shooting Federal’s 6.5 Creed Plus Peak.

It has been revealed that “At this time, SAAMI’s guidance stays the same,” SAAMI’s senior director of technical affairs, Alan Serven, tells Outdoor Life. “As this is not a standardized cartridge, we can’t really say anything definitive about it, so we are directing folks to the manufacturer of their firearm. And we do caution that an answer from one manufacturer cannot be interpreted as a blanket statement … It’s on a case-by-case basis with each of the manufacturers and potentially down to model.”.

According to recent reports, on Nov. 5 the sporting-goods retailer Scheels sent an internal memo to its employees announcing any Plus Peak ammo should not be stocked on store floors or made available to customers.

“As of yesterday morning we have added a ‘DNS’ Do not Stock rating to all SKUs of Federal 6.5 Creedmoor +Peak ammunition,” reads the memo, obtained by Outdoor Life. “The Kinetic Group [Federal’s parent firm], gun manufacturers and SAAMI are continuing to review this product. Once we have more information on their review and the stocking of the 6.5 Creedmoor +Peak, we will make a determination on how to proceed.”.

Scheels has put all direct orders for Plus Peak on hold, according to the memo. The retailer also instructed its ammo and gun teams to accept any returns from customers and put any received Plus Peak “somewhere where we can ensure it will not make its way to the floor to be sold.” When Outdoor Life called a Scheels store asking about Plus Peak availability and the possibility of ordering any, the employee who answered the phone replied that no, this was not possible because “corporate put the kibosh on this until SAAMI figures out the safety and pressure complications.” The store policy affects all five SKUs of Plus Peak.

“Federal’s Peak Alloy case technology is the wave of the future for rifle ammunition,” Kinetic Group’s VP of marketing Jason Nash tells Outdoor Life, noting that Federal sought to work with as many rifle makers as possible in its development of high-pressure loads. “Over the past seven years Federal has manufactured millions of rounds in multiple cartridges and firearms. Federal has the utmost confidence in this new technology and its function in today’s firearms.”.

In a recent development, some gunmakers have confirmed to OL that all their existing 6.5 Creedmoor rifles are compatible with Plus Peak and they have no safety concerns whatsoever. Others have remained quiet on the advisability of using Plus Peak in their 6.5 Creedmoor rifles. Bergara remains the only rifle maker who has publicly disallowed its use in its bolt-action rifles. (Break-action rifles from CVA, Bergara’s sister company, are also not approved for Plus Peak, according to Federal’s site.).

In a recent development, this about-face on the use of Plus Peak in Bergara rifles raises many more questions than it answers. For instance, is this hesitancy around the 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak rooted in legitimate concerns of consumer safety? Or is it ultimately driven by the potential threat that some companies see to their bottom lines? Here’s what to know.

In a recent development, although the conversations around Plus Peak in SAAMI’s working group are confidential, industry insiders are keyed into the crux of the issue. Here are two of the primary camps.

According to recent reports, no one seems to be disputing the performance gains of the Plus Peak ammo. Instead, the debate is over how to standardize it.

According to recent reports, “It definitely is an interesting idea what Federal is doing,” indicates one gun manufacturer who spoke on the condition of anonymity. “The industry itself is not politicking against it. The industry is not against new technology. We know and understand new products are what drive business. That’s not the glitch. There’s probably some ammunition companies that are bitter or angry they didn’t think of it first, but that’s also neither here nor there.”.

It has been revealed that according to this source, the problem is the fresh technology right now puts too much onus on gunmakers without the opportunity to earn revenue. In fact, it poses a big expense for bigger manufacturers.

“For those of us who played by the rules and built guns to SAAMI’s standards, now we have an ammunition out there that’s outside that spec. And we’re at a conundrum to say, ‘Is it safe or not safe in our guns,’” notes the gunmaker. “So one [option is] we have to go back and retest all our guns at an immense cost to verify those guns will pass these pressures.”.

Sources indicate that some guns will inevitably pass, they say, but other guns may not. This could result in a laundry list of liability concerns in which gun companies must painstakingly note — online and in owners manuals — which rifle models are compatible and incompatible with Plus Peak.

The biggest fear is that a customer will get hurt. It’s also a bad look for any existing guns that don’t pass, given that it “may expose ‘weaknesses’ that don’t exist” in rifles that were built to spec for standard 6.5 Creed loads.

Another option for gunmakers is to simply not retest guns and not comment on (or in Bergara’s case, publicly come out against) the 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak.

“It does kind of stand in the face of why we have SAAMI and why we self regulate,” notes the source. “So it’s a legitimate concern. We won’t approve [Plus Peak] either. Will our guns pass it? Most likely. But we’re not chomping at the bit to go through all the testing to verify that. We have other things we need to worry about.”.

The right way to have handled this upcoming ammo technology, in this gunmaker’s mind, was to have rolled out a new cartridge that could have more easily received SAAMI approval and allowed gunmakers to collaborate on new rifle builds.

Recent findings suggest that “We would have all happily engaged in a new caliber that did this, like the 7 Backcountry. We knew the pressures, and we could build a gun specifically to handle that caliber with those higher pressures. No problem. It’s the retro-fitting for everybody. Why should we go to a pile of work? Just build a new caliber. It’s a very cool technology. We’re all about that. We’re not dragging our feet because we’re old and crotchety. We’re trying to protect our business and this industry.”.

Industry observers note that in that scenario this ammunition wouldn’t be a 6.5 Creedmoor using Plus Peak technology — it would be a whole upcoming cartridge called, for instance, the 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak. Of course, this would require shooters to buy a new rifle.

“The difference is meaningful,” says Outdoor Life shooting editor John Snow of this hypothetical scenario. “And presumably, you’d have to have firearms marked with that newly introduced cartridge name in order to be in compliance with what SAAMI has deemed acceptable.”.

In a recent development, federal has treated the 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak not as a upcoming cartridge, but an improvement on existing 6.5 Creed ammo. The difference, again, is that it contains higher-than-SAAMI-approved pressures that drive bullets at higher velocities.

These souped-up loads give hunters and shooters the ability to get 6.5 PRC-like performance out of their existing 6.5 Creedmoor rifles.

To some, the nature of Plus Peak is so monumental that industry disruption is natural and even necessary.

According to recent reports, “We are embracing high-pressure technology like Peak Alloy,” claims Sean Murphy, director of sales and marketing for Proof Research (and an occasional OL contributor). “It’s a development similar to switching from black to smokeless powder.”.

In a recent development, some of the more nimble gunmakers, like Proof, have already tackled the testing they need to feel comfortable about giving customers approval to run the higher-pressure load in its guns. That’s because Proof predicts this high-pressure ammunition is going to be a major player in the future, and the company is working to develop barrel and rifle technology to complement it by maximizing accuracy and performance.

In a recent development, “Proof Research has extensively tested Federal Peak Alloy cases in multiple cartridges, including 6.5 Creedmoor and 7 Backcountry,” notes Murphy. “In 6.5 Creedmoor alone, thousands of rounds have been fired through hunting, target, and semi-automatic precision rifles with no case failures or firearm damage. Additionally, many thousands of rounds have been fired by Proof with Peak Alloy 5.56 ammunition, also without glitch … Chamber-bore obstruction testing across every Proof Research receiver design indicated Peak Alloy cases outperforming equivalent brass cases, with a greater safety margin at 80,000 psi than brass cases at 60,000 psi.”.

The Montana-based rifle maker is also one of the most advanced barrel makers in the country. It spent years developing its PXT barrel, which Proof says accomodates much higher pressures and velocities without shortening the barrel’s lifespan.

“During our PXT barrel testing and development, more than 10,000 rounds of 7 Backcountry were fired — including 5,000 and 3,500 on individual receivers — with no damage, and wear levels comparable to brass-cased ammunition,” says Murphy.

The company also issued an apparent rebuttal to Bergara’s announcement of Oct. 29 with posts to Instagram and Facebook that same day, declaring full support and formal endorsement of Peak Alloy cartridges in its rifles.

“We have tested all our rifles — and many from other manufacturers — extensively with the Plus Peak ammunition and it’s proven to be completely safe,” says Murphy.

As part of its development and testing of the Plus Peak, Federal worked with a dozen gunmakers and related businesses. Federal confirmed to American Rifleman this summer that certain rifles from five of those companies are compatible with Plus Peak: Christensen Arms, Weatherby, Seekins Precision, Geissele, and Nemo Arms. Federal matches guidance from SAAMI that hunters and shooters should contact their gunmaker to specify which models are approved.

“Our testing has shown 6.5 Creedmoor +Peak operates in a variety of 6.5 Creedmoor firearm platforms,” Federal advises in the Plus Peak guide on its website. “Refer to your rifle manufacturer for recommendations on compatibility with high-pressure ammunition.”.

Christensen Arms echoes similar language on its website. However, all existing Christensen Arms rifles chambered in 6.5 Creedmoor are compatible with the Plus Peak ammo, a spokesperson confirmed to Outdoor Life. The additional seven brands who worked with Federal include Area 419, Forster Products, Proof Research, Pure Precision, Hill Country Rifles, Short Action Customs, and Springfield Armory.

SAAMI has good cause to be extra cautious, points out Snow, since it’s a voluntary organization. The gun industry has regulated itself for a century — the result of a handshake deal with the government after World War I — and would like to continue avoiding federal oversight “like that of the auto industry,” claims Snow.

But one reason gunmakers may come out against Plus Peak in their rifles has nothing to do with safety, cost, or liability.

“It’s possible that companies could see poor accuracy with the Plus Peak ammo and not recommend it,” states another industry insider, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity. “High chamber pressures, especially with some barrels and rifling designs, can cause accuracy problems that aren’t safety problems.”.

Federal has patented its high-pressure cartridge technology, which means other ammunition makers can’t leverage it without paying for the privilege.

“There are rival companies that would arguably like to see this newly introduced and innovative technology put into a box and shoved off to the side,” says Snow. “Because they don’t have the ability to capitalize on this trend currently, and it’s potentially bad for their business if Plus Peak succeeds.”.

The Peak Alloy case technology used in the 6.5 Creed Plus Peak was pioneered in the relatively fresh 7mm Backcountry, which debuted in January 2025 and was rooted in development of high-pressure ammunition for the military.

When the 7mm Backcountry was introduced, we tested more of it than anyone (besides Federal’s engineers) by shooting every SKU and running it in a dozen rifles. Although the 7BC delivered on its promise of velocity and produced accuracy equivalent to factory ammo in other cartridges, we encountered one major problem with almost every rifle. After 40 to 120 rounds, the 7BC rifles developed very stiff primary and secondary extraction. It turned out this was a common concern for other testers and shooters, too.

In a recent development, this issue, ultimately, was rooted in the case dimensions of the cartridge — not poorly cut chambers, as some people have speculated. After receiving updated 7BC ammo and testing the fresh batches in rifles that were previously showing these issues, we’ve found that the extraction issues have been resolved.

Those initial extraction problems in the 7BC were — erroneously — interpreted as effects of the increased pressure of the cartridge on the guns themselves. That doesn’t appear to be the case. In reality, most rifles chambered in 7mm Backcountry aren’t constructed differently from similar models designed for brass-cased cartridges like the 6.5 Creed.

So in other words, concerns over pressure issues from the latest cartridge materials from the 7mm Backcountry to the 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak appear largely unfounded.

It has been revealed that the 7 Backcountry was accepted by SAAMI without the current speed bumps, in part, because it’s an entirely upcoming cartridge. It required brand-new guns manufactured specifically for the cartridge. Gunmakers could either opt to produce a gun chambered in 7BC — or not. Federal’s choice to offer the Plus Peak in an existing cartridge was a different route, but a calculated one.

“The reason Federal went with the 6.5 Creedmoor is because the 6.5 Creed was introduced in 2007 and is only available in modern firearms that are of recent vintage,” claims Snow. “So it is extraordinarily unlikely, I would almost say impossible, that we would see, for example, a Plus Peak .308 or .223 offered commercially. That’s because there are way too many actions and rifles of older vintages that cannot be vouched for.”.

Serven could not provide a timeline on when SAAMI’s Plus Peak working group might disclose its findings.

According to recent reports, “Our primary mission is safety, so we are proceeding with that in mind. That concern is the overriding factor,” claims Serven. “So we are not in a hurry. The priority is that we get the right answer, not a fast answer.”.

SAAMI’s acceptance of newly introduced cartridges standardizes the case and load across ammo makers. The organization’s blessing is not required for the sale and use of ammunition, and many niches of the hunting, shooting, and military world operate outside the bounds of SAAMI approval. This includes everyone from brands like Buffalo Bore Ammunition to wildcat cartridge developers to the federal government itself. It also means you can still get your hands on 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak.

Federal at the moment offers the Terminal Ascent Plus Peak for sale on its site at a limit of two boxes per customer. The four other loads are “currently unavailable.” Plenty of YouTubers have been able to get their hands on the ammo, and none we’ve seen have reported safety issues.

“The stakes are pretty consequential,” says Snow of how SAAMI decides to handle the Plus Peak ammo. “On the one hand, are we going to move with less friction and resistance into the era of high-pressure, high-performance cartridges? Or are there going to be speed bumps and other impediments put in place that effectively throttle or discourage the adoption of this fresh technology?”.

Recent findings suggest that read Next: I Shot the First Elk With the Newly introduced 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak Ammo. It’s an Undeniable Elk Hunting Cartridge.

According to recent reports, the push to adopt high-pressure rounds has come from the U.S. military, which has mandated it to maintain an advantage over “near peer” adversaries (such as Russia and China) on the battlefield. The military wants rifles capable of defeating newer body armor, and the way to do that is to drive bullets from existing guns at greater speeds.

“The government has been crystal clear about what they want and expect,” notes Snow, “which is that high-pressure cartridges are happening and need to be here sooner rather than later.”.

#9108. Industry News: A Bowhunt for Caribou Along Alaska’s Famed Haul Road Is Even Tougher Than It Sounds

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2817 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: A Bowhunt for Caribou Along Alaska’s Famed Haul Road Is Even Tougher Than It Sounds

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I picked my way through the rocks along the edge of the half-frozen creek, knowing that any minute I would intersect trails beaten into the snow by thousands of caribou hooves.
  • Recent findings suggest that the hundreds of caribou that we had tried to ambush were now moving away.
  • All we could do was look for another group of caribou to stalk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We had to be getting close. I picked my way through the rocks along the edge of the half-frozen creek, knowing that any minute I would intersect trails beaten into the snow by thousands of caribou hooves. But could we make it in time? We couldn’t see the trails as we hurried alongside the steep cut bank, although I knew they had to be right here somewhere. I climbed up a few feet to peek over the bank, only to see a hundred caribou about 50 yards away. They saw me too. The stalk was blown.

Recent findings suggest that the hundreds of caribou that we had tried to ambush were now moving away. Though we could hear the grunting, snorting, and occasional clash of antlers just over the hill, they might as well have been a mile away. They flowed like water over the tundra.

All we could do was look for another group of caribou to stalk. Luckily this shouldn’t be much of a problem, as thousands of caribou were migrating through this snowy stretch of rolling hills and wide valleys at the northern edge of the Brooks Range, within the largest bowhunting-only area on the continent.

Recent findings suggest that the Dalton Highway, or “Haul Road” as it is commonly referred to, could be considered an irreconcilable dichotomy. It’s where ambitious industry and true wilderness meet—and coexist. The 414-mile industrial road was constructed in 1974 to facilitate building the Trans-Alaska Pipeline and service the new oilfields in Prudhoe Bay. It provides the vital link that allows oil to flow all the way to the Port of Valdez to this day.

Although its primary function is still to service the pipeline and oil fields, the Haul Road was opened to the public in 1980 and has provided and created access to millions of acres of public land. The Dalton Highway Corridor Management Area extends five miles on either side of the road and stretches about 370 miles from the Yukon River north to Prudhoe Bay, in which only bowhunting for major game is allowed.

“This is going to be a long drive,” I told my dad and our videographer Tanner Denton as we loaded up our gear with the snow still falling.

With about 500 miles to go and six inches of wet snow on the ground, we had a challenging drive ahead. The Haul Road is not only the most remote highway in the U.S., but it also has a reputation for tough driving conditions. It’s been featured on highlights like Ice Road Truckers, and most rental vehicle contracts explicitly forbid driving on it. Even travel guides suggest bringing not one, but two newly introduced spare tires. For decades, the road was all gravel, and although some sections are now paved, much of the pavement is honestly worse than the gravel. On the drive, you’ll encounter huge potholes, frost heaves, rocks slung into your windshield from passing significant rigs, and a unique silty sludge that will coat your entire vehicle. It was early October, and we knew that wet, muddy, and icy conditions were going to be a fact of life.

Despite the relatively easy access, popularity, and long seasons, I hadn’t ever really given an honest effort to a Haul Road hunt. I’m usually distracted by sheep and moose hunting, and aside from sneaking away on days off while working in Prudhoe Bay a couple times, the last time I had made the drive was in 2009 with my dad. So it was fitting that Dad was coming along with me on this trip.

According to recent reports, even so, this was anything but a slam dunk. As migrators, caribou are where they are, and you find them when you find them.

Industry observers note that we hit the road shortly after first light. By the time the sun began to set, we were looking at more than a thousand caribou scattered across the barren hillsides in the northern foothills of the Brooks Range. With the temperature dropping quickly, it was time to set up camp, string our bows, and heat the wood stove. As we discussed our plan for the following morning, we hoped that the caribou tracks that littered the fresh snow around our camp were a good sign. I had been told by folks who are much more experienced than I, that this time of year, the herds of caribou will overnight up in the hills, then begin moving down in mid-morning. It looked like we were in a good position.

The next morning, we began gearing up as the coffee percolator thumped on the small wood stove. We periodically peeked outside the tent, looking for any major movement in the herds of caribou.

In a recent development, our basic strategy was simple and dictated almost entirely by the terrain and the nature of the caribou. In herds of hundreds or more, on completely barren tundra, it would be all but impossible to sneak close enough for a shot with our recurves. When caribou did pass by terrain features that might allow a stalk, the herds were almost constantly moving. At a feeding, strolling pace, it would be impossible for us to keep up or gain ground on them to get into position. Instead, this hunt had to be an ambush. We had to take advantage of any terrain feature we could hide in, and let the caribou come to us.

Industry observers note that “They’re pointed this direction,” I stated as I stuck my head out of the tent. “I think we need to get moving.”.

A herd of caribou was on its feet and moving on a low ridgeline about a mile away, angling for a ravine a few hundred yards from camp. Before we had much time to react, caribou began popping up onto the ridge on the other side of the creek, having already crossed. We had missed our opportunity.

“I think they’re going to drop down to the bottom eventually, so let’s work around and try to find a way to get in front of them,” I mentioned.

We promptly hooked to our left, just above the base of the hills that the herd was moving along. They didn’t seem to be in a hurry. I don’t often think of caribou as an especially vocal animal, so it’s always surprising to hear their bellowing and snorting. As we crested the top of the hill which had been covered in caribou minutes earlier, we saw the last animals of the herd cresting over another skyline, headed farther back into the mountains. The barnyard-like scent of caribou hung in the air as we walked back.

When I saw the trails converge into one spot crossing the ravine above camp, I knew that this place had everything we needed for an ambush. The caribou had to cross a hilltop, then drop down a tall, steep bank, then cross two different channels before climbing out on a single trail that exited the other side. We would be able to see the next herd coming from camp, then promptly move into position to intercept them.

Sources indicate that back at camp, the percolator hadn’t even started boiling when another herd came over the far ridgeline, headed right for that creek. We threw on our backpacks and grabbed our bows, the herd moving closer with every precious second. The animals were coming from the north and I wanted to be on the south edge of the ravine. We would be able to hide and have plenty of time to see bulls coming and get ready. I didn’t cross the creek soon enough though, and it quickly turned to deep pools covered by unstable ice. Crossing now was too risky, so we continued moving upstream against the steep bank. Just as we had almost reached the trail that the caribou were headed toward, I looked over that cut bank and spookedthe entire herd. It was so close. If we had been just one or two minutes earlier, the outcome might have been different.

It has been revealed that by that evening, the herds of caribou had abandoned their ridgetop route and began congregating in and moving through the valley below our camp. After rushing back and forth all day, we jumped in the truck and moved to a spot where we could see the entire valley. As evening began to fall, a big herd that had spent the day in the relative safety of the wide-open and flat valley began to move. Like spilled water trickling off a tabletop, a stream of caribou began to pull from the immense herd. In minutes, the line of caribou stretched as far as we could see into the mountains, crossing the creek just downhill of our camp. We tried one last time to slip into a gap in the herd, but that didn’t work either.

The next morning, we made the short drive from camp to where the road crested a nearby hill, giving us a good vantage of the whole valley. We could see hundreds (if not thousands) of caribou scattered across the foothills in the distance. They were beginning to move down to the valley floor. One cow would make the decision to go, followed by a single-file line of animals until the whole herd vanished. It was apparent that the whole mess of them was going to cross the road in a spot with virtually no cover and a howling 20 mph wind. To complicate matters, two other truckloads of hunters who were camped nearby were already positioning to try and have a crack at the approaching herd. We decided to wait where we were.

It was possible that some caribou could cross the creek we had been hunting, either above or below camp—we just needed to know which way they’d go.

In a recent development, as the caribou flowed across the road, we swiftly turned around, parked the truck, and began walking down the creek to intercept them. They were crossing the gulley in a shallow, flat spot, several hundred yards from the edge of any brush. We managed to slip into a sizeable gap in the herd and were frantically trying to find a position to hide and wait, when my dad (who was kneeling right next to me) whispered, “There’s antlers right there, about 30 yards!”.

If there’s one thing that’s a dead giveaway that a bull caribou is coming, it’s his set of tall antlers. If there’s any terrain between you, you’ll see his antlers long before he can see you.

According to recent reports, if there’s one thing that’s a dead giveaway that a bull caribou is coming, it’s his set of tall antlers. If there’s any terrain between you, you’ll see his antlers long before he can see you. And at that moment, there were antlers sticking up above the small embankment—very close. We were in a bad spot though. I nocked an arrow, but Dad had to move away from me slightly. When he did that, the caribou spotted us and spooked, circling wide and crossing the shallow depression.

Industry observers note that we cautiously stood and, not seeing any more caribou, tried to find a better position. Soon we spotted more antlers over a softly rolling rise in the tundra. Down on my knees, arrow nocked, I knew they were going to cross too far from us. In good conditions, 40 yards was pushing my reasonable limit with my recurve, but with a 20-mph wind, it was out of the question. One herd crossed at 75 yards, then another at 60, and then the herd fizzled out. After repositioning again and waiting, we decided to grab a cup of coffee and regroup. Each time we were getting closer, and we knew that something had to break our way sooner or later.

Before a much-needed lunch, I opted to drive back up to our vantage point and make sure nothing else was coming. Almost as soon as we got there, Dad and I saw yet another massive herd. This group was on a trajectory that would take them near the line of tall brush that lined much of the creek, and we might have a place to hide. Again, we parked and hurried, walking through the brush as rapidly as we could.

“We’re not going to make it in time,” I mentioned, frustrated by our constant race against the clock.

Industry observers note that I could see the backs of the caribou through the brush as they made their way across the open flat. They were just too fast, and we came to the end of the brush just as they started crossing the creek about 120 yards away.

It has been revealed that “Why don’t you just try sneaking up there by yourself,” my dad noted. “Three guys are too many, but one might be able to slip in there.”.

Recent findings suggest that it was worth a shot. Between us and the herd, the wash that the creek flowed through was about 3 to 4 feet deep, with a little bit of rolling terrain that might obscure the caribou that were coming. After a hundred or so had crossed, I began rapidly, but carefully, moving down the draw. Eventually, some of the caribou that had already crossed began to see me, but kept on their way. I was still obscured from most of the animals that hadn’t yet crossed. I was skeptical about my chances, but after a small group saw me at about 60 yards, flared, and crossed farther down, a gap in the herd appeared. With antlers just coming into view, I quickly covered the remaining distance and dropped to my knees. I hid next to a small bush, arms-length from the main trail the herd had created. I watched the antlers, which looked to be following the group I had just bumped. There was nothing I could do but wait. I quickly ranged a rock in the cut bank across the winding trails in front of me. It was 30 yards away. I told myself I wouldn’t shoot at anything beyond that.

Sources indicate that seeing the rest of the herd safely across the creek must have calmed the caribou, because they swiftly turned back toward me. All I could think as they closed the distance was: Don’t make eye contact.

It has been revealed that exposed, but holding absolutely still with my head tilted down, the cow that was leading the group came closer, followed by a nice bull. At under 10 yards I could hear her sniffing the air, even over the whipping wind. The bull was beyond her. As if I didn’t even exist, the cow walked past me, only paces away. My eyes shifted to the bull who was quartering to me, then to the rock I had ranged. He was only about 20-25 yards I figured, so I drew my bow.

According to recent reports, I was in a state of calm disbelief. Somehow I accepted that, aside from the timing and placement of my arrow, the situation was totally out of my control. I expected the bull to come out of his skin as soon as I moved, but he didn’t even notice me until I hit full draw. His head turned toward me at some point, but I only remember checking off my shot process. Anchor, good alignment, aim, expand—and the arrow disappeared into the bull. I wanted to hit him through the meat of the front shoulder to fully catch both lungs, but my arrow went a little high and left. The bull crossed the creek in a sprint then turned back. I stood to watch him as he ran about 150 yards back to meet the confused herd. The second the bull stopped running, another big bull ran up, hooked his antlers, and threw my bull on the ground, thrashing him as if my bull owed him money.

After the herd moved off, I walked up to my bull, still in disbelief. This beautiful white-caped bull at my feet was the true embodiment of the Arctic. As a hunter, I always experience a sense of thankfulness and relief when I can finally put my hands on an animal that I’ve hunted, and I felt that with this bull.

Industry observers note that but more than the thankfulness for possession, of meat, hide, antlers, there was something that I haven’t experienced so strongly in a long time. It was a raw appreciation of that moment, that every hunter feels right when it works out. The feeling transcends space and time and connects the hunter to the feeling of the arrow being released. That experience is a true gift that will last long after all the meat is gone.

#9106. How to Use a Stalker Decoy for Taking Bucks at Close Range

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1387 w)
