General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

How to Use a Stalker Decoy for Taking Bucks at Close Range

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1387 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that four long years were spent eating tag soup during my annual archery trip to the prairie in search of whitetail and mule deer.
  • It has been revealed that that’s when I came across the Ultimate Predator Stalker Decoy.
  • It has been revealed that ​While that sounds fine and dandy as a brief overview, I’d be lying if I noted it’s been easy to fill those tags.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that four long years were spent eating tag soup during my annual archery trip to the prairie in search of whitetail and mule deer. In the vast flatland, stalking with nothing more than ankle-high grass as cover proved to be more of a fool’s errand than a difficult hunting strategy. Getting to 100 yards was easy, but closing the final 50 to 60 yards was nearly impossible. Eventually, I had reached a point where enough was enough, and I began searching for a tool to help me close the distance.

It has been revealed that that’s when I came across the Ultimate Predator Stalker Decoy. This bow-mounted decoy attaches easily and is just realistic enough to trick a rutted-up buck in the middle of November. Since I began using the decoy on my annual trip, I’ve tagged out every year.

It has been revealed that ​While that sounds fine and dandy as a brief overview, I’d be lying if I noted it’s been easy to fill those tags. On rare occasions, the decoy helps finish the stalk for me and puts an unwary whitetail right in my lap. Most of the time, however, my stalks end the same way they did before I had the decoy, with the deer spooking and running into the next county.

On those adrenaline-pumping occasions that it works, it’s worth the countless heartbreaks leading up to that moment. Over the years, I’ve learned a few rules that can’t be broken if you want to be successful. Below are the five rules for reaping whitetail deer that you need to know.

According to recent reports, just like stalking in deep ravines or picking out a treestand location, factoring in the wind and thermals is a necessity when reaping whitetail deer. In my experience, there’s not a single product on the market that you can apply or wear that will beat a deer’s sense of smell when they’re directly downwind. Since you’re reaping from the ground, there’s nothing you can do other than to approach from an angle where your wind and thermals won’t be a factor.

In a recent development, when reaping deer, they’ll usually try to circle downwind. This is a natural movement pattern that is hardwired and unbreakable. Knowing this, you have to use the terrain and landmark features, like a thick treeline or fence row, to your advantage.

Recent findings suggest that once a buck locks on to you, it’s not going to want to lose sight of you when approaching. If you can get near a fence row that is perpendicular to the wind direction and in range, you’re increasing your odds of getting a shot off.

Industry observers note that aside from the wind, which applies to all forms of deer hunting, this rule is the most important rule of them all. If you’re trying to reap a deer in the big woods of the Northeast, or the prairie out West, a buck in lockdown is going to be the most willing to march your way.

It has been revealed that when a buck is in lockdown with a doe in estrus, he’s arguably at the peak of his aggression towards other bucks. In the multiple days of lockdown, it’s likely that he will fend off multiple different bucks trying to gain access to the doe. This natural instinct works in your favor when reaping.​.

Sources indicate that if you’re able to approach a lockdown buck with the wind in your favor, he’ll likely be willing to close the distance for you. That’s not always a guarantee, as factors like the doe running off or the buck not feeling aggressive in that moment may come into play, but lockdown is the scenario I crave when reaping whitetail deer.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve reaped spring gobblers, you’ve likely heard of popping the bubble. In essence, the bubble is an imaginary line in the landscape that you need to cross with your decoy to invade the bucks’ privacy. If you pop up 500 yards away on the skyline, he’s likely to pay you no mind, or simply retreat over the next ridge and play it safe.

Recent findings suggest that but if you use the terrain to your advantage and close the gap to 80 yards and then appear with the wind in your favor, your odds of triggering an aggressive reaction go up in a hurry. This is even more important in a lockdown scenario. Getting in close to the buck and doe prior to being seen and then popping out almost in bow range can force a rutting buck to pick a fight over flight just based on his instincts kicking in.

According to recent reports, in a lockdown scenario, your biggest threat of getting busted while reaping is always the doe. Unlike her male counterpart, she doesn’t have insanely high doses of testosterone that make her more susceptible to letting her guard down. Typically, she’s always on high alert.

Sources indicate that that means your approach with the decoy has to be very well thought out. Rather than just bullrushing in and trying to pop the bubble by any means necessary, a more subtle approach is to pop the bubble in a way where only the buck can see you. In most cases, the buck will bed within 15 to 20 yards of the doe. In the best-case scenario, this leaves you with a tight window to approach with the wind in your favor and pop the bubble without being visible to the doe. It’s not always possible, but I’m referring to the ideal setup here.

By approaching the buck and leaving the doe oblivious to your presence, you’re much more likely to elicit an aggressive reaction from the buck without the doe spooking and taking him with her. In the end, you must remember that no matter how realistic your decoy looks, the buck cares more about the doe than you and will skip out on a fight to stick with his doe without a moment’s notice.

It has been revealed that this final rule has been the difference maker for me on three of my four successful reapings. Whether you’re using a grunt tube to create low tending or loud challenging grunts, snort wheezing to elicit a reaction, or even just stomping the ground once you’ve popped the bubble, it’s pivotal that you act like a buck when reaping.

Recent findings suggest that A challenging buck doesn’t just meander in a straight line and walk right up to a lockdown buck and doe. They stomp, they grunt, and they slowly circle in preparation for a fight. Watch any video of bucks fighting, and pay close attention to the moments before the fight. Their body posture and positioning can cue you in on minute details to replicate when reaping.

Industry observers note that ​I’ve found most success in a stomp and snort wheeze combination. This typically convinces the buck that I’m there to challenge him for his doe, and that’s when he bristles up, pins his ears back, and begins marching in my direction. Once I see those telltale signs, my focus switches to my rangefinder and release.

This tactic isn’t very popular or mainstream. That’s for good reason. The success rate is admittedly low. For every successful reaping, there are 20 to 30 unsuccessful approaches in the rearview mirror. You have to be willing to fail time and time again in order to have one successful hunt.

I would also be remiss to not mention that safety is paramount when reaping. Do not, under any circumstances, reap on public land during a firearms season. Even in archery, deploying hunter’s orange on the decoy and your person would be a strong recommendation of mine. No deer is worth dying over.​.

It has been revealed that with that stated, reaping whitetail deer is something I look forward to attempting every year. It’s a wonderful way to break up the monotony of sitting in a treestand for hours on end. It’s physically and mentally challenging, and has led to some of the most exciting moments in my hunting career. There’s nothing better than tricking a mature buck into pinning his ears back and approaching you, ready for a fight.

#9104. ‘The Safety Was On!’ I Nearly Missed My Chance at a Substantial Adirondack Buck

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

‘The Safety Was On!’ I Nearly Missed My Chance at a Substantial Adirondack Buck

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3159 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Ho!” said Hugh, and he beat me to it by a split second.
  • A moment before, he had been a shadowy shape moving through the brush; now he was a picturebook buck.
  • I had first seen the buck 47 minutes before, and in those minutes the major deer had acted out a whole literature of whitetail lore.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Ho!” said Hugh, and he beat me to it by a split second. I had already puckered my lips to whistle. Hugh Fosburgh, who knows as much about whitetail deer as any man I know, had marked the little patch of sunlit runway as the place to stop the deer. The buck performed as though he had been trained in an obedience school. He stopped, keeping his nose to the trail for a long moment before he lifted his grizzled head and turned it slowly in our direction.

A moment before, he had been a shadowy shape moving through the brush; now he was a picturebook buck. Slanting rays of cold November sunlight picked out every point on his massive rack and colored them a rich antique ivory.

I had first seen the buck 47 minutes before, and in those minutes the major deer had acted out a whole literature of whitetail lore.

For a moment I thought I would kneel to shoot, but a little clump of beech brush wiped out that notion. I had raised the rifle with a kind of brainless calm, put the tapered post on his lung area, and squeezed the trigger. That trigger had always broken as cleanly as a glass swizzle stick, but now it resisted. I didn’t realize how excited I had become until I found myself jerking crazily on the trigger. A curtain of dark woods dropped into the sight picture, and the post was wavering and drifting. The safety was on!

In extenuation I must confess that in the previous 47 minutes I must have pressed the trigger-guard safety of the Remington 760 off and on at least seven times, and when I finally got a clear shot, I must have pressed it wrong.

Industry observers note that “Well, you had cause to be nervous,” Hugh remarked later. “I know all about that kind of thing. Remember, I missed one at 50 yards, standing, just two days before you arrived.”.

Hugh had told me that story at breakfast the day I got to camp. I had met him in a Manhattan restaurant the previous August. When he discovered that I was a fellow hunter, he noted, “You must come up and hunt a few days at the camp.” I needed no urging, and after a nine-mile ride over a rutty dirt-and-gravel track from Minerva, Newly introduced York, through deep forest, we emerged in a large clearing. I discovered I was visiting the 5,500-acre North Woods Club.

Hugh gave me a handsome printed map of that marvelous wilderness in the Adirondacks, and a legend told me that Winslow Homer, the American artist, had been a charter member and that all of his famous Adirondack paintings had been done there. There on the map were Mink Pond, Beaver Mountain, and the Outlet. Three Homer masterpieces—The Smudge Fire, The Young Huntsman, and The Blue Boat—loomed up in my mind’s eye.

According to recent reports, the first day, we drove Hugh’s four-wheel-drive to where he had missed his buck. Two does and two fawns came out into full view, and a buck ran into the swamp behind a little rise of ground. I saw his antlers at the top of each bound, but that was all.

On the third day I hunted alone in the morning and had a fine experience with a massive doe that walked daintily to within 12 yards of me as I sat on a fallen log above a marsh.

That afternoon Hugh noted he would drive me over woods roads to give me a better look at the country. Then he would put me on stand to hunt until dark. We drove around to look at the views that Winslow Homer had painted, looked at two cubby-pen fisher sets (a trap arrangement involving a baited shelter arranged near a watercourse), visited the highest beaver dam I had ever seen, and drove a woods road onto a steep shoulder of Beaver Mountain. We got out and walked down toward some scraggly second-growth bottoms.

Recent findings suggest that “I think we’ll just sit here for a while,” Hugh said. “That little flat is a good deer crossing.”.

The sun had broken through the heavy overcast, and we were grateful for its quick warmth. We chatted in low tones. The dry humor sprinkled through Hugh’s low-voiced comments was diverting, but I did hear the sharp snap of a dry branch. It was the kind of noise a heavy animal makes.

According to recent reports, “There’s a deer,” Hugh noted perfunctorily, as if seeing a deer was a routine matter. I saw the deer at the same time, and it was no routine deer. I couldn’t see antlers, but even in the brush at about 140 yards, the animal’s body was burly and male. In two quick steps the deer vanished. It was exactly 2:45; I looked at my watch and recorded the time and many other things in my journal that night.

Recent findings suggest that while the deer was out of sight, I swung my legs around the butt of the log so I could face in the right direction. I did it slowly, and I remember thinking: Hey, my right leg hasn’t started to tremble yet. My right knee always knocks all by itself whenever I see or hear game, especially deer.

Recent findings suggest that the buck was puttering around like a cranky old bachelor doing chores. First one piece of brush moved, then another swayed. A whole mass of brush moved violently in a jerky but rhythmic fashion. I sweated out four to five minutes of this. I must have started to rise, for Hugh whispered, “Take it easy; he’ll show himself.”.

In a recent development, he did, but only for a second. I saw two legs, then two more from the knees down as he passed a low opening in the cover.

I strained my eyes to pick him out through the half-light that filtered down through the scattering of substantial and small pines, beech brush, and hazel bushes. He seemed to be moving to our left.

Recent findings suggest that I pushed off the pumpgun’s safety and held on a narrow opening, but the buck turned before he reached it and angled toward us. He was still 100 yards away, but I was alarmed because Hugh and I were just high enough above the flat so that the rim would soon blot out the deer.

Time went by, and then Hugh jabbed a finger at a spot much farther to the left.

Sources indicate that “It’s a buck—and a good one,” he said. Then I saw the head. The animal raised it just once and rapidly lowered it, but the glimpse of the huge antlers was enough. My right knee began to perform.

Industry observers note that all this while I was raising and lowering the rifle to squint through the 22X Weaver scope, but it was useless. Then the deer walked right out into the open and stood quite still. When I swung the rifle to cover him, I saw that “he” had no antlers—it was a massive doe! The buck was still hidden. This quite unnerved me, and my second symptom of buck fever hit. My arms seemed suddenly drained of all strength and took on that sickly spaghettilike feeling. I managed to whisper, “My God, another one!” Just then the buck walked through the same narrow opening and was gone. Miraculously, he seemed to walk through the opening again, going in the same direction. I was flabbergasted but it was a second doe.

In a recent development, our problem was complicated by a factor of three. There were three deer in the brushy tangle, and while I was trying to find the needle in the haystack, I must have had every view of a deer that a man can see in the woods—a patch of brown, a glimmer of white, a dark-gray fleeting shadow, a leg, a flicking ear, a backline moving with measured stride and then hurrying across an opening in the thick second growth. Here a motion, there a contour. It went on and on while the three deer went through their annual rutting ritual. The does were playing hard to get, but the buck was persistent, and I hoped against hope that one of the does would submit and that the buck would rise above the brush as he mounted her.

According to recent reports, and it did happen. In a rising lunge, the buck’s body heaved above the cover as he mounted a doe. Head, antlers, bulging neck, and shoulders were all in sight. I could have fired had I not hesitated for a moment to appreciate the startling sight. As I rose, the doe evidently slid and skittered out from under the eager buck because he dropped from sight. I could hear the deer, but I could no longer see them. They were cracking twigs and rustling dry bushes. The swaying bushes showed that the buck was now chasing one or both does.

Once or twice Hugh pointed, but finally, even from his slightly different angle, he could see only the swaying bushes. The wind was blowing directly across our front, and I knew our scent would soon alarm the deer because they were angling to our left and coming much closer. Soon the animals would be under the bank that dropped off below us and directly downwind as well. Then there was silence—nothing. I felt the breeze on my right cheek.

Industry observers note that hugh rose slowly and motioned me forward to the edge of the dropoff. By pointing to himself and gesturing, he indicated that he would circle around to our left to see if he could move the deer back past me. I was doubtful; if he moved that way, I thought he would give them his wind. But I slipped toward the dropoff.

Recent findings suggest that hugh noiselessly edged to our left, and then one and another of the deer blew. The ragged exhale of breath of the second snort ended in an angry, screeching whistle. The deer were close under the dropoff, and they went out in wild confusion. One doe bounded off in the open to my right. Then I saw the flag of another deer going away. Buck or doe, I could not tell.

Hugh came back chagrined because he had spooked them.

“Did you see him?” he asked. I shook my head. “I thought not,” he whispered. “I think the buck ran off to our left. I think he’s still in there.”.

Figuring nothing ventured, nothing gained, I gave the long, rasping gutteral Brrkkkk sound that rutting bucks sometimes make. Instantly the does blew almost in unison far up the little valley.

“They didn’t like what they heard,” Hugh said ruefully.

I waited two or three minutes and then made the Brrrrrkkkk sound again, hoping our lovesick quarry would think he had a rival nearby and challenge him. Hugh took a dim view of my calling.

Recent findings suggest that “Let’s smoke another cigaret and then go back to the Jeep,” he told me. “Then I’ll drive you out on that woods road and put you on stand for the evening.”.

According to recent reports, it was 3:30 when we settled down again, chatting in low tones and listening to the slow yank, yank of a nuthatch. Far up the narrow part of the little valley where the two does had gone, I heard the long, drawn-out churr and bark of a short-tempered red squirrel. I glanced in that direction and caught a motion in the brush. It materialized into a deer walking precisely through the little glade where we had first seen the buck. It was another doe.

“There’s another,” Hugh stated and pointed. Sauntering behind the first one was a second doe, and just behind her I saw a third deer—a six-point buck. He took a little hop or two, caught up with the doe, and, with his nose nudging her tail, followed her.

“The woods are full of deer,” I murmured.

According to recent reports, hugh noted, “Get up on the road if you want that six-pointer.” He was saying it when a yearling buck came along behind the first buck. I had risen and was starting toward the woods road when the hatrack buck that had shaken me earlier stepped into the clearing behind the yearling. His head was down, but he was in full view, walking rapidly in the wake of the four deer ahead of him.

According to recent reports, as he went out of the scope’s circle behind the cover, I swung ahead and held on another sunlit clearing. I was getting set to whistle to stop him when he came into view, but Hugh whispered, “I’ll stop him when he gets into the clearing.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Ho!” said Hugh, just as the buck came into full view at what I later determined was 140 yards. At the sound the buck stopped dead, and raised and turned his head toward us. I saw the ivory tips of his broad antlers, but he seemed a long way off. Curiously, I was suddenly calm. The post covered his lung area, and I began the squeeze—with the crazy results already described.

Industry observers note that when I discovered that the safety was on, I lost my wits. My arms seemed weak again, and my right knee bounced wildly. The post wandered all over the deer after I finally pushed the safety off. When the rifle roared, I knew the hold was too far back.

The rifle went up in recoil, but then I saw the buck swinging away from me. I pumped another .30/06 cartridge into the 760, but the buck was gone.

“You hit him,” Hugh stated matter-of-factly. I was amazed.

Industry observers note that “If I did, I don’t know where. The post was all over him.” I felt a mounting disgust with myself. It had been 14 years and seven massive-game animals since I had failed to kill with one hit.

Industry observers note that “You hit him hard,” Hugh told me. “I saw him flinch. Didn’t you see how heavily he moved?”.

Recent findings suggest that hugh was right. The deer had not gone off in major, high bounds. “Maybe—maybe,” I ventured.

“Oh, I’m sure of it,” Hugh remarked with an easy grin.

According to recent reports, “We ought to wait a while and let him stiffen up,” I mentioned. “He may be hit too far back—if he is hit. That was pretty poor shooting.”.

“We’ll smoke another cigaret, and then see,” Hugh replied.

In a recent development, after 10 or 15 minutes Hugh said, “I’ll spot you from here. Go down and see what happened.” I thought it a bit early and decided to go only as far as the spot where the buck had stood when I’d fired.

When I got there I found nothing. I walked a bit farther in spite of myself and then went another five yards. I found a tuft of hair.

Sources indicate that but it was pure white hair. My heart sank. “A belly shot, low down,” I stated to myself.

I moved alongside the scuffed leaves, and then I saw a 10-inch patch of blood. But it didn’t look like lung blood. Too dark.

With a heavy heart I went back to where the deer had stood and waved Hugh toward me. When he walked up, I pointed out the hair, and Hugh picked it up.

“He’s hit too low, but there’s blood ahead,” I told him.

Hugh followed me to the first patch of blood, reached down in the little hollow where the blood was already coagulating, and picked up a piece of tissue.

In a recent development, “This is a piece of lung,” he said. And it did look like it and feel like it, but I was dubious.

Sources indicate that “Let’s work ahead slowly,” Hugh suggested. We did, and found a few red drops here and there. One of us stood at the last drop until the other located the next. We were being very quiet. Twice we found puddles of blood. At one, we could see that the buck had lain down or had fallen down. I also noticed that the wounded buck had stirred up the leaves in a continuous disturbed line by dragging his feet.

It has been revealed that we had come perhaps 150 yards on the blood trail when we heard a rustling and thrashing in front of us and to the left. Then it stopped. We listened but heard nothing more until a nuthatch suddenly gave its wild alarm cries.

It has been revealed that we stopped beside a significant boulder a few feet from a fallen yellow birch. In getting over it the buck had left a smudge of blood. We stood still and listened again.

In a recent development, “Let’s be patient,” Hugh noted. “He didn’t get up, I’m sure, and with the vitality deer have during the rut, I’d just as soon he didn’t get on his feet again.”.

Recent findings suggest that I was more than agreeable. Frankly, I thought we had followed too far and too soon.

Industry observers note that we sat in silence on the boulder for 10 more minutes and then worked ahead a few yards. Peering intently into the dark woods, I finally spotted him through my scope or thought I did.

Recent findings suggest that read Next: Forget Trail Cameras and Feeders. Try Hunting Wilderness Whitetails the Old Way.

Industry observers note that “He’s right there,” Hugh said with certainty. And the deer never moved. He was dead, probably from loss of blood.

Sources indicate that the buck was a fine, significant, swollen-necked nine-pointer, and Hugh held out a big hand for a congratulatory shake. The buck had been hit high in the ham, and the exit wound was in the flank on the other side. The paunch was broken. Certainly the tissue Hugh and I had taken for lung was not. But the buck was ours, and I realized again how important it is to follow up whenever you fire at game.

It has been revealed that during the dressing out and the drag, I kept thinking of Winslow Homer’s painting, The Young Huntsman. I could see the youthful hunter and a significant buck’s head partly rolled up in the deerskin. It was a strange feeling to live again a scene that had been painted many years before.

According to recent reports, this story was originally published in the November 1976 problem of Outdoor Life. Angus Cameron, the author, was 68 years old at the time of publication. He was an editor for Alfred A. Knopf, the prestigious Fresh York City book publisher.

#9103. Breaking: We Decoyed Substantial Bull Moose in the Alaska High Country

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3557 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: We Decoyed Substantial Bull Moose in the Alaska High Country

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that as we loaded our gear into the bush planes, Bruce Werba offered one last piece of advice.
  • I’d spent enough time in the Alaskan backcountry over the years that he wasn’t going to get an argument from me.
  • It has been revealed that our squadron consisted of three Super Cubs with tundra tires.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as we loaded our gear into the bush planes, Bruce Werba offered one last piece of advice. “Be sure to use all 44 stakes. It’ll get windy up there—I guarantee it.”.

I’d spent enough time in the Alaskan backcountry over the years that he wasn’t going to get an argument from me.

It has been revealed that our squadron consisted of three Super Cubs with tundra tires. I folded myself into the cramped space behind the pilot where the rest of my gear was stored, my shoulders touching both sides of the fuselage. We lifted off the gravel runway that’s the primary connection between the 160 souls who call Holy Cross, Alaska, home and the rest of the world, and banked over the wide and muddy Yukon River before my pilot, Matt, put us on a westerly bearing.

Sources indicate that we were in the air for nearly an hour, heading into the Yukon Delta National Wildlife Refuge, a massive region that borders the Bering Sea and is bigger than the state of Maine. I took mental note of the terrain we flew over, a mix of pine-­covered mountains, tundra, vast patches of willows, and countless bogs, ponds, and rivers. It occurred to me that if, for whatever reason, we had to trek out on foot, we’d probably never make it back.

It has been revealed that over the roar of the engine, Matt shouted that we were approaching our landing zone. He made a large circle over an exposed flat that was surrounded by mountains on three sides to make sure he could put us down safely.

Recent findings suggest that he pointed the nose of the plane into the stiff easterly wind for the final approach, and we bounced to a standstill in a matter of feet. He jumped out of the cockpit and signaled by hand to the other pilots to help them land.

As soon as the three planes were down, the pilots rapidly pitched our gear onto the tundra and just as quickly took off. “Good luck,” Matt mentioned before firing up his engine. Time is money for these guys, and they weren’t wasting any of it.

Industry observers note that the three of us looked around at the place that would be home for the next 12 days. I was with my longtime friend Jason Nash, who works at Federal Ammunition, and photographer Tom Fowlks. This was Jason’s first moose hunt, and we had decided to do it on our own terms: getting dropped off in the wilderness during the rut and calling bulls.

According to recent reports, we had to manhandle our tent, which was bucking in the strong wind, to get it set up. The forecast said the prevailing winds for the next 10 days would be out of the south, so we oriented the entrance toward the north and, with Werba’s admonition in mind, pounded all 44 stakes deep into the rocky soil with large stones.

According to recent reports, werba, who runs Alaska Pike Safaris with his wife, Connie, is a bit of a legend in Alaskan outfitting circles. He has the friendly demeanor of everyone’s favorite grandpa (he’s in his 70s), but is almost inhumanly tough. That spring, a few months before our trip, he’d had a heart attack while guiding pike fishermen and wasn’t able to get to a doctor in Anchorage until four days later—yet he was back on the job in a matter of days, doing work that would grind down a man half his age. His reputation for putting both his guided and self-guided hunters on big bulls is why I sought him out. I’ve been on half a dozen moose hunts over the years and have killed three, but I’d never had a chance on a true monster—one of those gaggers in the mid-60s that just takes your breath away—until now.

While Jason and Tom set up the cots in the tent, I dug a pit and lined it with a tarp that I weighted down with rocks to collect drinking water from the rains that were sure to come. Once the camp was set, we fired up the stove, heated water, and ate freeze-dried spaghetti and beef stroganoff straight from the bag. We had some bourbon to celebrate the start of the adventure, half a bottle disappearing with alarming speed. We’d only purchased two bottles back in Anchorage, a nod to modesty that the three of us instantly regretted. For the rest of the trip, we invoked emergency rationing.

According to recent reports, it rained heavily that first night, and the wind beat on our tent, making the rainfly snap and pop like a flag in a gale. The next morning, I fiddled with the guide lines until I got the rigging right, and the tent quieted down.

Industry observers note that after downing mugs of instant coffee, we explored our outpost. The broad flat was covered in tundra with patches of gravel and a few small stands of pine and willow. Everywhere I looked I could see bushes laden with ripe blueberries, and dark crowberries carpeted the ground.

Industry observers note that both ends of the flat, which was about three-quarters of a mile long, gave commanding vistas of the country. The north end overlooked a long, broad valley rimmed by mountains that descended to a river about a mile away. To the south, we had views of more mountains and the upper reaches of a pine-forested draw that dropped steeply down to god knows where. I hoped that if a good bull were down there, I could coax it out of the timber—because there was no way on Earth I’d chase one into that hellhole.

A large grizzly came through our camp at lunch. We were back at the tent, comparing notes and eating sandwiches, when he appeared. He angled slowly toward our tent, head down, eating berries. He was a big brute: small ears, broad across his shoulders and rump, sagging belly. I couldn’t tell what his hide would have squared—I’m not particularly good at that—but he was a toad. If I were chasing grizzlies, he’s exactly the kind of bear I’d be looking for.

As it was, the three of us just watched him strut our way. The wind was at his back, and he hadn’t noticed the interlopers on his turf. He dropped down and rolled on his back like an enormous dog, trying to deal with the swarm of bugs around him. We stood there, Jason and I, with rounds chambered in our .30/06s, as he cruised past us at 75 yards. Later that afternoon, while glassing for bulls, I saw him through the spotter about 2 miles away on a mountain, still going.

It has been revealed that our hunting technique wasn’t complicated. We had two cow moose decoys and a makeshift moose paddle that consisted of a white mesh game bag I had stretched over a wire hanger. Because the wind rarely let up, we put one decoy in a small willow-choked gap on the edge of the northern lookout, where any bull to the north or west of us would see it.

From a spot above and behind the decoy, we’d glass while calling every 10 minutes or so. Cupping my hands over my mouth, I’d wail like a lonely estrous moose, emptying my lungs for all they were worth. Sometimes I’d mix in bull calls, a deep, guttural mwah that to me always sounds like an old man grieving some terrible loss.

The wind picked up, and fog and rain rolled in, which cut our visibility to a couple hundred yards but provided relief from the swarms of tiny black flies that pounced whenever the breeze died. We had Thermacells to help with the mosquitos, but they didn’t dissuade those psychotic little bloodsuckers. Only our full-face bug nets and a liberal dousing with pure DEET kept them at bay.

Recent findings suggest that on the fourth day, I spotted my first moose. I was trudging across the tundra, working toward the south end of the flat to glass, when I saw the cow in a small patch of willows. She’d spotted me too, and even though 700 yards separated us, that was too close for her, so she turned around and loped over the hill and out of view. Watching moose cover ground is an impressive sight. Standing still, they are awkward-looking creatures, but nothing moves through rough terrain the way they can, like skaters on ice. They can run through timber blowdowns that would stop any two-legged hunter in their tracks.

Sources indicate that I posted up on an exposed knob that was flanked by several large willows, giving me some cover from which to glass the area. At one point, I watched a nervous-­looking black bear work back and forth across the hillside that dropped into the hellhole. He was eating berries in the same patch I’d walked through a couple of days before. Between mouthfuls, he’d pop up on his hind legs and look around before grabbing some more. After 20 minutes, he saw or smelled something he didn’t like and beelined into the depths of the dark timber.

By the end of the day, I was tired and scanning on autopilot. So when I swung my binocular to the right and got a full-frame view of a grizzly walking toward me, the adrenaline surge felt like a physical blow.

In a recent development, once my lungs and heart started to work in concert again, I took another look. Like the grizzly that had strolled through our camp, he was a massive bear, walking with the assured saunter of an apex predator.

He was 300 yards away, and while he wasn’t walking fast, his every step was bringing him right to me. It was getting late, and the light was failing. Even though I was well-armed with both my .30/06 and a .44 on my hip, I wanted to give the bear his space. So in the spirit of General O.P. Smith, commander of the 1st Marine Division at the Chosin Reservoir, who said, “Retreat, hell! We’re not retreating, we’re just advancing in another direction,” I packed my gear and headed back toward the tent, glancing over my shoulder every few seconds to make sure the griz wasn’t closing the gap.

Before I could make it to camp, I spotted Jason and Tom walking toward me. They were both grinning.

Jason told me that earlier that day, he had called in a bull and gotten a good look at him. He judged it at slightly larger than 50 inches. Many places in Alaska impose a 50-inch minimum on nonresidents, but we happened to be in an any-bull area, so his main concern was just making sure it was a mature bull. The most common way to size up a moose’s rack is to wait for it to face you, then compare the width of the antlers to the distance between its eyes.

Sources indicate that measured from the outside corners, a bull moose’s eyes are about 10 inches apart. So, if the antlers extend at least two eye-widths off the side of its head, you’re at 50 inches.

Sources indicate that during that first encounter, Jason let the bull melt back into the willows. We still had many days to hunt, the rut hadn’t hit its peak, and the promise of a mythical 65-incher kept his finger off the trigger.

It has been revealed that but later, when the bull reappeared, again drawn by Jason’s calls, that logic flew out the window. Jason couldn’t resist, and his 160-yard shot took the bull through the shoulder, and it piled up in a shallow ravine in the willows. His smile told me he had no regrets.

The grizzly that had been trailing behind me vanished, but we still had bears on our mind as we put on our headlamps to recover the bull. The terrain down in the willow thickets is featureless in daylight; at night, it’s a maze.

In a recent development, eventually, we found the moose and got to work. It was a long, wet night. A pea-soup fog rolled in and gave the kill site an otherworldly feel. We managed to get the hide off, the moose quartered, and the first loads—the rear hinds—strapped to our backs. The fog rendered our headlamps nearly useless, blinding us more than lighting our way.

In a recent development, the hike to camp was less than half a mile, but it was all uphill and through the boggy tundra with more than 130 pounds of meat and bone on our backs. By the time we crested the final hill, my legs were shaking, and it was 5 a.m.

Jason groaned. “That’s some Navy SEAL shit.”.

Industry observers note that we each took a shot of bourbon and tried to dry off as best as possible before crawling into our sleeping bags, but by this point in the hunt, everything was wet, and our tent smelled like a sweatshop. The next day, we hauled the remaining meat, cape, and antlers back to camp. By then it was raining hard, and our first priority was to protect the venison. Tom took the camp ax and cut down a few small pine trees so we could build a lean-to against the side of the tent to keep the meat dry. We chopped off the boughs to make a bed, and tied sections of the trunks together with paracord to form a frame over which we draped tarps.

After removing the meat from the bags, we dumped a Costco-size container of pepper on it to keep the flies away. We spread the game bags on the branches and put the meat on top of the bags. As the smell of the spiced fresh meat hit my nostrils, I salivated like one of Pavlov’s dogs.

I called Bruce Werba on the sat phone to let him know we had a batch of meat to fly out. But the clouds and fog were keeping all the planes grounded.

It has been revealed that when I asked when the conditions might shift, he mentioned, “Be patient.” When I told him about our scant moose sightings, he repeated that mantra. “Be patient. It can change at any moment.”.

Of course, we didn’t have a choice in the matter. The weather was going to do what it would do, and the same with the moose. So we went back to glassing as the rain and the temperature fell.

The very next day, I spotted a good bull high on the mountains behind us to the east. He was feeding up a draw to a saddle. I cow-called and he paused but didn’t turn around or look my way. Eventually, he crested the ridge and vanished.

It has been revealed that it rained nonstop for the next three days, a cold downpour that finally managed to defeat my Gore-Tex rainwear, making for some truly miserable glassing. Every few hours I’d return to the tent to heat water and make coffee or hot cider to stop the shivering.

At night, our tent offered a fragile haven from the elements, rocking back and forth like a ship in the violent winds that Werba had predicted. The lantern above our heads created a small pocket of warm air at the top of the tent, and we hung our wet gloves and socks around it each night in the hopes they would dry. Much of our conversation turned to how best to stay warm. We stuffed the edges of our sleeping bags with extra clothes, and I started wearing my down jacket as I slept, even though it, too, was wet.

Read Next: A DIY Caribou Hunting Adventure in Alaska.

On day 10, I saw two more bulls. The first looked to be in the mid-50s and had three brow tines on each side. He was angling toward the river, and I last saw him at 500 yards as he went into the timber. I figured he’d show again later so I could get a better look at his antlers, but I was wrong—he was gone for good.

Recent findings suggest that at the end of the day, I called in a bull in the low 50s. It had gotten foggy again, so we didn’t have much visibility, but I watched him come my way through the willows as he tipped his rack from one side to the other. He walked right below my perch, almost within bow shot.

That night, another bear came into camp and dragged Jason’s rack away. We found it 50 yards downhill the next morning. A couple of the points on one paddle had been chewed, and we could see where the bear had scraped bits of meat off the skull. Fortunately, the bear hadn’t worked up the courage to raid our stash of meat under the tarp’s lean-to. He had, however, left an impressive pile of brilliant purple scat next to the tent that, in my addled state, looked like the filling for a delicious blueberry cobbler.

Industry observers note that the fog that morning was the thickest it had been. We couldn’t see more than a hundred yards in any direction. But this was the last full day of the hunt, so I went to the northern lookout and stared into the mist. Eventually, the clouds lifted, and I glassed a pair of antlers that appeared like the sails on a man-of-war emerging from a fog bank about 800 yards away.

He was with three other moose: a cow, her calf, and a spindly-horned young bull. After a closer look, I realized he was the smaller bull that we’d already called in several times. There was no calling him today, however: His intentions regarding the cow were unmistakable. He separated her from the calf like a cutting horse. She tried to get back to her calf a dozen times, but he was faster and stronger and herded her off into the willows as the younger bull and the calf watched.

And that was the last moose of the trip.

That night we polished off the bourbon and ate the final bags of Mountain House lasagna, which we had saved for the occasion. I got Werba on the sat phone the next morning. The good news was the weather had cleared and the Super Cubs could take off from Holy Cross to collect us. More good news came in that his self-guided hunters who had been on the river had done well. One shot a 68-inch bull, and another had dropped a 74-incher.

According to recent reports, werba mentioned he was sorry the big boys hadn’t worked their way up higher, and that none of the mountain hunters had shot toads. The weather had been too warm to get the huge bulls moving, and that was that. Whenever your heart is set on a trophy animal, leaving with an unpunched tag is always a possibility. Truth is, I didn’t mind. Jason got a terrific bull, we’d had the great adventure we came for, and I knew at some point I’d return to the Lower Yukon to try again.

After I hung up with Werba, the three of us pulled the 44 stakes from the ground, packed up, and looked to the sky, waiting to hear the drone of motors of the airplanes that would take us home.

According to recent reports, moose are substantial animals, but they aren’t especially difficult to bring down. Even moderate cartridges work well on them. In Sweden and Canada, more moose have been killed with the 6.5×55 Swede and the .303 British than anything else, and neither are punishing to shoot. As always, shot placement and bullet construction are the key factors.

Sources indicate that on this hunt, Jason and I were both carrying .30/06s. My rifle (above) was built for the elements. I used a stainless Shilen DGR action and Shilen barrel with a Manner’s EH-1A stock and topped it with a 2.5–15×44 Maven RS.1. The rig handled the cold and wet without any problems.

Sources indicate that one reason I went with the .30/06 was to try out some of Federal’s new loads. After several years’ hiatus, Federal is working with bullet-makers beyond the Vista Outdoor family of brands. (Vista is Federal’s parent company.) So, once again, hunters can get Federal Premium cartridges topped with bullets from Barnes, Nosler, Hornady, Berger, and others. I’m glad these companies have decided to kiss and make up.

Read Next: I Spent 12 Days Trapped with a Moose Guide Who Wouldn’t Give Up.

I shot the 165-grain Barnes TSX, which, thanks to its monolithic construction, plows deep into whatever you’re shooting, smashing through hide and bones, and retains nearly all of its weight.

It has been revealed that jason used a 180-grain Nosler Accubond, which I think is about the best all-around big-game bullet made. It is accurate, mushrooms beautifully, penetrates well, and does everything a bullet is supposed to. Another benefit of these projectiles is they would work well on grizzlies. Just in case.

This story was originally published in a 2019 Glitch of Outdoor Life.

Latest Update: How Two WWII Fighter Pilots Hacked Through the Fresh Guinea Jungle for the Best Duck Hunt of Their Lives

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “Ducks Can Improve Any War,” appeared in the December 1944 problem of Outdoor Life.
  • Recent findings suggest that A duck hunter is always a duck hunter.
  • Industry observers note that you duck hunters know exactly what I mean, but I doubt if any of you ever felt the old longing as much as I did that day in Fresh Guinea in February, 1943.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “Ducks Can Improve Any War,” appeared in the December 1944 problem of Outdoor Life.

Recent findings suggest that A duck hunter is always a duck hunter. No matter how long he’s been away from the sport, he still longs for that song of the wind on the lake reeds. He craves the acrid smell of burning powder and the comfortable feel of his favorite gun. He never forgets the beauty of the cold gray mists of dawn, the hazy silhouettes of decoys, the tense, exciting wait, and finally, the sight of fast gray wings above him.

Industry observers note that you duck hunters know exactly what I mean, but I doubt if any of you ever felt the old longing as much as I did that day in Fresh Guinea in February, 1943. Yes, New Guinea — hot, steaming, sultry. I had been in the Pacific area for eighteen months, flying a fighter. Four of those months were combat flying. I was getting in plenty of hunting — a serious kind of hunting that I enjoyed — when late one afternoon while sitting on alert, a flock of ducks, real live ducks, passed right over our pilot’s hut and lit in a near-by swamp.

Sources indicate that when those ducks flew over, two old-time duck hunters jumped to their feet and watched ’em till they’d disappeared. Then they turned and looked at each other. They didn’t say anything; they didn’t have to. One of those duck hunters was Lieut. Fred Sibley from Maine. I was the other one. And right then and there the war we were in had improved 1,000 percent.

When we opened the boxes of No. 6s we found that half the shells were bloated by the damp atmosphere, and wouldn’t fit into the guns. So we had to take our knives and patiently whittle each shell down until it would slip into the chamber.

We started right in, lining things up for our next day off. We dug up a couple of old double-barrel guns from the squadron supply and, after making the rounds through several camps, found some honest-to-goodness 12 gauge ammunition a pilot had bought in Australia. We finally succeeded in heckling the officer into turning some of it over to us — by promising him a big fat duck for dinner.

Now, this was really an effective offer, since his squadron had been practically living on bully beef for six months. It didn’t hurt our consciences to take advantage of the poor man, as we knew we could feed a lot of hungry soldiers if we could get him to come across.

Anyway, we got back to camp with two boxes of No. 6’s. Later, when we opened them we found that half the shells were bloated by the damp atmosphere, and wouldn’t fit into the guns. So we had to take our knives and patiently whittle each shell down until it would slip into the chamber. Then we gave every shell a coat of grease to protect it from the humidity until the big day.

Recent findings suggest that we had found previously from wandering around in the jungle that it was absolutely imperative for a man to sprinkle himself with some kind of sulphur as a protection against the chiggers and ticks. These tiny parasites were dangerous not only because their bites caused infections which took weeks to heal in that climate, but because they were known to carry a tropical disease. We also knew it was necessary to use mosquito lotion as millions of these pests swarmed everywhere.

In a recent development, our problem, then, was to concoct something that wouldn’t wash off our bodies when we were wading through swamps and marsh land after those ducks. We hit on the bright idea of mixing the sulphur powder with vaseline, and it worked like a charm. The mosquito lotion was no problem as we could carry plenty of it along in a small bottle. For extra protection we each obtained a mosquito head net and a pair of leggings. Two canteens of water completed our preparations in the way of equipment for the unique duck hunt.

Sources indicate that we still had a couple of days to go before our day off, so we decided to do some aërial scouting. We knew we’d be doing some flying in those remaining days, and that while on our landing patterns we would have an opportunity to study the swamp and determine the best possible way of getting into it from our camp.

In a recent development, to appreciate the importance of this, one must imagine a typical Florida swamp surrounded by the most dense undergrowth in which, every five or six feet, giant trees rear their heads. Undergrowth and trees are connected by a maze of hanging moss and tough vines, the only trails being pig runs and an occasional hidden native trail that no white man can follow. The only way a white man can get through such stuff is to cut and fight his way through. So our problem was to determine the spot where we could cut our way through with the least effort. We studied the jungle carefully during the next two days’ flying, and found that a few miles from our camp a grassy hill cut through the jungle to within about a quarter of a mile of the swamp. We could get to this hill easily from the camp, and figured that with the aid of a compass we should be able to bore through the jungle to the swamp itself in two or three hours. Our intends were now complete.

The major day came at last. It dawned misty and cool — for Latest Guinea — as near a perfect duck-hunting day as that part of the world could have provided. And it found Fred and me hacking our way into the jungle surrounding the swamp. We looked more like a couple of jungle soldiers than we did duck hunters. We had our .45’s on our belts for use on snakes or crocodiles, and also because neither of us was sure there might not be a stray Japanese pilot hiding in the brush. We knew several had recently bailed out or crash-landed in the vicinity.

We looked more like a couple of jungle soldiers than we did duck hunters. We had our .45’s on our belts for use on snakes or crocodiles, and also because neither of us was sure there might not be a stray Japanese pilot hiding in the brush.

Our heads were covered by our mosquito nets, and our canteen and ammunition belts rattled as we whacked at the undergrowth with a substantial jungle knife, taking turns at hacking and resting.

All through the jungle we encountered many varieties of beautiful birds. Most of them were of the parrot or pigeon families, and were of every color of the rainbow. Some were as small as wrens, others much larger than domestic pigeons. Once we caught a glimpse of an Australian jungle turkey, a magnificent bird almost as large as the American wild turkey, but were unable to get a shot at it in the thick undergrowth. We also saw a couple of dark brown jungle chickens of the grouse variety. Later, in another part of New Guinea, I was fortunate enough to kill several of these birds, and they were very delicious, the meat being light and tender. But this story is about duck hunting — and what duck hunting!

In exactly one hour and thirty minutes after the first swing of our jungle knife we broke into the swamp — and, believe me, it was beautiful to behold.

“Look at them, Dave, look at them!” Fred was wild with excitement.

“Gee, it’s been a long time,” I said.

Ducks were everywhere — circling the swamps by the hundreds, quacking, whistling, and splashing down into the open spot among the tall reeds.

Sources indicate that we stood there just looking for a long time. Then Fred said, “Dave, you know what we’ve got to do?”.

Ducks were everywhere — circling the swamps by the hundreds, quacking, whistling, and splashing down into the open spot among the tall reeds.

Sources indicate that “Yes, I’m afraid I do,” I replied. “But it’s sure going to be hard to remember all the hungry people at camp when those singles start flying over. Boy! I wish we had plenty of shells.”.

“Yeah,” sighed Fred, “or not such a large family to feed.”.

It has been revealed that I had an idea. “I’ll tell you what let’s do,” I said. “Let’s each of us get fifteen ducks with as few shells as possible, and then use the rest of the shells for singles. That will give us at least thirty ducks to feed the sixty guys back at camp.”.

Sources indicate that “O.K., Dave, we’ve got to do it, I guess,” agreed Fred. “It’s going to seem real unsportsmanlike to take pot-shots, but bully beef is sure getting tiresome. Let’s go!”.

Neither of us relished shooting those beautiful birds on the water, but this was one time we had to bring home the bacon.

It has been revealed that we decided that since the length of the swamp lay north and south we would separate, Fred going south and I going north, this way keeping the ducks moving back and forth between us. So, out we started. The water in the swamp proved to be from ankle to almost waist deep. The bottom, however, was solid, so walking was not difficult. Most of the swamp was covered with thick dead reeds about six feet high that broke easily as we waded through them. In the midst of these reeds were a great many small open spots where some kind of short green water grass grew which the ducks fed upon. These openings were also the feeding grounds of many different kinds of wading birds which swarmed up with the ducks as we approached. Then there were several flocks of large white herons that seemed almost psychic, as they would take wing long before we reached their resting place, circle, climb high into the sky, and disappear into the distance. They alone seemed to leave the swamp. All other birds, including the ducks, would fly to some other clearing in the swamp and settle there.

Related: We Had a Week Off from Active Combat, So I Went Trout Fishing. I Got Pinned Down by a Sniper.

According to recent reports, hundreds of large coots were present too. They were about twice the size of any I had seen before, and looked like American birds, except they had brilliant red bills.

Before I had made my way very far into the swamp I heard Fred fire twice and, looking in his direction, saw hundreds of ducks getting up. A dozen black mallards passed right over my head. How I wanted to shoot! But didn’t, remembering my promise to Fred to get my first fifteen with as few shells as possible.

Industry observers note that most of the ducks lit about 100 yards north of me, so I began creeping in that direction, making as little noise as possible. As I crept closer through very thick reeds I came to a small opening no more than ten yards in diameter, and, lo and behold, there sat about twenty honest-to-goodness greenwing teal. They saw me and shot up like a covey of quail. I caught them just as they rose, and fired once, knocking down three. I had a tough time recovering them in the reeds, but finally found them all. At the sound of the shot the mallards got up about seventy-five yards away and circled for some ten minutes, settling back down in the same place about the time I had recovered my last teal. With the teal in my belt I crept toward the mallards, crawling through the ankle-deep water on my knees and one hand, holding my gun in the other, as the reeds were not tall in this area.

How I wanted to shoot! But didn’t, remembering my promise to Fred to get my first fifteen with as few shells as possible.

When I reached the edge of the clearing where the mallards were I saw they were all about fifty yards away on the opposite side. About halfway across the clearing was a small clump of tall reeds that I thought I might be able to keep between the mallards and myself until I could get them a little more in range.

I started crawling toward those reeds, making every effort to keep the ducks from seeing me but, alas, ducks seem to be as wary in one part of the world as another. Just as I got started they spotted me, and off they went in every direction. The largest bunch of them circled over the edge of the swamp and then seemed to disappear into the trees. This I believed to be an illusion — ducks don’t light on trees, especially mallards.

By this time I had decided that it was too hot for crawling and that I would let Fred do the work for awhile. So I took my station in the clump of reeds in the center of the clearing and waited for him to send some ducks my way. I took off my head net, wiped the perspiration from my face, applied some mosquito lotion, and put the net into my pocket, deciding I could shoot better without it.

After about ten minutes’ waiting I heard Fred open up again, firing three times, and, looking in his direction, I saw them coming. There they were, hundreds of them! And from then on, things went too fast to tell about. All the ducks seemed to want to light in the clearing I commanded — and I did command every inch of it!

Industry observers note that there they were, hundreds of them. And from then on, things went too fast to tell about. All the ducks seemed to want to light in the clearing I commanded — and I did command every inch of it.

First, a substantial flock of mallards tried to light within ten yards of me, and I opened up with both barrels just as they were settling, getting four of them. A bunch of pintails came in right after them; then teal, and more mallards. I was firing as fast as I could reload. I could hear Fred doing the same thing and knew he was in their favorite clearing at the other end of the swamp. I had never seen so many ducks at one time, and they were flying back and forth between the two of us. The boys at camp were all going to get a real meal.

After about fifteen minutes of the fastest shooting I have ever done I took inventory. I found I had seventeen ducks — and four shells left! And I actually had four black mallards, a couple of beautiful little ducks that I couldn’t identify, three pintails, and several greenwing, bluewing, and cinnamon teal. The teal were larger than any I had seen in the states, but were exactly like our teal in every other respect.

Recent findings suggest that since I had more than my quota of fifteen birds I felt I could use the remaining four precious shells for the tough shots that I have always loved so much. So I took my station and waited.

Recent findings suggest that A high flying mallard came in fast and weaving. It was one of those shots you make once in a lifetime and never forget. I led him plenty and just hoped. He came down from way up there like a rock, and I felt a thrill inside I hadn’t come close to feeling for two years.

A minute later two teal came in fast and low. I caught one with the first shot, but missed the second. But the first bird came down so clean I didn’t feel badly about the miss. With my remaining shell I stopped another mallard, not as high as the first, but it was a sweet shot.

Recent findings suggest that I gathered up my birds and started back to meet Fred. We met just in front of our trail that led back into the jungle, and as we waded through the last few yards of swamp Fred said, “Look at ’em, Dave. We’ve got thirty-five of the most beautiful ducks I ever saw!”.

“Heavy, too,” I mentioned, laughing.

A bunch of pintails came in right after them; then teal, and more mallards. I was firing as fast as I could reload. I could hear Fred doing the same thing and knew he was in their favorite clearing at the other end of the swamp.

We reached the edge of the jungle and sat down to rest. As we sat there we beheld a most astonishing sight — about ten black mallards flew right out of the tree we were sitting under and winged their way back into the swamp. Believe it or not! Mallards do light in trees, in New Guinea anyway.

It has been revealed that we started home and Fred said, “It’s a funny war, isn’t it? Black mallards lighting in trees; our belts loaded with ducks, and a bunch of hungry boys back at camp to appreciate them more than any ducks were ever appreciated before. I think, Dave, today has been the most wonderful day of my life.”.

I was glad Fred said that, because it was his last duck hunt. Fred went down fighting — doing his bit to guarantee a free and fearless future full of “wonderful days” for all of us.

#9099. To Win the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, Try Being … Vulnerable?

To Win the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, Try Being … Vulnerable?

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2222 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that author Dan England spoke with five members of Team USA after they won the 2026 Substantial’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship on October 22.
  • According to recent reports, early into the second night of the 2026 Massive’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, Mark Dowdle turned to U.S.
  • According to recent reports, before the start, Harvey Lewis, a two-time individual backyard ultra world champion whom many on the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that author Dan England spoke with five members of Team USA after they won the 2026 Substantial’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship on October 22. A rough start forced the team to abandon the fundamentals of competition and ask for help, be honest about their problems, and sacrifice for others. It paid off: the U.S. came from behind to defeat Australia and Belgium, who took second and third, respectively.

According to recent reports, early into the second night of the 2026 Massive’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, Mark Dowdle turned to U.S. teammate Levi Yoder and admitted that he was so tired he might fall asleep and into the nearby ditch. Yoder replied that he was so tired he was hallucinating and might wind up in that same ditch.

According to recent reports, before the start, Harvey Lewis, a two-time individual backyard ultra world champion whom many on the U.S. squad thought of as their de facto captain, told his teammates to lean on one another. But Dowdle hesitated the first day, and so, he thought, did many others. It made sense: Backyard ultras are usually individual events predicated on you staying strong while others give up.

For the uninitiated, backyard ultra rules are pretty simple: Run a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour, until only one remains. (That runner must complete one final loop, also called a yard, to be declared the winner.) At the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, which alternates every other year with the individual championship, each participating country simultaneously hosts its own backyard ultra with 15 runners. The team with the most cumulative laps wins.

According to recent reports, typically at backyard ultras, competitors are wolves looking for the elk with a limp. No one wants to look weak. No one demonstrated this formidable exterior better than Dowdle in the Last Soul Ultra this April, when his gamesmanship created the event’s most talked-about moment. But his competitive side was ubiquitous among the 15 elite backyard runners on Team USA. They each won backyard ultras to qualify; they were wolves, not elk.

Yet Team USA struggled from the start. With daytime temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit, it felt warmer than they thought it would. The course was hilly, with over 400 feet of climbing per loop, costing them a minute or two per loop in a format where extra seconds are precious. Indeed, over the first 40 laps when all runners from all 67 countries were still in the race, the U.S. had the slowest average lap speed of 52:21—nearly seven minutes slower than the fastest country, Slovakia.

Recent findings suggest that struggling through that second night, the U.S. decided to try a different tactic. They decided to be vulnerable.

Lewis urged the team to be honest about how they were feeling because there was a good chance others could help. It took Dowdle a bit to believe, even after watching how others supported each other.

“It did take encouragement from my team to even be more of a teammate,” Dowdle told Trail Runner.

But Dowdle was enthused when, after his admission that he was struggling, Yoder suggested that they look out for each other over the next 3 miles they had to complete to keep going. Dowdle got the message: This would be a different backyard than he’d ever run before. They talked to each other through the loop and by the end they had caught up to their teammates.

“That turned the corner for me,” Dowdle said. “In a normal race, I would never say that I was falling asleep to another runner. You just would never give up that information. But that opened the door for me to be more vocal about how I was doing.”.

According to recent reports, several other members of the U.S. squad admitted that being honest with each other and asking for help when they needed it was key to them winning the world title. Instead of acting like individuals in a last-man-standing race, they were a unit. That helped many of them run farther than they ever had before—eight Americans ran over 80 yards, or 333.3 miles—when it looked like Australia might literally run away with victory.

“When some were feeling strong, we would help those who were not feeling OK,” stated Megan Smyth, who set a PR with 82 yards and was the last woman standing. “I’m pretty sure that’s how so many of us got over 80 yards.”.

Sources indicate that the backyard, despite its do-or-die nature, lends itself to camaraderie because of the way runners all start the next 4.167-mile loop together on the hour, every hour. Jon Noll qualified for Team USA by running over 440 miles at the individual world championship last year. Even there most competitors congratulated each other after each lap. “The ultra community, in general, is not exactly a cutthroat environment for the most part,” Noll noted. He especially felt that sense of camaraderie this time as the miles piled up.

This is why Smyth loves the backyard format.

“There’s no incentive to win a lap, so you really do wind up cheering for each other,” Smyth remarked.

In a recent development, still, Team USA had to get comfortable with each other in a hurry. Even with seven returning members from the third-place 2024 team it was a little awkward at first: Some had previously competed against each other, and some called each other friends. Some were rivals. Other first-timers felt a sense of awe: Smyth had imposter syndrome, which doesn’t make it easy to talk about, say, a sore ankle.

But she also welcomed the unique race set up. If a typical backyard ultra can feel crowded and chaotic, the team race with its 15 competitors feels sparse, even intimate. Smyth got her wish right away.

Sources indicate that “I haven’t gotten to do true team running since my cross-country days,” she noted. “It was just a magical experience.”.

A couple team meetings over Zoom, as well as an in-person meeting before the race, helped shoo away some of the awkwardness, Lewis thought. But Smyth said Lewis helped bring the team together during the event, too, with little (even corny) things like running in a fighter jet formation and chanting “U.S.A!” for a lap.

Smyth remembers walking at night and nearly falling asleep before the Ron Express came up behind her. Ron Wireman, competing in his second team championship, struggled early in the race and needed help from others. That first night, he was eager to pay his teammates back and named himself after a train to help them through the dark.

“He mentioned, ‘MEGAN ARE YOU AWAKE?,’” Smyth said.

Recent findings suggest that smyth, just like Dowdle, learned how to ask for help. Later in the race, as the prospect of doing another lap on the steep trail, she requested a “hill sherpa.”.

The team cohesion would be tested right away as Lewis insisted they answer a question democratically: Should they run the road or the trail?

Team USA competes on the original Big’s Backyard Ultra course in mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s literal backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee. On odd years during the individual championship, racers run a trail loop during the day and a road loop at night. This time it was runners’ choice throughout the race.

The road was flatter and easier, but the hard, smooth surface can be problematic for trail runners. Smyth, for instance, said she didn’t bring many pairs of road shoes. But Laz recently made “improvements” to the trail loop that made it steeper, tougher, and slower. The precious minutes saved on the road loop could be the difference between having time to recover, fuel, sleep, and even go to the bathroom, and to DNF.

“There isn’t a lot of wiggle room in a backyard,” Lewis said.

Communication was key as the team tried to accommodate runners struggling with the trail by adding more laps on the road.

According to recent reports, “We were changing things as the race went on,” Noll stated. “Sometimes you didn’t know what course you were doing [on the next lap]. Mentally that can be hard.”.

Ultimately, the back and forth paid off. Eventually emphasizing the road over the trail helped the team squeeze yards from people who may not have been able to continue otherwise.

“If we hadn’t moved to the road, I don’t know if we would have won the race,” Lewis said.

As the third day burned off its final few hours, Australia had a commanding lead of 58 yards over the U.S. The Aussies still had 11 runners in the race; the U.S. was down to 9. Nicholas Steel kept announcing to his U.S. teammates just how far behind they were. More than one American admitted later that they found these updates annoying. Dowdle told himself he didn’t care and tried to enjoy the experience.

But backyard veterans will tell you that the race doesn’t end at hour 70; that’s really when it starts. One Aussie dropped at yard 70, another at 72, two at 73, and two more at 75. By yard 80, nine Aussies had dropped. They had only two runners left—a precarious place to be, given the final runner can only complete one additional lap after the penultimate runner drops. Sure enough, Australia was out by yard 88. We’re not being judgy about this: They were on their third day of running without sleep. But that brutal attrition gave the U.S. a shot.

Sources indicate that suddenly Steel’s updates were inspiring. They would need Dowdle and Noll, the workhorses, to keep doing their magic. But the Americans realized that they could win if they got at least half their runners to yard 75 and several past yard 80.

“The possibility that we could catch up lit a fire under my belly,” Dowdle said, “and I remember thinking, ‘Oh, maybe I do care.’”.

It has been revealed that even the Americans who dropped relatively early decided to stay at the campsite to cheer. This was substantial: Dowdle finished one lap with 15 seconds to go, riding the wave of exhortation to get him across the line in time.

In a recent development, lewis did what he could to keep as many runners out there as possible. He ran with those who were close to dropping, even to his detriment. At times he finished the lap with less than three minutes to go. Lewis, famously, sleeps for a few minutes after every loop, but running with others meant he wasn’t able to do that. Ultimately, he went out for yard 84 but didn’t finish it, a result that Lewis found disappointing.

Industry observers note that “I didn’t have my own rhythm because I was helping others,” Lewis said. “My ultimate goal was to be there for the team, so I sacrificed myself and my own best race for that.”.

That kind of support from teammates, along with the competitive boost the Americans got chasing down Australia, helped push some to their backyard ultra PRs. Nick Petterson made it to 84 yards, 19 more than his previous best. That’s nearly a full day more of running.

According to recent reports, “The team needed you, and that was a really easy thing to grab onto,” Petterson said. “We needed everyone to crank up the numbers. That motivation outside of just myself was really helpful.”.

Petterson thrives off that external focus anyway. During backyards, he enjoys asking others how they’re doing, even though it’s not always reciprocated.

“The team factor was a major driver when times got hard for me,” he said. “I might have gone out earlier if it wasn’t for that.”.

According to recent reports, yoder made it 86 yards, 11 more than his qualifying mark. Ryan Snickles went 69 yards after qualifying with 55. Smyth set a PR by five yards and quit only after her ankle swelled like a balloon. Jeff Walker got 75 yards, 30 more than his qualifier. Even Steel seemed inspired by his own updates. He went 94 yards—177% of his 53-yard qualifier.

Ultimately the U.S. won by a landslide with 1,120 yards to Australia’s 1,069.

Recent findings suggest that it’s the second world title for Team USA in this rapidly developing sub-sport. When the U.S. won in 2022, it was with only 860 yards. Belgium, which has won the other two team titles, took third this year—although two of their runners set the individual backyard ultra world record of 124 yards, or 516.7 miles over five days of running.

“When other runners are hanging on longer,” Lewis noted, “it impacts everyone to hang on longer.”.

Ultimately, Dowdle was the last American standing with 107 yards—a personal best by 13 yards, or 54 miles. Noll got the assist with 106 yards. Despite his initial reticence, Dowdle notes he values moments with his teammates more than his individual national title.

“There was one lap where I broke down crying,” Dowdle said, “and Nick Petterson saw me and put his arm around me and was just with me during that time.”.

Dowdle wouldn’t want the backyard format to be flooded with team events, but he wants to go back:.

“I’m bummed that you have to wait two years for it again.”.
