💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Department of the Interior released a five-year strategic plan Tuesday that outlines the federal government’s intentions to sell public lands, further reduce the workforce at its agencies, and continue to pursue natural resource development for energy dominance.
  • It has been revealed that the 28-page document lists four key goals for fiscal years 2026 through 2030.
  • It has been revealed that “The Department will consolidate its workforce to advance operational efficiencies,” reads the plan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Department of the Interior released a five-year strategic plan Tuesday that outlines the federal government’s intentions to sell public lands, further reduce the workforce at its agencies, and continue to pursue natural resource development for energy dominance.

It has been revealed that the 28-page document lists four key goals for fiscal years 2026 through 2030. One of the most critical sections of the document for the conservation community is nested under the fourth goal of collaborating with states, tribes, and communities:.

It has been revealed that “The Department will consolidate its workforce to advance operational efficiencies,” reads the plan. “The Department will work to decrease the size of the federal estate by offering to states, localities and Tribes the opportunity to purchase federal lands. Through these sales, the Department will be able to focus its resources on primary federal responsibilities and nationally significant federal lands.”.

According to the Interior, the proceeds from sales of lands that aren’t considered “nationally significant” will go toward “purchasing entities to use for conservation purposes elsewhere” for “improved recreation access for American citizens, while at the same time decreasing the federal taxpayer’s financial responsibility to manage federal lands.”.

Industry observers note that “From a hunting and angling perspective, we love the places that are not of national significance,” Backcountry Hunters and Anglers president and CEO Ryan Callaghan tells Outdoor Life (we interviewed him while he was deer hunting a piece of no-name BLM ground out West). “Because they don’t have a big spotlight on them, and that’s where we go to hunt and fish.”.

Selling and transferring federal lands — of any significance — is also wildly unpopular with American outdoorsmen and women.

Recent findings suggest that “I’d need to see the criteria for disposal, but at first blush this flies in the face of overwhelming positive appreciation and sentiment for America’s public lands,” notes Callaghan. “We’ve proved that middle-of-nowhere BLM land in Utah is of national significance during last summer’s budget reconciliation process. From an end-user standpoint, the American people want more public land and a workforce that can manage them responsibly.”.

The staff cuts to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, National Park Service, Bureau of Land Management (as well as the U.S. Forest Service, which is managed by the USDA) have also been a point of contention for hunters and anglers. As we reported in September, key public land agencies have already been chronically understaffed and underfunded for decades, with an accelerated decline under the second Trump administration.

Agency Staff CutsMeasured by direct civilian full-time equivalent.

According to recent reports, the only sectors where the DOI’s strategic proposal promises to add staff are law enforcement and public safety — not conservation roles. That includes building a larger Park Police presence in Washington, D.C. The plan includes no staffing numbers or targets. These priorities are the heart of the objective: “Interior protects Americans and public lands.”.

Transferring federal lands to states poses both the risk of further sell-off to private entities — and greater regulation for hunters, anglers, and outdoor owners in general.

“People have got to understand [the restrictions of state land],” says Callaghan. “You can’t camp on state land in Colorado or Wyoming unless posted. You can’t drive on state land even on established roads unless they’re signed here in Montana. It’s illegal to shoot clay pigeons on state land in Montana. We just literally got de facto public access to our state lands in Montana about 20 years ago. State lands are private lands first, and the public access components come second to the ability to make money off those state lands. You’re not going to have [default state] public access unless it’s compatible in some way.”.

The plan also merges wildland fire programs into the new U.S. Wildland Fire Service as part of a massive restructure of how the federal government fights wildfires.

Burgum also emphasizes the role of “super intelligence” throughout the DOI’s strategic plan.

According to recent reports, “For the first time in human history, we can turn electricity into intelligence,” he writes, in the only bolded line in his letter that prefaces the plan. (Nowhere in the document does the DOI use the phrase “artificial intelligence.”).

The Trump administration is considering proposals for no fewer than a dozen data center projects on public land, as we reported in September. Together, those data centers could impact at least 17,600 acres of public land in the West.

According to recent reports, “At every turn, the proposal prioritizes extraction over conservation, emphasizing the need to pillage our public lands in order to power AI data centers,” Center for Western Priorities communications director Kate Groetzinger remarked in a statement Wednesday. “Of course, that’s no surprise given Burgum’s financial ties to the AI industry. But it flies in the face of the American public, who have made their feelings about data centers abundantly clear.”.

Related: The Rush to Build Data Centers on Public Lands Is Worse Than You Thought.

According to recent reports, in the strategy Burgum directs DOI employees to “harness technology to power efficiency,” pointing to efforts to replace manpower with artificial intelligence. The directive comes just days after the USFWS announced it wanted more “boots on the ground” to better manage our national wildlife refuges.

“Our team is actively expanding domestic energy production and securing our critical minerals supply chain — reducing reliance on foreign adversaries, accelerating innovation and protecting the global environment,” writes Burgum in the proposal. “…Timber, grazing, geothermal energy, hydropower, outdoor recreation, hunting and fishing, mining, oil and gas and more contribute mightily to every facet of American life. As President Theodore Roosevelt, who helped shape and define our department, explained: ‘Conservation means development as much as it does protection.’”.

Burgum is referencing a speech then-former President Roosevelt gave in 1910, in which he spoke forcefully against private interests. The full quote from Roosevelt reads:.

It has been revealed that “Conservation means development as much as it does protection. I recognize the right and duty of this generation to develop and use the natural resources of our land; but I do not recognize the right to waste them, or to rob, by wasteful use, the generations that come after us.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Releasing this [blueprint] anytime would not get positive feedback. Releasing this during the middle of hunting season is absolute proof the people administrating our public lands right now are extremely out of touch with the American people and their needs,” states Callaghan. “You’re not going to stop at a diner, a truck stop, a bar in America right now and find someone wearing hunter orange who says, ‘You know what? I want less of this. What would be good for me, and my kids, and my hunting season now and in the future, would be less land.”.

The DOI’s strategic plan was released on the same day the BLM proposed a rule that would make the goals defined in this plan easier to execute.

Sources indicate that the potential rule is rooted in public-land rule making, but it would essentially overhaul the guidelines for writing BLM resource management prepares. That includes eliminating the 90-day public comment period for major plans, throw out the right now required draft proposal for public comment period, and potentially replace public comment periods with public meetings.

According to recent reports, related: Public Comment Periods Don’t Usually Matter Much to the Feds. Duck Hunters Made a Difference Anyway — for Now.

Sources indicate that “Those plans decide where drilling, mining, and grazing can happen on public lands, and which lands can be sold,” according to the Center for Western Priorities. “Under the Federal Land Policy Management Act, BLM can sell land only after a resource management proposal identifies it for disposal.”.

The proposed BLM rule is open for public comment through Jan. 11, 2027.

Two Hikers Were Killed by a Sow Grizzly with Cubs in ‘Very Rare’ Predatory Attack

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (721 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that two women and four grizzlies are dead near Bella Coola, British Columbia after an unusual and horrific predatory attack.
  • It doesn’t seem real,” Josh Balcarras, a family member, told CBC News.
  • In a recent development, the remains of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, were found November 2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that two women and four grizzlies are dead near Bella Coola, British Columbia after an unusual and horrific predatory attack. A sow with three cubs killed two hikers, a mother-daughter pair who had been missing since November 1. DNA tests confirm the women were killed by the bears.

“It’s surreal. It doesn’t seem real,” Josh Balcarras, a family member, told CBC News. “The way it starts is a few hours of not hearing from them. That turns into a day, and then a night. Then a second night comes and it becomes a real thing.”.

In a recent development, the remains of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, were found November 2. The remains of her daughter, 20-year-old Selah Reed, were found November 3. The two were not far from a trail  in the steep and heavily-wooded Snooka Trail System. Both were buried in caches, something bears often do to hide their food from other animals. Investigators consider the attack to be motivated by predation.

“This attack involved predatory behavior, which I can tell you is very rare,” Jeff Tyre, British Columbia Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) inspector noted in a recorded statement issued November 10. “That is to say, we don’t know how it started but we know how it ended. Out of respect for the family, I’m going to decline to answer what predatory behavior looks like specifically in this case.”.

The mother grizzly bear was in her late teens. Her three cubs were born this year. BCCOS unveiled November 10 that all four were captured and euthanized for their predatory behavior. A week after finding the remains of the second woman, the case is considered closed and trapping equipment has been removed. Nuxalk Nation cultural leaders will decide how the bear remains will be used.

“They all had to be destroyed because bears that are involved in attacks on people cannot be rehabilitated or relocated,” Tyre noted. “This type of behavior presents an extreme risk to the public and such bears are dispatched to protect the public and prevent similar attacks in the future.”.

Industry observers note that this most recent attack happened nearly a year after a grizzly attacked a group of tribal school children who were having lunch in the same region last November. In that case covered by OL, three students and one adult were hospitalized after a grizzly raided their picnic.

Despite the two high-profile incidents, investigators say grizzly bear attacks are not increasing near Bella Coola. They also cross-checked DNA from bears involved in both cases. None of the grizzlies euthanized this year were involved in the group attack last year. That bear was never located.

The tribe renewed its safety protocol during this year’s investigation. It has since lifted curfew but continues nightly patrols and offers escorts to take kids to school.

“This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year’s attack,” stated Samuel Schooner, Nuxalk Nation elected chief. “Our focus continues to be on taking care of our community members.”.

Bella Coola is in the coastal region of British Columbia. Coastal bears and interior bears are genetically the same grizzly species, but their size and diet are different. Coastal bears have access to salmon, a nutrient-rich food source.

“Individual bears with increased access to salmon tend to be larger, have bigger litters, have lower stress hormone levels, and exist at higher densities at a population level,” reads an October 2025 study by Lauren Henson and Kris Christensen published in the scientific journal G3: Genes, Genomes and Genetics. “Interior grizzlies [have] smaller body mass and skull size than coastal individuals.”.

Read Next: These Alaskans Stopped a Charging Grizzly at 5 Yards with Their 10mm Pistols.

It has been revealed that BC’s combined coastal and interior grizzly bear population has increased from 6,600 in the 1970s to 15,000 in 2018. In 2017, BC implemented a controversial grizzly bear hunting ban. Those in favor of the ban believe that a lack of grizzly hunting does not lead to more human fatalities, but organizations opposing the ban refer to recent attacks as reason to re-open the hunt.

Sources indicate that “We have to do something,” Jesse Zeman, B.C. Wildlife Federation executive director told CBC News. “What we’re currently doing is very clearly not working.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, one summer evening, I was hiking a trail near Marias Pass in Glacier National Park, returning to the car after a few hours of wildlife photography at a lake— nothing but deer and mosquitoes to show for it—when I noticed something blondish-brown moving toward me. It barely registered. I felt relaxed, though, truthfully, I’m never fully relaxed.

And then we were on top of each other.

A grizzly cub, massive as an overgrown Saint Bernard. I was fascinated—until reality hit. The mother wouldn’t be far behind.

“Hey, bear,” I shouted, my voice cracking. The cub woofed an alarm and took off to my left, a dark blur swallowed by the forest.

Sources indicate that I turned toward the trail ahead. And—boom—there she was. Running at me, substantial and fast and flat to the ground.

I grabbed the bear spray strapped to my chest, fumbled the can free, and held it out like a pistol. She closed in. I could see the whites.

#9092. A Deer for My Dad: It Was the Biggest Buck of My Life — But Would It Mean Anything to My Fading Father?

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2126 w)
📖 Baca

A Deer for My Dad: It Was the Biggest Buck of My Life — But Would It Mean Anything to My Fading Father?

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the first three deer to come by me were ridge-flat regulars—I’d seen them before, both on trail camera and in person.
  • But I never thought that the cool-looking little deer would be capable of running the gauntlet of hunters during general firearms season, so it was good to see him in this final hour of the final day.
  • In a recent development, it’s always exciting to see deer on the last day of the season, but missing was any rush of adrenaline—for good reason.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the first three deer to come by me were ridge-flat regulars—I’d seen them before, both on trail camera and in person. The lead whitetail, a piebald button buck, was a welcome sight, even though I had cursed him so many times these past few weeks. At first a curiosity, the little buck had become something of a nuisance during bow season due to his ravenous appetite for the apples that covered the leaves near my stone-wall ground stand and his proclivity for busting every good setup.

But I never thought that the cool-looking little deer would be capable of running the gauntlet of hunters during general firearms season, so it was good to see him in this final hour of the final day. A doe and an I’d-probably-shoot-him-on-any-other-day 8-pointer followed, each glowering at their backtrails as they picked their way toward my food plots several hundred yards down the hill.

In a recent development, it’s always exciting to see deer on the last day of the season, but missing was any rush of adrenaline—for good reason. There was another deer around, or at least I hoped that he was still around. It was a buck the likes of which I’d waited my entire life to take. It’s why I never even thought to flick the safety off on the 8-point.

It has been revealed that that other buck had haunted my trail camera for a solid month and left me day- (and night) dreaming of killing him. In a land of dinks and almost-shooters, this was a bona fide stud. Hell, he’d qualify as such in Kansas. He was a perfect 10-point, so symmetrical that I thought my buddies were playing some sort of cruel practical joke on me when I first saw the photos. What would he score? Who knew? Who cared? I surely didn’t. But what I did know was that I’d never seen a larger rack on any buck on my family’s property in all the years of living there—nor had anyone else who hunted our little patch of Latest England deer woods.

I barely had time to wonder why those first three deer might be so unnerved when a single thought screamed in my brain….

Sources indicate that that simple word and a thin smile were pretty much the only signs of acknowledgement Dad had been capable of during Thanksgiving dinner two weeks earlier. In addition to some snapshots I’d taken of our deer camp, I had downloaded a couple dozen trail-camera photos to my phone to show him in the hope that seeing a photo of that buck on his property might ignite a spark of recognition in his brain—that he’d somehow come back to me even if only for a moment or two. You see, that’s mostly what we—families of Alzheimer’s sufferers—pray for. Something. Anything. A glimpse or a glint, some little part of the old Dad would do. And I got that little gift.

If there’s a more insidious disease than Alzheimer’s, I certainly can’t conceive of it. What other ailment kills a host’s loved ones years before actually killing the host? And make no mistake, my family (no different from any other Alzheimer’s family) has been dying in fits and starts for more than a decade. No one is capable of standing by helplessly while watching a father, a spouse, or a dear friend fight their own mind without losing a part of themselves. Even harder is watching a once-brilliant engineer, capable of taking anything apart and putting it back together, struggle for hours on end to solve simple word-search puzzles.

In a recent development, truth be known, Dad wasn’t really a deer nut—never shot one, actually—but he did hunt with me each season and both tolerated and nurtured my addiction to chasing whitetails. He bought me my first deer-hunting coat when I was 15, and he lugged an extension ladder a half mile through the woods to build my first treestand. We drove three hours through a ferocious ice storm in his brown Buick LeSabre one Thanksgiving night just because I told him that the bowhunting the next morning would be incredible after such a weather event. He gave me my first sip of whiskey after I spent too many hours in that same stand during a blizzard. Even though it’s been years since Dad has hunted, he always liked to hear my stories of deer missed or deer killed and other adventures at our family’s little hunting camp—or at least it seemed as if he did.

Recent findings suggest that somehow, the trail-camera photo of the huge buck brought that particular Dad back to me, if only for a moment before he went away again. But it was enough—I knew that he knew. And so it was that after 1 ½ months of frustration during bow season, and much of the same during the firearms hunt, I felt the sort of motivation I remember feeling two decades ago, when he and I used to sit within sight of each other in the deer woods and I wished for a buck to walk by so that I could do my dad proud. I decided that I needed to show Dad one more photo—the one in which I’m holding that buck’s rack in my hands in front of the camp where he and I had spent the greatest days of our lives.

Just five minutes or so after the last of the three deer walked out of sight, I finally spotted the reason for their preoccupation. Even at 80 yards there was no mistaking him—that magnificent rack, burly body, and gait of dominance. It was the one I had come to think of as Dad’s deer. Whether it was the cautiousness of his years or my impatience, I still can’t be sure, but the damned buck seemed not to move no matter how hard I wished him to—neither­ would he give me a broadside shot. This stasis lasted long minutes and was physically draining. I didn’t dare stare him directly in the eyes, but I didn’t dare look away either. When he’d finally take a noiseless step, he’d stop to scrutinize the frozen woods, and it seemed his intensity bored right into me. He closed from 80 to 50 yards but I still hadn’t heard a footfall on the frost-brittle leaves. He still would not turn broadside.

Okay, I’ll shoot you dead-on facing me if I need to, you substantial bastard, I thought. It’s not ideal, but if you get too close I’m going to shoot. I’m not gonna blow this one.

Industry observers note that as if eavesdropping on my conversation with myself, the buck somehow cut the distance to 35 yards, though I swear I didn’t see him take a step. And then he turned. Using my knee as a solid rest, I snicked the safety forward, put the shotgun’s bead on his chest, and squeezed it off. The major buck kicked high with his rear legs—a good thing—before tearing off for parts unknown—a very bad thing. Then the woods became still again. I sat there in agony listening for many soundless minutes and fighting off the urge to run to the place where the buck last stood. As much as I wished to see him lying there dead in the light skiff of snow, to run my hands along his main beams, I feared more the agonizing what-ifs.

What if he was still alive and I pushed him to a nearby hunter, who shot him?

What if he was still alive and I pushed him into some far-off thicket, never to be recovered?

What if I missed him completely?

What if I wouldn’t be able to show Dad that single, all-revealing photograph?

Diminishing daylight made the decision to give the buck time a bit easier. Judging from his size on the trail camera, I’d need help getting him out of the woods anyway. I’d go back to camp, have a beer or two to calm down, and make a few phone calls.

Three torment-filled hours later, I finally received a return call.

It has been revealed that “You got him,” stated a familiar voice on the other end of the line, not in the form of a question, but rather a statement. “We’re all at a Christmas party, but give me 20 minutes and I’ll be there.” I never got the chance to respond before the phone clicked. The cavalry was on its way. If anyone could help me find the buck, it was my friend Rich Hamilton.

Industry observers note that in typical subdued fashion, Rich walked through the door, asked to hear the story, then wasted no time heading out the door again. Although he’d not been there with me, he took the lead in our search for blood.

Recent findings suggest that “Well, this ain’t worth a sh&$,” he said when the beam of his flashlight hit a single drop on the snow. “Not worth a sh&$ at all.”.

Sources indicate that and he was right. Even with the skiff of snow on the ground, it was difficult to find a second drop. The hoped-for salvation of all sunset shooters—a blood trail a blind man could follow—was not revealing itself. My heart sank.

Sources indicate that “Well, he fell here,” Rich deadpanned, now following the running tracks in the windblown spots of snow. “Fell here, too.”.

Our flashlight beams fell on the giant rack simultaneously. He hadn’t gone more than 50 yards.

According to recent reports, “Look at that giant son of a bitch,” Rich said. “Oh…my…God.”.

I’d never before seen a more magnificent sight. Dad’s deer had come to rest in a boggy thicket amid a jungle of briars, his rack seemingly floating 5 feet above the ground. Under the moonlight, we could see the faint lights of camp and billowing woodsmoke pouring from the chimney. We unashamedly hugged and shouted, then struggled to get the major deer onto a dry hummock for field dressing. In all honesty, I was of no help.

In a recent development, “Here, hold the flashlight,” Rich stated after my first header into the muck. “I need to gut this deer. I want to gut this deer.”.

An hour later, and too tired to move him any farther, much less hang him up, Rich and I wrestled the buck to the top of the basement woodpile. We stepped back a few feet to simply stare at the deer for the first time in full light—at a complete loss for words.

Recent findings suggest that after Rich left, I stood and stared some more—long into the night—just me with the buck and thoughts of a hunting season incomparable and unreproducible. And of my Dad. By the next day, everyone who cared to hear the story, and some who didn’t, came by the house. After a while, 10 of us—each grabbing an antler, a hoof, a leg, or the tail—carried the buck outside and into the sunshine. Embarrassingly unprepared for a photo session, I handed my camera phone to one of the kids and asked him to click off a few pictures. I really only needed one.

Instead of fading with time, my exhilaration seemed to grow in the days that followed. I told the story countless dozens of times and emailed photos to friends around the country, but it wouldn’t be until Christmas Day, two weeks later, that I would see Mom and Dad.

Recent findings suggest that “He’s not having such a good day today,” my mom mentioned when she hugged me at the front door. “Just sit with him for a while.”.

And I did. I told him our story and demonstrated him our buck, but his eyes remained focused on the word-search puzzle book in his lap, as he haltingly circled letters—the sound of my voice either unheard or completely foreign.

Somehow, my daughter, Amy, has always been able to garner Dad’s instant attention, and she did again on Christmas Day.

“Merry Christmas,” Dad noted as Amy hugged him in his chair, word-search book falling to the floor. The hours Mom spent rehearsing those two words with him had paid off. Tears welled in his eyes as he smiled at a face he fought his own brain to recognize.

Read Next: ‘The Safety Was On!’ I Nearly Missed My Chance at a Big Adirondack Buck.

I picked up his book as they hugged, Amy trying in vain to engage Dad in conversation but getting no response. Glancing down at the crumpled page, my eyes focused on three circled letters: D-O-E.

My Dad was back, if only for a moment or two, before he was gone again.

Recent findings suggest that “He jumped but never knew what hit him. He moved away at a fast walk, got behind some cover and I thought I heard him crash, but it was wet and rainy, so I wasn’t sure.”.

In a recent development, the best winter hiking and snowshoeing pants are highly breathable softshell pants that prevent perspiration from accumulating when hiking, snowshoeing, climbing/mountaineering, or even ski touring in winter. They’re made with woven nylon or polyester, which is warmer and more windproof than standard three-season hiking pants, and are treated with an exterior DWR coating to help repel water. Many softshell pants have features that can be used for multiple winter sports, while others are more hiking-specific. The fit also varies by activity: climbing-style pants tend to run slim, while hiking/snowshoeing pants are roomier and easier to layer. Popular features include a buried/integrated belt providing for hipbelt and climbing harness compatibility, zippered side vents, zippered pockets, and ankle adjustability. Be sure to read our FAQ below about how to choose the best softshell winter pants for your needs.

Here are the 10 best softshell winter hiking and snowshoeing pants that we recommend.

According to recent reports, many experienced winter hikers prefer softshell winter pants because they’re simpler to use than wearing rain pants over a pair of long underwear. Softshell pants are also more form-fitting and don’t make any noise. The problem with rain pants and long underwear is that it can be difficult to vent your rain pants or take off your long underwear without first removing your rain pants and boots. Softshell pants are breathable enough, meaning that your sweat will evaporate through them if you start to warm up and perspire.

Sources indicate that softshell pants are good for snow because they have a DWR coating on the exterior that repels water and they’re highly breathable so you don’t overheat. Hiking in snow or snowshoeing requires a lot of energy and it’s easy to overheat and perspire. You want to avoid getting too warm and sweating because it will wet your clothing and reduce its ability to insulate you.

In a recent development, softshell pants are far more breathable than the waterproof rain pants that some hikers wear, so you’ll stay cooler and perspire less when working hard when hiking up mountains or snowshoeing. While they have an external DWR repellent coating for enhanced rain resistance, they are not waterproof or as windproof as hard shell rain pants. We recommend carrying both softshell pants and rain pants on cold-weather hikes, the latter for rain and wind protection, as well as added warmth when layered over the softshell pants.

Softshell pants are more windproof and warmer than regular hiking pants, but they’re designed to be highly breathable and let some wind through. If you need protection from the wind, we’d recommend layering a pair of wind pants or rain pants over a pair of softshell pants when you need added wind protection.

You can wear a baselayer (long underwear) under softshell pants, but it’s often not necessary except on extremely cold days. Softshell pants are warmer than regular hiking pants and usually sufficient to keep you warm when you’re actively hiking or snowshoeing. If you need additional warmth because you’re being chilled by the wind or because you’re standing still and not moving and generating heat, you can warm up by wearing a pair of rain pants over your softshell pants. Also, if you wear a baselayer under softshell pants and find yourself overheating, it’s very difficult to delayer without taking off your boots and pants, unless your baselayer long underwear has side zips and is removable without requiring that you get undressed.

It has been revealed that ski pants are usually much heavier, bulkier, and warmer since there is so much start and stop activity involved especially if you’re skiing at a resort with chair lifts. many ski pants also have internal gaiters which are hot and awkward to use when hiking and snowshoeing.

It has been revealed that A buried or integrated pants belt loops around your waist like a regular belt but is covered with fabric around the back and sides of the pant. This makes the belt compatible with a climbing harness or a backpack hipbelt. When climbing higher mountains, you may be required to rope-in with a climbing harness.

Softshell pants have zippered pockets that are usually located in front of the pants and are positioned so they can be easily accessed even if you’re wearing a climbing harness. Zippered pockets are more streamlined than regular pockets and less likely to interfere with gear hanging from a climbing harness.

Some softshell pants have a built-in ankle cuff on the inside of the legs to provide crampon protection when climbing, backcountry skiing, or winter hiking. The ankle cuff isn’t as substantial as a high gaiter and doesn’t replace wearing them, but can be a useful convenience for winter use, especially if you want to use the same pants for ski touring.

Articulated knees are baggier than the knees in regular pants and provide more freedom of movement especially for climbing.

Gussetted pants have added fabric panels, usually triangular, that add more width to the crotch, making it easier to raise your knee when taking large steps or climbing vertical surfaces.

Palmer was midspan on the Tunitas Creek Bridge, southbound, when the boat came into view through the gunsight notch of the arroyo. It was a Whaler circling clockwise fast and tight, maybe a quarter mile beyond the surf.

He’d wanted to ride a few waves at a sandbar that had been assembling itself over the past few days at Pomponio. A quick lunch-break session before the wind came up. But then he got the call about the boat, and now that he saw it spinning he also saw that his day was officially fucked. He crossed the bridge and powered up the Coast Highway to the overlook at the top of the rise. He lifted his Bushnells from the dashboard and got out of the truck and glassed the vessel.

It has been revealed that the wake’s widening spiral told him the wheel had been hard to starboard a good long while. It looked to be stirring up some kind of suicidal whirlpool.

It has been revealed that since our very first issue published in 1898, Outdoor Life has covered outdoor gear with independence and rigor. From Jack O’Connor’s old gun columns to today’s in-depth video reviews, field testing gear and reporting the results has always been part of our publication’s DNA.

It has been revealed that which is why I am excited to now introduce our upcoming online gear shop, which represents the culmination of more than a century of gear coverage. This new online retail site will carry a wide variety of quality outdoor products, and purchases made from the site will help to power the Outdoor Life you know and love into the future. There are a few key points that longtime OL readers should know.

According to recent reports, if you’ve followed Outdoor Life closely, you know that we’re not scared to piss off folks on occasion. This often includes manufacturers who have overhyped their products. That’s because we believe that reader trust is OL’s single most important asset. If we report the truth, good or bad, we have faith that you will keep coming back. This has been the promise that the OL editors made at the very beginning, and it’s the contract we uphold today.

It has been revealed that in all of our gear reviews and buying guides, we will continue to celebrate the top-performing products (whether they are carried in the Outdoor Life shop or not). Likewise, if a product falls short, we’ll continue to call out those flaws.

Industry observers note that unlike some other media outlets in our space, we have no editorial obligation to a single brand. We shoot, hunt with, and wear whatever is latest and noteworthy, because that makes the most interesting content. This will continue, regardless of which brands are carried in the shop. Simply scan a few of our recent gear reviews (like our rifle scope test or binocular test) and you will find this to be true.

It has been revealed that over time, the shop will begin to host content from the hundreds of gear reviews we’ve written through the years. Beyond basic specs and product descriptions, the Outdoor Life shop will include details about how the products actually performed during testing. Our “editor’s picks” will highlight the top performing items in a category. Video reviews will show how products work (or don’t work) in the field.

Our aim will be to educate the reader, or potential customer, about the gear they are considering buying, whether they end up buying it from us or someone else.

The OL team is proud that we already spend a ton of time and effort producing the most in-depth gun and gear reviews in the outdoor space. We have been able to fund these efforts by linking to online retailers who sell the gear that we cover. If one of our readers purchases a product from these online retailers, we made a small commission. Added up over the course of the year, these commissions become a meaningful source of revenue that powers our editorial team to create more content.

At its best, it’s a system of meritocracy. Those who create the best content grow the biggest audiences and, in turn, make the most money — to make more content.

According to recent reports, but that system has been corrupted with the popularization of Artificial Intelligence. Now, more and more folks are simply asking ChatGPT or Claude, “what’s the best wader for duck hunting?” These chatbots scrape online articles to produce an answer for the user, who then makes their purchase. That hunter will rarely see the original source material. In other words they will never come to our reviews and field tests at Outdoor Life.

According to recent reports, and the chatbots don’t much care if they are lifting content from OutdoorLife.com or someone’s basement blog, or even a manufacturer’s own website. In time, this will lead to the degradation (I believe the modern term is “enshittification”) of  gear reviews, and, well, first-hand expert information in general.

In a recent development, our way to combat this is to own the online shop ourselves. We believe that so long as we have the best and most thorough information, and the best available products, the reader will end up with us.

Sources indicate that in the weeks and months to come, we will be adding many more brands and gear categories to the shop. We’ll be offering deals on select products that have performed admirably in our field testing. And we’ll be turning out a lot more stories and videos.

If you’re looking to purchase some new gear, I do hope you check out the OL shop. But the truth is, there are many reasons to love the outdoors and our passion for quality gear is only a sliver of Outdoor Life. So, after all these years, thank you for reading, following, and watching.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in quite the feat of boots-on-the-ground journalism, author Dan England raced Jess’ Backyard Ultra on August 9, 2024. (Don’t ask him about the race name grammar.) He also spoke with backyard ultra mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell, several other backyard ultra race directors, and key backyard ultra runners, including Harvey Lewis and Maggie Guterl. What he found is that the format of running a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour until only one runner remains is about so much more than running in circles. Since this article was originally published on Outside Run in 2024, backyard ultras have further entered the mainstream with the rise of figures like Mark Dowdle, Belgium resetting the world record, and Team USA winning the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship.

It’s 8:55 P.M. on Friday, August 9, and I’m with a small group of runners huddled together in a tent on a farm near Greeley, Colorado, that momentarily shelters us from our bad life decisions.

Outside the tent awaits pouring rain and a mushy race course complete with the “Plank of Doom”—a pink makeshift “bridge” adorned in purple twinkle lights suspended four feet over a drainage ditch full of stormwater.

Before the starting gun of this backyard ultra goes off in five minutes, Jessy Nelson needs to make an announcement. I’m assuming it will be about safety. Instead, she tells us that she is not a narcissist.

Yes, Jess’ Backyard Ultra does carry her name. But she named the race for about a dozen friends, all named Jess. (Seriously!). She met them all in an online chat group during a 1,000-kilometer Great Virtual Race Across The States.

Nelson started the race on her farm for them in 2021 with the hope that one Jess could run far enough to qualify for Massive’s Backyard Ultra—the original Bell Buckle, Tennessee, “backyard ultra” event that pioneered a quirky latest kind of endurance racing format in which runners must complete a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour until they can no longer accomplish the task.

For the record, this event is Jess’ Big Backyard Ultra, not Jessy’s. Understand?

It has been revealed that we nod as the rain comes down harder. It would be a fun, goofy, quaint little race that seems to match the aesthetic of many backyard ultras across the world, except it’s been raining for three days, transforming the dirt roads on which we will run into what seems like gooey Jello pudding.

Industry observers note that nelson is worried. The Plank of Doom is seriously dangerous, she tells us. Sure, it’s pink and twinkly, but the four-foot fall that could result with any misstep could mean a broken ankle or, according to Nelson’s narrowed eyes, instant death. Nelson is so serious about the plank that she forces the four of us competing to vote to keep it on the course instead of bypassing it through a paved road 100 yards to the south. We vote to keep it, 3-1.

Recent findings suggest that it’s hard to take anything Nelson indicates seriously, given that this is a race seemingly held on the set of Little House on the Prairie and that a stuffed toy squirrel named Skittles awaits us in a rocking chair at the turnaround to our 4-ish-mile loop. One of the Jesses befriended a squirrel in her backyard, you see, and that’s a tribute to her. Nelson once befriended an eagle, who would follow her during her daily 10-mile loops around her property. But now, she presumes, the eagle is taking cover. We are about to do the opposite.

Nelson’s odd race is now one of an estimated 500 backyard ultras held around the world that are certified by concept creator Gary Cantrell. You may know him as Lazarus Lake, or simply Laz. He is  probably the sport’s most famous race director and certainly  the quirkiest. Cantrell is known first and foremost for creating the Barkley Marathons, a grueling 100-plus-mile largely off-trail race in Tennessee that’s considered to be the world’s hardest running race to complete. While there’s only one Barkley Marathons, Cantrell’s backyard race format has boomed over the past five years or so.

According to recent reports, there is no predefined end length or time in a backyard ultra, as long as multiple runners can complete each 4.167-mile loop within an hour. (Cantrell chose that peculiar distance because running 4.167 miles per hour is exactly what it takes to run 100 miles in 24 hours.) A race ends when only one runner remains to complete a lap and is declared the winner, while all other runners are relegated to did not finish (DNF) status with whatever total number of laps they are able to complete. The runner who completes the second-most laps in a race is often referred to as the “assist,” in the sense that their effort is ultimately what determines how long the race is allowed to continue.

Most backyard races are not like Cantrell’s Significant’s Backyard Ultra, which, even though it maintains a grassroots feel, has gained worldwide fame and is filled with elite runners. Most backyard races are more like Nelson’s: small, fun and grueling little get-togethers that last a couple days and bring most runners to tears. Most backyard race directors are like Nelson, too; they have“real” jobs outside of race directing and simply love the format and camaraderie their events foster amid runners of all ability levels pushing  themselves beyond what they ever thought possible.

When Cantrell started his race and named it after his pit bull, Significant, in 2012, he hoped to have enough interest for just one event. He was pleasantly surprised when people asked if there would be another race the following  year. Now tens of thousands will likely tune in to the livestream to watch this year’s race on October 19. Cantrell guesstimates more than 25,000 people have run in a backyard ultra event this year, and those are just in the races he’s certified: He knows there are probably dozens more who don’t bother with the paperwork.

“The continued growth really has been a surprise for me,” Cantrell noted. Indeed, there are backyard races in 83 countries now. Even the renowned Tarahumara tribe of Indigenous people from Chihuahua, Mexico, (aka the Raramuri people, who were profiled in the 2009 Fresh York Times bestseller Born to Run,) have their own race, Cantrell noted.

Recent findings suggest that cantrell relishes putting on the world’s hardest events, almost to a sadistic degree. Only 20 individuals have finished the Barkley Marathons since he began it in 1986. It’s a race as ominous as its location, Frozen Head State Park in Tennessee. The race, over 100 miles with a staggering 65,000-feet-plus of elevation gain, is a miserable quest for survival through thorn-infested bramble, often terrible weather, and ridiculously steep hills on a “course” with no real route.

It has been revealed that he started Massive’s as another way to test people, and at times, it resembles Stephen King’s The Long Walk, a fictional horror story about 100 walkers who are forced to trudge hundreds of miles and are shot when they quit. Big’s format is also horrifyingly simple: Run 4.167 miles, a “yard,” in under an hour, and then line up and do it again, and again, and again, on the hour, until one person is left. No breaks from the on-the-hour start are allowed, not even to use the porta-potty, but if you finish the yard early, you can eat and drink to your heart’s content, sleep a few minutes, and yes, answer nature’s call. Last year’s winner, accomplished Cinncinnati ultrarunner Harvey Lewis, set a world record by running 450 miles over 108 hours—or four and a half days.

Sources indicate that cantrell now finds himself surprised not only by the race format’s popularity but also the allure many runners have found in the design. These backyard races are, like Nelson’s race, more about community and the comradery of people pushing each other to go farther than they ever have than about fighting your competitors to the near death. While the format becomes exponentially more grueling over time as variables like sleep deprivation escalate, for the first 24 hours or so, the backyard ultra format is an approachable way for many to cover a very long distance. And Cantrell admits that he likes what these mom and pop backyard races have become.

“There are a lot of aspects to it that I didn’t really consider,” he mentioned. “I do know we get a lot of people who never thought they could ever run an ultra. It’s a race for everyone.”.

Cantrell thought of the idea for a backyard race close to 50 years ago, when he was in high school struggling to keep up with the fast kids on his track team during interval workouts. He noticed by the end of an interval he was often a little closer to their heels.

In a recent development, “I’d get left in the dust early, but eventually, I’d wear them down,” he remarked. “So in a 4-mph race, I thought I could beat everybody.”.

The idea stayed in the recesses of his mind until he could do something about it on his property in central Tennessee. He didn’t have the money to put on a big race, but with the format, all he needed was a stopwatch.

“This format doesn’t require very much,” Cantrell stated. “I think that’s why it’s caught on.”.

It has been revealed that it’s also caught on because it’s spectator-friendly—both online and in person—perhaps more so than any other race not on a track. It not only made a household name out of Lewis but acted as a coming-out party for Courtney Dauwalter when the two went head-to-head for nearly 20 hours in 2020 and ran a total of 283 miles before Dauwalter outlasted him by a lap and won. Cantrell stated this was another aspect of the race he didn’t consider, and it’s partly what makes it fun.

“Women are on an equal competitive footing with men,” he said, and indeed, Maggie Guterl also won Major’s Backyard Ultra, now considered the format’s national championship, in 2019.

The format, Cantrell mentioned, is supposed to measure willpower, not VO2 max or speed or other aspects of physiological talent. There are enough races for that. Instead, Big’s measures grit—the one thing he had over those speedy, more talented guys on the track in high school.

“The most challenging part,” Cantrell said, “should be the distance between the chair and the starting corral.”.

It has been revealed that tens of thousands were captivated last year by Lewis’s win, his second at Significant’s Backyard, which Cantrell now livestreams and provides real-time written commentary. Lewis was already well known for winning the 135-mile Badwater Ultramarathon in 2014, but he wasn’t taken seriously as a trail runner when he first entered Big’s in 2017, he remarked.

“I like the trails though,” Lewis mentioned. “I’m very strategic. They were doing it wrong. Everyone was running up the first hill, and I was in the back, just walking up. The next day, everyone walked up the hill.”.

It has been revealed that lewis kept going even after making a lap by just a second. He eventually gave in after 200 miles, taking the assist, but it made him wonder just how far he could go. He decided to devote part of his life to it.

“Significant’s is so great,” Lewis remarked. “You’re walking into an ultimate game board, with strategy, perseverance, and skill level. The course itself is nothing special, and it’s usually that way with a lot of them. The genius is behind the format.”.

According to recent reports, lewis races at Significant’s to win, no doubt, but as a teacher at the School for Creative and Performing Arts in Cincinnati his living does not depend on it. (Good thing, as there’s no prize money anyway.), Despite his competitive drive, he’s learned to relish in the non-competitive moments on the course and treasures his two assists as much as his wins.

Last year, he indicates his goal was as much to help get runners through the third night as it was to outlast them all. He remembers 2020 mostly for the way he and Dauwalter spent nearly a full day and night taking turns leading the race and pushing each other to approach 300 miles, a number that was, at the time, unheard of to run in this format. Lewis called it a “collaboration” instead of a race. It was a much-needed feel-good story during the pandemic delivered by two nice people.

“We were very encouraging of each other,” Lewis noted.

This is one of the evolutions of the race that took Cantrell by surprise: Backyard races build community among runners with different ability levels because of the unique format. Many other ultras around the world are in intimidating places for beginners, but the accessible four-mile loop obliterates those fears.

Mandy Mullen, the owner of run.Windsor in Windsor, Colorado, changed the format from a 50K to a backyard race for her Weld Your Mettle ultramarathon because it helped foster that community aspect.

Industry observers note that “There’s so much more to running than just running,” Mullen noted. “In this the competition goes away, and it’s more teamwork. There’s zero of, ‘I want to beat this person.’”.

According to recent reports, katie Stroud is the president of a running and walking club that’s existed since 1979 in Alice Springs, a small town in the desert of Australia. She hosted the second annual backyard ultra this year as a part of the races the club puts on.

“It’s such a terrific format for people to push their distance in such a wonderful and supportive way,” Stroud said. “It’s so much more than people running in circles.”.

In a recent development, indeed, Cantrell believes more people ran 100 miles in 24 hours, a benchmark so elite that races usually give out special belt buckles to those who do it, this year in backyard events than all the other ultramarathons around the world combined. The final two left standing this year in Alice Springs, Stroud said, were running buddies who just wanted to push each other to 100 miles.

“There are all these little moments like that in our event every year,” Stroud said. “It’s really cool to be there for that.”.

Carl Worth was another one who caught the backyard bug. Even though he’d never run more than a half marathon, he ran the virtual backyard race during the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020 and astonished himself by covering 54 miles. He liked the camaraderie and community of backyard running so much he began organizing the Banana Slug Backyard Ultra the following year in Oregon’s Champoeg State Park.

At this year’s event, the winner ran for 49 hours and 200 miles for a “Silver Ticket,” which qualifies him for Big’s Backyard, since the Slug was one of the six events where the winner qualified him for the World Team Championships.

But Worth prefers not to focus only on the winner. During the race, he puts up a spreadsheet on a TV—he’s a software engineer by trade—and posts everyone’s longest distance they’ve run. Whenever they break it, and many do, they can ring a bell, a tradition that Cantrell established at his own race. At this year’s Banana Slug event, 34 runners surpassed their personal bests.

“It’s a really satisfying thing to put on as a race director,” Worth remarked. “You get to see some amazing things.”.

This is true for Jess’ Backyard Ultra as well. The sun rises, illuminating the gray sky and shining some welcome light on our muddy trails. Nelson decides to take a small nap at the house. Our fourth competitor rolled her ankle in the wee hours of the morning, making my friend, Bret Naber, the winner after 30 miles, but we decided to run through the night and see how far we could go. At 9 A.M., after 12 hours and 50 miles of running through the mud, we go home for a shower and some sleep.

In a recent development, this year’s Substantial’s Backyard Ultra on October 19 is the biannual international team competition, called the World Satellite Backyard Team Competition. Team USA will compete at Cantrell’s event in Tennessee, and the 15-member U.S. roster will have at least two women, Megan Eckert, who won the Saguaro Showdown Backyard Ultra in Mesa, Arizona, and Jennifer Russo, who won Ohio’s Backyard Ultra, as well as Lewis and Scott Martin, the three-time winner of the Banana Slug race put on by Worth.

It has been revealed that cantrell said there are 68 national teams, the members of which will compete simultaneously in backyard ultras in their home countries to earn points for their teams. It’s much like the Olympics—with each country enjoying a home field advantage—and it makes you wonder if this event will finally get ultrarunning there.

It has been revealed that “I think you have to reasonably see how it goes,” Cantrell said. “A lot of things start up, and they are really popular, and then they fade out. Maybe somebody more politically skilled than me could get it there.”.

But Cantrell’s favorite part about the race format isn’t the superstars, even if his own includes some of the most elite ultrarunners in the world. It’s that time isn’t a factor. It’s about the distance you run, and if you run a personal best, you get recognized for it, even if you finish 30 seconds before the bell.

“The age groups in other races are won by the same people over and over,” Cantrell said. “But in this one, everyone has their day.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

According to recent reports, some people dream of assembling a long-range rifle capable of ringing one-MOA targets at 1,000 yards. Others dream of an ultralight mountain rifle that’s easy to carry for miles and can make a single precision shot. I dream of an ultra-quiet, accurate, and handy rifle for dropping squirrels out of trees. Here’s how I turned a CZ 457 into my dream gun and how it performed in my testing this fall.

Industry observers note that the base rifle for this build is a CZ 457 American. I kept the American’s stock because I love a wood stock on a hunting rifle, and its ergonomics work great for squirrel hunting. There are a ton of ultralight chassis you can go with, but wood and squirrel hunting just go together. I did have to sand down the inside of the stock to create room for the upcoming barrel, but that’s easy to do with a palm sander, a dowel wrapped in sandpaper, or every garage gunsmith’s favorite tool: a Dremel.

Read Next: CZ 457 American Review.

Lilja makes CZ 457 pre-fit barrels that are fantastic for competition shooting, but I wanted something lighter. That’s why I went with a 16-inch Proof Research pre-fit barrel. One of the great things about the CZ 457 is that the barrel changes are a piece of cake. You simply loosen two set screws to remove the barrel and the fresh one slides right into the action.

Recent findings suggest that the entire Nightforce NX6 line is fantastic, and the 2-12x F1 variant is perfect for a versatile rimfire. It can take a 50-yard head shot on a squirrel or snap shoot one up close. It also makes this rifle excellent for shooting long range. Dialing in to 300 yards and ringing steel is quite easy with this setup. The scope is fairly light and short, so I don’t think I’m giving up much in terms of weight compared to a traditional 3-9x, but I’m gaining a lot of capability and versatility.

In a recent development, this suppressor is quiet, light, relatively affordable, and easy to clean — everything I look for in a .22 can. There are plenty of other great options like the Dead Air RXD22Ti and the CAT BEN 22 Ti. A .22 silencer is a must-have accessory because it makes shooting a rimfire significantly more fun.

Recent findings suggest that I added an Area 419 CZ 457 Scope Base and bolt handle to my 457 action. The rail makes it much easier to mount scopes and adds some elevation, so I can plink with this rifle out to 300 yards. The bolt handle makes running the bolt easier than the stock round one. One final upgrade I’d like to make is the Timney CZ 457 Trigger.

Recent findings suggest that for accuracy testing, I shot SK Rifle Match, Lapua Center X, and CCI Select. I shot five, five-shot groups with each. All three averaged around a 1/2-inch group at 50 yards. I was most impressed by how well this barrel shot CCI Select, which is relatively inexpensive compared to other ammo I shot.

The new barrel is definitely accurate, and it also made this rifle significantly easier to maneuver in the woods. With the rifle slung over my shoulder it was unobtrusive as I weaved my way through thick cover. When I saw a squirrel, the rifle came to my shoulder rapidly and was easy to get stable.

The result of this build is a rifle that’s fun to shoot on the range and a joy to carry in the woods. To me, it perfectly blends a nostalgic wood-stock rifle with modern features. Is it a bit extreme for a squirrel gun? You betcha. But I love this rifle all the same.

#9082. Tech Report: No Cameras, No Bait. Old-School Tactics Pay Off for Ohio Bowhunter with 190-Class Buck

Tech Report: No Cameras, No Bait. Old-School Tactics Pay Off for Ohio Bowhunter with 190-Class Buck

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (656 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was Dave Talbott’s first year hunting a small farm in southeast Ohio.
  • In a recent development, “I never walked the farm until the week just before bow season opened,” says Talbott, who lives in Logan.
  • Talbott didn’t set any trail cameras or bait.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was Dave Talbott’s first year hunting a small farm in southeast Ohio. The property, which is owned by a family friend, has rolling hills and steep hardwoods and is scattered with hayfields.

In a recent development, “I never walked the farm until the week just before bow season opened,” says Talbott, who lives in Logan. “I found good deer sign, with lots of buck rubs on trees.”.

Talbott didn’t set any trail cameras or bait. Instead, when the season opened, he just walked the woods, scouting and hunting different locations. He used a lightweight tree saddle and climbing sticks to check areas swiftly and quietly.

“I sat in six different trees over 12 hunts, moving according to wind and weather conditions,” says the 26-year-old, who works in heavy construction.

On the morning of Nov. 7, he hunted a pinch point where he knew a few does were bedded.

“But I didn’t like the place and started walking the farm again when I climbed down that morning.”.

Industry observers note that it was the first cold day of autumn, cloudy and with temperatures around 40 degrees. Talbott located a couple of fresh scrapes, and climbed into a nearby tree around 1:30 p.m. to hunt that afternoon. He didn’t see much until about 4:30. That’s when he spotted a massive deer headed his way along the field edge.

“I knew he was big, and a shooter, and it all happened very fast.”.

Sources indicate that when the buck stepped behind some brush 15 yards from Talbott, he drew. The deer stepped into an opening, and Talbott released his arrow.

Recent findings suggest that talbott saw the deer run about 30 yards and, pouring blood, enter the timber toward a distant hayfield. Then it disappeared over a hill.

Recent findings suggest that “I was shaking uncontrollably when I called my wife, dad, and best friend [Brady Garren] and told them what had happened,” Talbott notes. “Dad and Brady got there after sunset to help me look.”.

Industry observers note that carrying flashlights, the three men followed a blood trail for about 150 yards. But the trail petered out. Then they heard thrashing in a nearby ravine. Thinking it might be Talbott’s buck, they backed out and called in Triple BC Deer Drone Recovery for assistance.

“They got there with a drone a couple hours later,” says Talbott. “They flew the drone to where we last found blood and in just a minute the buck was found in the ravine, but its head was up.”.

Recent findings suggest that they waited an hour and flew the drone again but saw just a slight movement from the buck. An hour later when they flew the drone a third and final time, they saw the buck was dead.

By then, around 11:30 p.m., more friends had arrived and seven people went into the ravine to help haul out Talbott’s huge buck.

It has been revealed that “I knew he was a great buck, but I had no idea he was that massive until I walked up to him,” Talbott notes. “I was beyond ecstatic.”.

According to recent reports, it was after midnight by the time they field dressed the buck and dragged it 600 yards to the truck. They loaded it and drove to a friend’s cooler.

The next day Talbott’s wife, Alison, took photos before they caped the buck and processed the meat. The buck has 16 points and is an estimated 5.5 years old.

Read Next: Counter Drone Technology Has Come to Deer Hunting and Landowners Are Starting to Fight Back.

“My taxidermist says it should score about 190 inches,” says Talbott. “The whole thing is so unreal I can’t explain how I feel. I spent a lot of time there hunting and learning the farm, how to use the wind and where the deer were bedding and scraping … It’s just an incredible experience.”.

#9081. The 11 Best Mid-Priced Hunting Rifles of 2026
